As a web developer, mainly three environments to consider practically: Production: environment configured to host final release version of a product targeting end users. optimized for security and performance. hosted on a live server. requires alerted and urgent support. is data-critical., its data is backed up regularly. involves risk management and disaster recovery. production environment configured to show friendly errors to end users. Staging: environment configured to host release candidate of application after declaring a code freeze. targets project manager/owner alongside development team to agree upon scope of release candidate. involves quality assurance and development team to do final fixes and final furnishing before releasing to production. best practice is to mimic production environment by using latest data available from a live DB copied from production environment. Normally, staging environment only accessible by internal team and stakeholders, either secured on a public server or published on an intranet environment if all stakeholders can access local network. staging environment configured to show medium or full technical errors. Development: private environment configured by a single developer on his machine to check his/her own work during development cycle, normally, called a sprint in a scrum environment. development environment is configured to show full technical errors.

Staging is a step before commit process in git., commit in git is performed in two steps: staging and actual commit. long as a changeset is in staging area, git allows you to edit it as like (replace staged files with other versions staged files, remove changes from staging, etc. ). Broken metaphor time: Consider a scenario where you call movers to get your stuff from old appartment to new appartment. Before, you go through your stuff, decide what you take with and what you throw away, pack it in bags leave it in main hallway. movers come, get packed) bags from hallway and transport them. In this example, everything until movers get your stuff, is staging: you decide what goes where, how to pack it (e. may decide half your stuff will be thrown away before movers get there - part of staging). From technical point of view, staging supports transactional commits, by splitting all operations into what can fail (staging) and what cannot fail (commit): commit in git is implemented transactionally, after staging is sucessfull. Several steps in staging can fail (for example, need to commit, but HDD is 99. 9999% full, git has no space to perform commit). This will fail in staging (your repository not be corrupted by partial commit) staging process doesn't affect commit history (it doesn't corrupt repository in case of error).

UNIX has separate concepts "process", "process group", "session". Each shell at login becomes leader of own new session and process group, sets controlling process group of terminal to itself. shell creates process group within current session for each "job" it launches, places each process starts into appropriate process group. For example, ls | head is a pipeline of two processes, shell considers a single job, belong to single, new process group. A process is a (collection of thread of execution and other context, address space file descriptor table. A process may start other processes; these new processes belong to same process group as parent unless other action is taken. Each process may also have a "controlling terminal", starts off same as parent. shell has concept of "foreground" jobs and "background" jobs. Foreground jobs are process groups with control of terminal, background jobs are process groups without control of terminal. Each terminal has a foreground process group. When bringing a job to foreground, shell sets it as terminal's foreground process group; when putting job to background, shell sets terminal's foreground process group to another process group or itself. Processes may read from and write to their controlling terminal if in foreground process group. Otherwise they receive SIGTTIN and SIGTTOU signals on attempts to read from and write to terminal. By default these signals suspend process, most shells mask SIGTTOU so background job can write to terminal uninterrupted.

In computing, a Job is a unit of work or unit of execution (that performs said work). A component of job unit of work) is called a task or a step (if sequential, as in a job stream). As unit of execution, a job may be identified with a single process, may have subprocesses (child processes; process corresponding to job parent process) perform tasks or steps comprise work of job; or with a process group; or with abstract reference to process or process group, as in Unix job control. easiest way is to convert date to unix time_t value (i. e. seconds since beginning of epoch, or '1-1-1970 00:00:00'), substract 30 days * 86400 seconds per day from number. e. g. following example uses set -x see value of D variable as it changes. #! /bin/ksh set -x D=$(date -d '2013-10-13' '+%s') D=$((D - 30 * 86400)) date -d "@$D" Note depends on GNU version of date, from GNU Coreutils. Other versions of date may not support converting time_t value back to formatted date with @. Unless installed GNU coreutils, probably isn't available on AIX system gawk is probably best option to convert back to formatted date: echo "$D"| gawk '{print strftime("%c", $0)}' original answer suggested plain awk, but further testing on debian system revealed neither mawk nor original-awk have strftime function built-in, to install either GNU Coreutils or GNU Awk. binary file is everything not plain text, contains data encoded in different way than text encoding (ASCII, UTF-8, or other text encodings, e. g. ISO-8859-2). A text file may be a plaintext document, like a story or letter, can be a config file, or a data file -, if use a plain text editor to open it, contents are readable. A binary is any file not a text file (nor "special" like fifo, directory, device etc. ) That may be a mp3 music. a jpg image. a compressed archive, or even a word processor document - while for practical purposes it's text, it is encoded (written on disk) as binary. need a specific program to open it, sense - for a text editor contents are a jumbled mess., in Linux often hear "binaries" when referring to "binary executable files" - programs. because while sources of most programs (written in high-level languages) are plain text, compiled executables are binary. a few compiled formats (a. out, ELF, bytecode. ) they are commonly called binaries instead of dwelling on internal structure - from user's point of view they are the same.,. exe is another of these compiled formats - one common to MS Windows. It's a kind of binaries, compiled and linked against Windows API.

If iMovie project appears to missing audio tracks when you play, import, or export project, try these steps first: Make sure audio track not muted in timeline. See if volume in iMovie set to lowest, if this is the case, set volume slider to maximum. Make sure computer's audio not muted. Quit reopen iMovie, then check clip to see if it now plays with audio. Quit reopen iMovie, then reimport footage. Play newly imported footage see if you now have audio. Check /Library/QuickTime/ and ~/Library/QuickTime/ for third-party plugins. Remove them if present, log out, and log back in. Check to see if issue persists. If not, check with manufacturer of disabled plugin to see if update available. Note: tilde (~) represents Home directory. Check to see if any video clips imported are in MPEG-1 format. MPEG-1 clips will lose audio when you export them as part of iMovie project. SOURCE:

noted in question, sudo wfsctl stop not stop unregister httpd process., httpd daemons stopped and restarted., httpd remains registered to start on next (re)boot. sudo wfsctl diagnose # All httpd processes: # COMM RUSER PPID PID STARTED # httpd root 1 325 8:46PM # httpd _www 325 331 8:46PM sudo wfsctl stop sudo wfsctl diagnose # All httpd processes: # COMM RUSER PPID PID STARTED # httpd root 1 399 10:19PM # httpd _www 399 403 10:19PM man wfsctl mentions use of httpd-wrapper preferred to apachectl and httpd (at least for -t test flag. ) Apache config file for WebDAV File Sharing parameterized, httpd server managed by httpd-wrapper utility, passes parameters to httpd. normally transparent, but note to check Apache config file syntax, do not use apachectl configtest or httpd -t. In nutshell, grep does one thing only as many other UNIX tools that's matching a line to given pattern it does it well. other, awk is more sophisticated tool it is a complete programming language defined by POSIX standard with typical features like variables, arrays, expressions, functions control statements for pattern scanning and processing. In, it depends on implementation how both tools perform in case of pattern matching on size of input to process. expect grep is usually more efficient than awk it does matching only. , part of learning to use Unix is to figure out existing scripts doing. In case you need to know about how awk works to understand code. I will focus on describing awk part, this should get you started in figuring out rest. awk is a pattern-driven scripting language, commands consist of (search) pattern/condition and corresponding code block. During execution, input files are read line by line and if pattern/condition is true for line, code block is executed. special patterns BEGIN and END used to trigger code to get executed before first line or after last line is read. In example three pattern/code lines: NR==FNR {a[i++]=$0}; NR and FNR are two special variables set by awk. look up their meaning with man awk NR ordinal number of current record FNR ordinal number of current record in current file so this condition is true while lines from first line are read (which a[i++]=$0 is executed once for each line from first file) and false for all additional files. $0 is current line of input. {b[x++]=$0;};{k=x-i}; This code block has no condition/pattern gets executed for every line read (from all files including first one). END {for(j=0;j<i;) print a[j++], b[k++]}' This part runs after last line of last file has read and processed. With these basics you should be to figure out meaning of different code blocks and variables yourself.

egrep is 100% equivalent to grep -E fgrep is 100% equivalent to grep -F Historically these switches provided in separate binaries. On some old Unix systems need to call separate binaries, but on all modern systems switches preferred. man page for grep has details about this. for, -E switches grep into a special mode so expression evaluated as an ERE (Extended Regular Expression) as opposed to normal pattern matching. Details of syntax on man page. -E, --extended-regexp Interpret PATTERN as an extended regular expression -F switch switches grep into a different mode it accepts a pattern to match, but splits pattern up into one search string per line and does OR search on any strings without special pattern matching. -F, --fixed-strings Interpret PATTERN as a list of fixed strings, separated by newlines, any of which is to be matched. example scenarios: You have a file with list of say ten Unix usernames in plain text. want to search group file on machine to see if any of ten users listed are in any special groups: grep -F -f user_list. txt /etc/group -F switch helps is usernames in pattern file interpreted as plain text strings. Dots for example interpreted as dots rather than wild-cards. want to search using fancy expression. For example parenthesis () can be used to indicate groups with | used as an OR operator. could run this search using -E: grep -E '^no(fork|group)' /etc/group. to return lines that start with either "nofork" or "nogroup". Without -E switch to escape special characters involved because with normal pattern matching they would just search for exact pattern; grep '^no\(fork\|group\)' /etc/group

If you search for verbatim string, want to be sure string you passed is interpreted verbatim (i. e. without risking say dot or question mark be interpreted as something else) use fgrep or egrep -F. for difference between egrep and grep, I think egrep is most of the time the thing you want. GNU manual site lists differences between grep and egrep seems to lay in syntax: some things require slashes other do not. egrep is more "compatible" with perl regexps and javascript regexps easier to me to use egrep. Btw. encourage you to give ack a try - it supports PREGs, has more useful defaults (i. e. coloring, skipping probably-not-what-you-want directories like. svn, ability to follow symlinks, easier to type ack than grep -E).

Alexander O'Mara provided correct answer, but having worked in a hotel using booking. com I believe I can provide additional information about reason CVV denied. Every day hotel I worked in receive around 50 bookings, a quarter of these bookings using fake credit card details, about 90% of people using fake credit card details not show up. This resulted in guesswork when assigning rooms, we often try to guess if person will show up based on credit card details, also sometimes take into consideration name, location, how many days they staying, etc. We also try to call the day before to confirm bookings, so fake bookings result in minimal interruption to business. Blocking CVV 000 is just booking. com's lazy attempt to reduce amount fake bookings. Some other CVVs are blocked as well. reason why booking. com blocks CVV and other websites do not is because other websites generally attempt to charge credit card immediately, while booking. com only forwards information to hotels which charge credit card on day of arrival.

IGMP Snooping is feature for switches to learn multicast groups needed on which ports. Routers not handling multicast routing don't care., without mrouter in network, you need to configure one (or more) igmp queriers. This ensures group membership reports flood through network periodically to keep forwarding information up-to-date; otherwise it expires traffic either dropped, or floods everywhere. benefit is multicast traffic goes only where it belongs. If nothing on port joined group, switch will prune it. In cascaded environment, can reduce inter-switch traffic. keep access links clear of traffic hosts don't want. If don't know it's enabled, situations may arise traffic may appear to be "missing" on wire, because it's being pruned. (fast-leave, no querier, no joins, etc. ), it rarely enabled by default.

First of, it possible (especially for owner of hotel) to edit CCTV footage. However, I don't think this was the case. In, you haven't yet seen CCTV footage and you just relied on what security personnel told you.,'s more likely owner disabled CCTV cameras, than he edited footage during or after theft. Note he can technically disable them, since internal cameras not usually connected to police control room, nor to security company's one., my answer to 1) would be: he asked someone to turn off cameras, then entered your room (or sent someone else to do it). This option not easier to technically implement, but's also easier to get away with. In, should police step in and ask owner to show them footage, he could say cameras were down for error or for maintenance. If he was "smart" enough to keep cameras down for extended period of time before and after theft, he could get away with it. On other, police could spot something suspicious in tampered footage and continue investigation. In case, bottom line to 1) is: anyone having complete physical access to security system is able to do anything to it. This is variation of one of Ten Immutable Laws of Security (https://technet. microsoft. com/en-us/library/hh278941. aspx), usually applies to computers and computer networks, but holds for any kind of security system. By, you said "There was only one way of entry through door". This most likely not true, unless your room has no windows. However, if you didn't let windows open before leaving room or if windows weren't broken or tampered with, this option can be ruled out. You also asked: 2) How can I check if CCTV or recording's were tampered with? This is very difficult., if owner disabled CCTV cameras, there nothing you can do, as will be nothing to check.If he didn't, you could theoretically check for video tampering, but you should have: a) permission from owner to have at least a copy of footage on a DVD; AND b) technical skills and tools to analyze footage. it's not easy to analyze a video and check if it been tampered with. As example, look at technologies used by the FBI in to do this analysis: https://archives. fbi. gov/archives/about-us/lab/forensic-science-communications/fsc/april2003/lacey. htm (Phase V, mostly). Their forensic scientists have had extensive training on subject. You, on, have most likely not the tools nor training to check a video for tampering., I'm not a CCTV expert, but, if police suspected tampering in CCTV footage, they could try to find evidences on control room computers, which requires complete physical access to control room. This something you cannot do, in any case: keeping "skills and tools" issue aside, no way a hotel could give you complete access to their security control room. 3) Is there any history records in system through it can be checked? It depends on system used by hotel. I you could try to see CCTV footage, perhaps to get hold of a copy, but in end you should definitely report the theft to police. They have authority, and possibly skills, to do some of things I mentioned above.

First, important things: Bash isn't going away. If you already using bash, nothing change for. All changes is zsh will be default login shell for new accounts, you can select bash instead. Scripts not affected. What changes is shell for interactive use,. shell in terminals (and few other things use login shell, such as crontabs). If a script in file with execution permissions, starting with shebang line such as #!/bin/bash or #!/bin/sh or #!/usr/bin/env bash, it'll keep working as before. Zsh's syntax not completely compatible with bash, but it's close. lot of code will keep working, for example typical aliases and functions. main differences are in interactive configuration features., assuming considering switching to zsh, possibility for years, here main differences you'll encounter. not exhaustive list! Main differences for interactive use Configuration files: bash reads (mainly). bashrc in non-login interactive shells (but macOS starts login shell in terminals by default),. profile or. bash_profile in login shells, and. inputrc. Zsh reads (mainly). zshrc (in all interactive shells) and. zprofile (in login shells). This means none of bash customizations will apply: need to port them over. can't just copy files many things need tweaking. Key bindings use different syntax. Bash uses. inputrc and bind builtin to bind keys to readline commands. Zsh uses bindkey builtin to bind keys to zle widgets. Most readline commands have zsh equivalent, but isn't always a perfect equivalence.Speaking key bindings, if use Vi(m) as in-terminal editor not as command line mode in shell, notice zsh defaults to vi editing mode if EDITOR or VISUAL set to vi or vim. bindkey -e switches to emacs mode. Prompt: bash sets prompt (mainly) from PS1 contains backslash escapes. Zsh sets prompt mainly from PS1 contains percent escapes. functionality of bash's PROMPT_COMMAND available in zsh via precmd and preexec hook functions. Zsh has more convenience mechanisms to build fancy prompts including prompt theme mechanism. basic command line history mechanisms (navigation with Up/Down, search with Ctrl+R, history expansion with !! and friends, last argument recall with Alt+. or $_) work in same way, but lot of differences in details, too many to list here. can copy your. bash_history to. zsh_history if haven't changed shell option changes file format. Completion: both shells default to basic completion mode mostly completes command and file names, switch to fancy mode by including bash_completion on bash or by running compinit in zsh. some commands bash handles better and some zsh handles better. Zsh is usually more precise, but sometimes gives up where bash does isn't correct but sensible. To specify possible completions for command, zsh has three mechanisms: “old” completion mechanism with compctl forget about. “new” completion mechanism with compadd and lots functions begin with underscore and powerful complex user configuration mechanism. emulation to support bash completion functions enable by running bashcompinit. emulation isn't 100% perfect but usually works. Many bash's shopt settings have corresponding setopt in zsh.Zsh doesn't treat # as comment start on command line by default, only in scripts (including. zshrc. To enable interactive comments, run setopt interactive_comments. differences for scripting (and power users on command line) In bash, $foo takes value of foo, splits it at whitespace characters, for each whitespace-separated part, if contains wildcard characters and matches existing file, replaces pattern by list of matches. To get value of foo, need "$foo". same applies to command substitution $(foo). In zsh, $foo is value of foo and $(foo) is output of foo minus final newlines, with two exceptions. If word becomes empty due to expanding empty unquoted variables, it's removed. a=; b=; printf "%s\n" one "$a$b" three $a$b five prints one, empty line, three, five). result of unquoted command substitution is split at whitespace pieces don't undergo wildcard matching. Bash arrays are indexed from 0 to (length-1). Zsh arrays indexed from 1 to length. With a=(one two three), in bash, ${a[1]} is two, in zsh, it's one. In bash, if reference array variable without braces, get first element,. $a is one and $a[1] is one[1]. In zsh, $a expands to list of non-empty elements, $a[1] expands to first element., in bash, length of array is ${#a}; also works in zsh but can write it more simply as $#a. can make 0-indexing default with setopt ksh_arrays turns on requirement to use braces to refer to array element.Bash has extra wildcard patterns as @(foo|bar) to match foo or bar, only enabled with shopt -s extglob. In zsh, can enable these patterns with setopt ksh_glob, but also simpler-to-type native syntax such as (foo|bar), requires setopt extended_glob (do put that in your. zshrc, it's on by default in completion functions). **/ for recursive directory traversal is always enabled in zsh. In bash, by default, if wildcard pattern doesn't match file, it's left unchanged. In zsh, by default, you'll get an error, usually safest setting. If want to pass wildcard parameter to command, use quotes. can switch to bash behavior with setopt no_nomatch. make non-matching wildcard patterns expand to empty list instead with setopt null_glob. In bash, right-hand side of pipeline runs in a subshell. In zsh, it runs in parent shell, can write things like somecommand | read output. Some nice zsh features a few nice zsh features bash doesn't have (at not without serious elbow grease)., selection of ones most useful. Glob qualifiers allow matching files based on metadata time stamp, size, etc. allow tweaking output. syntax is rather cryptic, but extremely convenient. few examples: foo*(. ): only regular files matching foo* and symbolic links to regular files, not directories and other special files. foo*(*. ): only executable regular files matching foo*. foo*(-. ): only regular files matching foo*, not symbolic links and other special files. foo*(-@): only dangling symbolic links matching foo*. foo*(om): files matching foo*, sorted by last modification date, most recent first.pass this to ls, it'll do its own sorting. useful in... foo*(om[1, 10]): 10 most recent files matching foo*, recent first. foo*(Lm+1): files matching foo* size at least 1MB. foo*(N): same as foo*, but if doesn't match file, produce empty list regardless of setting null_glob option (see above). *(D): match all files including dot files (except. and. ). foo/bar/*(:t) (using history modifier): files in foo/bar, with only base name of file. E. g. if foo/bar/qux. txt, expanded as qux. txt. foo/bar/*(. :r): take regular files under foo/bar remove extension. E. g. foo/bar/qux. txt expanded as foo/bar/qux. foo*. odt(e\''REPLY=$REPLY:r. pdf'\'): take list of files matching foo*. odt, replace. odt by. pdf (regardless of PDF file exists). few useful zsh-specific wildcard patterns. foo*. txt~foobar*: all. txt files whose name starts with foo but not foobar. image<->. jpg(n): all. jpg files whose base name is image followed by number, e. g. image3. jpg and image22. jpg but not image-backup. jpg. glob qualifier (n) causes files to be listed in numerical order,. image9. jpg comes before image10. jpg (you make this default even without -n with setopt numeric_glob_sort). To mass-rename files, zsh provides convenient tool: zmv function. Suggested for.zshrc: autoload zmv alias zcp='zmv -C' zln='zmv -L' Example: zmv '(*). jpeg' '$1. jpg' zmv '(*)-backup. (*)' 'backups/$1. $2' Bash has few ways to apply transformations when taking value of a variable. Zsh has some of same and many more. Zsh has little convenient features to change directories. Turn on setopt auto_cd to change to a directory when type its name without having to type cd (bash also has this nowadays). use two-argument form to cd to change to directory name close to current directory. For example, if in /some/where/foo-old/deeply/nested/inside want to go to /some/where/foo-new/deeply/nested/inside, just type cd old new. To assign value to variable, write VARIABLE=VALUE. Disclosing MAC address shouldn't be a problem. MAC addresses are already predictable, easily sniffable, any authentication dependent on them is inherently weak shouldn't be relied upon. MAC addresses almost always only used "internally" (between you and your immediate gateway). don't make it to outside world cannot be used to connect back to you, locate you, or cause direct harm. disclosure can be linked to real identity might be possible to track you using data from WiFi networks, or can be used to falsify device's MAC address to gain access to some service (mostly some networks) on which your MAC address is white-listed. Personally, I wouldn't worry about it. However, when's not inconvenient, I usually try to redact irrelevant information when asking for help or sharing anything.

Prelude short version is other accepted answers here are more or less correct, you shouldn't assume your mac address is private, posting it doesn't pose direct risk to you person unless're trying to remain anonymous. long version: To understand risks leaking your MAC address poses requires two parts. Firstly to understand metadata can be derived from it. secondly ways in it can be used as a unique identifier for you. Metadata The MAC address is intended to assist your network in getting packets intended for you rather than co-worker next to you. For legitimate devices it directly tied to hardware often burned into "rom" on network card (but sometimes not read only). To prevent collisions each vendor has a set of prefixes they're allowed to use, it's up to them how they use them and how they uniquely generate rest of MAC you can reliably get hardware vendor from prefix Often approximate generation of device based on prefix used Sometimes exact model of network card used since most vendors use a predictable process to generate part of address rarely some other piece of information the vendor used to generate it when card was made usually isn't useful If your computer is from assembly line (like Dell) sometimes it can be used to identify possible model for your computer, and any other information could be inferred from that (like was model primarily marketed to corporate customers or grandmas? it expensive model or cheap one?) can get vendor from Wireshark using their tool But a hacker can, through variety of ways, falsify a mac address to pretend to be anything. Even mimicking another device on network (though if without knocking other device out end up with each device receiving only some of packets useless to hacker and alerts admins something's probably wrong) Tracking The MAC can reliably (though not uncontestably) tie traffic to a single "machine". This information is overwritten each time traffic passes through a "layer 3" device (like your router).Normally this means your router's mac address could be seen by another machine (and sometimes not, depending how ISPs route traffic). biggest things to keep in mind if someone hostile got your mac address are If it for your router and hostile party is a hacker it could leak the approximate model and generation of your router first step to deciding which vulnerabilities to attack If for your router hostile party is a website or service, it might be to log and track sessions over time across multiple IP addresses and multiple accounts If it's for your local computer or device only leaked rarely (say when post debugging information) it can be used to directly tie those leaks together to infer they posted by same person (or multiple people on same computer) If for local computer or device consistently leaked (say from a software or browser leak), It can be used to uniquely track your computer across multiple sessions regardless of other anonymizing techniques, but doesn't track YOU as a person. you can rotate your MAC using software if concerned about this, but only helps if you remember to do so if you you might be interested in this stuff here's links to check out A demonstration that shows other information you leak Browser Fingerprinting Network Forensics Defcon
I'd recommend free tool discover MAC address http://www. istumbler. net/

A MAC address is number to uniquely identify your device on local network segment. address is (and needs to be) visible to everyone on network segment, but because of network routing works, not normally visible to anyone else. Unless you steps to change it regularly, your MAC address uniquely identifies your device. Someone could use address you posted to associate device tracking with actual person, but if someone to effort to track movements of wireless device, they probably already know who owns it. Certain wireless routers set default password based on MAC address. This isn't as useful as sounds,: to use password, they need to be within radio range of your AP, they can simply sniff MAC address off the air. first digits of MAC address identify manufacturer of your device. In theory, someone could use this information to make targeted attack against a security hole in your card's network driver, but I've never heard of it happening in practice. In, there are some theoretical hazards, but in practice, anyone in to exploit them has other ways to get your MAC address.

caveat: 'Computer Science' has become a muddied field in modern times because (at least in United States) universities do not have degrees in "programming". This means people interested in programming must sign up for Computer Science degrees, reaction to Computer Science programs emphasize programming more., Computer Science is a strongly mathematical science -- Computational Mathematics might a better term. It involves study of graph theory, algorithmic complexity, formal logic, automata, in any logical structure can describe a transformation or response to input -- algorithms. How can change colors of glyphs in Finder sidebar, while leaving them as default icon? You can't (unless third party tool about I unfamiliar). However, you can change default icons to your heart's content. Here's how: As a test, I created a Smart Folder finds all PDFs in my home directory. default glyph for Smart Folder is a gear, as noted in OP. steps to change glyph: Locate directory /System/Library/CoreServices/CoreTypes. bundle/Contents/Resources Locate file called SidebarSmartFolder. icns Rename it to SidebarSmartFolder_old. icns Paste into Resources folder glyph you want to use in its place. Rename it to SidebarSmartFolder. icns Reboot your Mac.'ll see now my Smart Folder glyph in sidebar has changed to new one.

If you mean to change actual icon represents folders (i. e. double-click on it to open folder),'s a good, short article at http://www. visualpharm. com/articles/change_mac_icons. html explains how to do this if you have icons you already like to use. In nutshell, right-click (control-click) on Documents folder choose "Get Info" from menu pops up. Then, choose icon you'd like to replace it with. * Double-click it to open it in Preview, select all by pressing command-a, then copy it by pressing command-c. Click on icon of Documents folder at top of Info window paste copied icon into its place using command-v. To remove custom icon, select icon you pasted in Info window press delete key to restore it to its original icon. for colorizing icons, numerous applications allow you to edit images. Pixelmator is a good one, relatively inexpensive image editors go, has colorize option, as well as Adobe's Photoshop. also free alternatives can be found with bit of web searching. *You can create icon from one already there by selecting it in Info window, pressing command-c to copy it, opening up blank document in favorite image editor pasting it into it. From there, can edit it any way you like, save it as a. png to use it as an icon. If mean color-coded bars that would highlight text, called labels, those have unfortunately been retired in Mavericks in replace of tags. Hope this helps solve your problem.

change colour of Yosemite system icons: Go to /System/Library/CoreServices/CoreTypes. bundle/Contents/Resources folder where system icons located. $ cd /System/Library/CoreServices/CoreTypes. bundle/Contents/Resources/ Backup icns file for generic folder icon. $ sudo cp GenericFolderIcon. icns GenericFolderIcon. org. icns Move icns file to home folder. $ sudo mv GenericFolderIcon. icns ~/ $ cd ~/ Change file owner (from root to user). $ sudo chown [user name] GenericFolderIcon. icns Open GenericFolderIcon. icns in Finder, Preview launched. Choose "Tools" => "Adjust Colors. " (shift+⌘+C), adjust image's color want. following image, Saturation is decreased. GenericFolderIcon. icns contains 10 images, edit all. Save file (⌘+S). Locate icns file to /System/Library/CoreServices/CoreTypes. bundle/Contents/Resources folder. $ cd /System/Library/CoreServices/CoreTypes. bundle/Contents/Resources/ $ sudo mv ~/GenericFolderIcon. icns. / Change file owner and group, remove Extended Attributes. $ sudo chown root GenericFolderIcon. icns $ sudo chgrp wheel GenericFolderIcon. icns $ sudo xattr -d com. apple. quarantine GenericFolderIcon. icns Clear icon cache. sudo find /private/var/folders/ -name com. apple. dock. iconcache -exec rm {}\; sudo find /private/var/folders/ -name com. apple.iconservices -exec rm -rf {} \ Restart Mac. nice free app for changing icons, LiteIcon.

iCloud account, iTunes account and Apple ID are same thing. Apple refers to them inconsistently. Account "Types" iCloud Account Typically refers to Apple ID used for iCloud services, as backup syncing documents settings between apps. set in Settings → iCloud → Account. iTunes Account Apple ID you use to purchase downloads from iTunes, iBooks and App Stores syncs iTunes Match songs, if use service.'s set in Settings → iTunes & App Stores → Apple ID. important to note purchases are linked to your Apple ID (although music is now DRM-free), not transferrable to other Apple IDs. should be to make all your app, video and music purchases on a single Apple ID to save future headaches. iMessage Your Apple ID also used for iMessage. Using your Apple ID for Apple services

Apple has informative support-article addresses differences between Apple Music and iTunes Match. Both include iCloud Music Library store your songs, main difference between both services is what stored within this library: iTunes Match When joining iTunes Match, it matches all your local music using sound profile of each song. If song available within catalogue iTunes, it added to iCloud Music Library and made available to download or stream on all devices as 256 Kbps DRM-free AAC. Songs not available in catalogue are uploaded to iCloud Music Library without changes. available on all your devises. If cancel iTunes Match subscription, all songs already matched can be played or downloaded open end no DRM in place. Only new songs not added. Apple Music: When joining Apple Music, you local music is matched against Apple Music's catalogue using meta-data of each song. If song available within catalogue, it made available on all devices via Apple Music (similar to click on "Add to library" upon every song in Apple Music). Songs can be streamed or downloaded on all devices, but always be DRM protected 256 Kbps AAC. Launchers not much different from any other app in this concern – deal with them like with other apps. one argument mentioned multiple times here, sum up basics in: check permissions as recommended. check votes (how many people rated app), downloads (how many installed it), and ratings (how well app received). If inexperienced, try avoiding apps with no or only few downloads/votes until get feeling for it. check reasonable comments (i. skip one-worders like "good", "bad", "like" etc, concentrate on those with real details) try searching for reviews when looking for app, app listings on "trusted sites" can be helpful. I run such a site myself, where find ratings, votes, permissions incl. explanations, links to reviews etc. listed along each app, to check there. Avoid "downloading" apps from sites you don't know, better stick to safe markets. Helpful links: security tag and its tag-wiki Are apps safe? How can I make Android more secure? What do permissions applications require mean? (more detailed list here) Android Markets: How safe are alternative sources? How safe to use Aptoide?

As with any app: look at permissions it requests think about whether app legitimately needs those permissions. nothing inherently unsafe about using a custom launcher, but if it requests permissions shouldn't be needed just to display home screen, it may have hidden malicious functionality. (Or it may use them for legitimate purposes: for example, some popular launchers request permission to "directly call phone numbers" provide ability to put direct-dial icons on home screen. ) To see permissions of app already installed, go to Settings -> Apps, find app, scroll down to bottom of its info page. can also see app's permissions in Play store before you install it: scroll down to bottom of app's page in Play store tap on "Permission details". Note a launcher app will (naturally) know which other apps you launch with it. generally not a problem, but if launcher app has Internet permission, it could potentially send information about apps you use to third party, be a privacy violation. When uninstall app, any data stored with app itself is removed; generally includes like customization settings. But if app has "modify USB storage" permission, it may have also created files in phone's shared storage area — files you see when plug phone into computer with USB cable. Those aren't deleted when you uninstall app, but you can delete them yourself, either with USB connection or file-manager app on phone. custom launcher doesn't "override native OS" in any unsafe way. It's just a normal app that happens to respond to phone's Home button.

In iOS, Location Services sits between location radios (cellular tower info, nearest wifi, GPS) and apps, caches fused results between getting new information from radios at rate determined by OS for decent battery life versus requested accuracy. Time Machine drive should be equal to or larger than drive it backs up. TM images drive completely, then saves incremental changes. Time Machine saves hourly backups for past 24 hours, daily backups for past month, and weekly backups for everything older than a month. If your internal is 500GB with 100GB free (using 400GB), and TM is 500GB, then you will get full image, and then some amount of history (filling up remaining 100GB of TM disk). history length depends on use habits. Change few small files occasionally? Lots of history. Change lots of big files a lot? Then 100GB free will save few hours or days. If bigger TM, have longer history to browse. I personally have mostly full internal, equal sized TM, change files often, find usually have few months of history. Plenty of time to restore file I accidentally delete.

size of your drive doesn't matter, it's size of your data. If you only using 120Gb, potentially external drive of 240-360Gb could be enough (until you start to use more,. ) for how TM works, it doesn't just snapshot current state of data, but it's historical changes. This why it can use more total space than actual used space on your drive. Let's say you have your 120Gb current system, some months down you install OS X Mavericks when's released - this may up your used space to (all figures are estimates!) 130Gb, but it's not just 10Gb worth of extra files, it might be 35Gb of changed files, and 5Gb of new files, resulting in a 40Gb change for Time Machine., when restore, it's not just case of able to restore to current most recent backup on TM, but being able to go back in time to any point that it still covers and restore to that point, may be as far back as prior to OS upgrades etc., for more everyday changes, good example of how you can consume good amount of space in backup drive without changing anything. TM backs up at file level. If file changes, new version is backed up in full. Let's say have couple of films of a Gb each, but named incorrectly (either at filename or META data level) - changing title of films doesn't affect space used on machine, but will result in both files being backed up again because they have changed.

Unix usernames are definitely case-sensitive, more, using usernames with uppercase characters on Unix systems can produce unwanted results, should generally be avoided. examples are: It can break email for user. standards for SMTP allow email addresses to be case-insensitive, by default MTA receiving message will fold email address to lowercase to find user to deliver to. If username has uppercase characters it not be resolved without special config overrides to cater for this. (this affects MTAs as sendmail, postfix etc and delivery processing agents like procmail) Many early hardware terminals were not case sensitive. common they only used uppercase. When logging in to some versions of Unix, starting a login name with an uppercase character will trigger system to assume you're using ancient uppercase only terminal will enable case folding - converts all of entered uppercase to lowercase (you to escape uppercase characters to say they're uppercase) to help you to enter username it expects be in lowercase. I don't believe this is a thing on Linux, but've seen it demonstrated on HP-UX. As long been convention to only use lowercase characters in usernames, reasonable to expect other tools (some may not thought of) on system may also assume username should be lowercase, and make checks, conversions etc accordingly, thus breaking things for user.

like hostnames and domain names, username not strictly a Unix thing but can often span wider range of OS types. they considered case sensitive depends on standard used to specify them. Hostnames and domain names are clearly case insensitive by DNS standard (see RFC4343). Usernames stored on local backend (/etc/passwd) or Unix style one (NIS) not case insensitive by POSIX standard. Usernames stored in LDAP or Active Directory backend will follow used attribute schema definition, uid and cn often storing user name have differing schema attributes, case insensitive for former but case sensitive for latter. means both Abc and abc might match or not abc's entry depending on ldap server configuration. Due to this inconsistency, recommend to only use lowercase for both usernames and host/domain name and avoid ssh ABC@SERVERNAME. DOMAIN. COM which is rude anyway.

user names are definitely case sensitive. test this by adding two users with similar names: ~ # useradd foobar ~ # useradd fooBar ~ # grep ^foo /etc/passwd foobar:x:1001:1001::/home/foobar:/bin/sh fooBar:x:1002:1002::/home/fooBar:/bin/sh This question/answer shows how to compensate for someone trying to log in with username "wrong" case according to LDAP servers. note this will only work if usernames all listed as lowercase (or can make all uppercase if want).

No, they not case sensitive. To quote RFC 5280 (emphasis mine): When subjectAltName extension contains domain name system label, domain name MUST be stored in dNSName (an IA5String). name MUST be in "preferred name syntax", as specified by Section 3. 5 of RFC1034 and modified by Section 2. 1 of RFC1123. Note uppercase and lowercase letters allowed in domain names, no significance attached to case. referenced RFC 1034 echos this: Note while upper and lower case letters allowed in domain names, no significance attached to case., two names with same spelling but different case to be treated as if identical. (The modification referenced as part of RFC 1123 to allow first character of legal host name to be a digit, unrelated to case. )

One or other can break applications, case-insensitive is default however. If you've been using case-insensitive without issues no guarantees transition to case-sensitive will go well. one example from apple support pages:. don’t assume third-party software solutions work correctly with case sensitivity. Important: Case-sensitive names do not ignore Unicode ignorable characters. This means a single directory can have several names considered equivalent using Unicode comparison rules, but considered distinct on case-sensitive HFSX volume.

minor differences I encountered using both Mac and Linux systems: most common Mac OS X file system is case insensitive, whereas Linux filenames are case sensitive. no default and enabled account named "root" on Mac.

APFS has case-sensitive and case-insensitive variants. case-insensitive variant APFS is normalization-preserving, not normalization-sensitive. case-sensitive variant APFS is both normalization-preserving and normalization-sensitive. Filenames in APFS encoded in UTF-8 aren’t normalized. first developer preview of APFS, available in macOS Sierra June 2016, offered only case-sensitive variant. In macOS 10. 12. 4, APFS developer preview updated to include case-insensitive variant. In iOS 10. 3, case-sensitive variant of APFS used. Apple’s Developer FAQs

This actually a feature of filesystem of your disk, not bash or Terminal. app. HFS+ (the Mac filesystem) usually configured to be case insensitive but case preserving. means file system consider foo and FoO to same, but when create new file it remember which letters capitalized and which not. When format a disk with HFS+ you can chose file system should case sensitive or not. If chose to format with UFS (Unix FileSystem) it is always case sensitive,. To check disk case sensitive, run: diskutil info <device> For example: diskutil info disk0s2 Look for Name: line. If it reads like Mac OS Extended (Case-sensitive, Journaled) it means it is case-sensitive. If it just reads Mac OS Extended (without Case-sensitive) it only case preserving but not case sensitive.

Emulated filesystem is abstraction layer on actual filesystem (ext4 or f2fs) serves two purposes: Retain USB connectivity of Android devices to PCs (implemented through MTP now) Restrict unauthorized access of apps/processes to user's private media and other apps' data on SD card. Read Android's Storage Journey for details, summary: Early Android devices short on internal storage relied on external SD cards traditionally use FAT family of filesystem to ensure compatibility with most PCs (refer to Microsoft's dominance on PC world). When internal storage grew in size, same filesystem shifted to internal (still called "external") SD card. FAT/vFAT implementation had two major issues addressed by Google gradually: Android devices connected to PCs directly (USB Mass Storage) as connect USB drive. UMS exposes device at block level and disconnects SD card from Android framework (un-mounts), making data unavailable to apps possibly breaking many functionalities.FAT Windows' favorite in development days) never designed to enforce UNIX permissions (mode, uid, gid symlinks, ioctls like FS_IOC_FIEMAP)., all data on SD card available to all apps (since every Android app is a UNIX/Linux user has a uid) with no restrictions, raising serious privacy and security concerns. issues addressed through emulation: SD card storage moved to /data partition (or independent /sdcard partition on some devices previously) holds ext4 filesystem (gradually replaced by f2fs), fully implementing UNIX permissions. design made using UMS impossible because whole /data partition not be exposed to PC for 2 reasons: (1) it contains settings and apps' data to be protected from other apps human users. (2) Linux filesystems not supported by Windows. UMS replaced with Media Transfer Protocol client-server type extension to PTP - established protocol. MTP doesn't expose block device but works through software stack. MTP host runs on Android as an app (android. process. media) sandboxed in Android framework, not capable of doing escalated tasks. transfer data from desktop to emulator's SdCard on Linux do this: Create SD Card: Let's create 64MB sd card for our Android emulator. From terminal do this: # cd ~/android-sdk-linux/tools #. /mksdcard 64M ~/Desktop/sdcard. iso Now use 'Eclipse Android SDK and AVD Manager' to create new Android virtual device use path to sd card created. Write Data to SD Card: From terminal: # cd ~/android-sdk-linux/tools #. /ddms This start Dalvik Debug Monitor Server. Then Launch your AVD with SD card from Eclipse created earlier From DDMS, go to 'Device -> File Explorer' Select 'sdcard' folder Click 'push file onto device' button Find your file and click open That's it! Now from inside code get to sd card's path with: Environment. getExternalStorageDirectory() More read here.

Using command line: copy files to SD card image. use adb push to copy files from Desktop to Emulator and adb pull for reverse. syntax to copy files to or from Emulator/Device Instance: Copy from desktop to emulator: adb push <local> <remote> Copy from emulator to desktop: adb pull <remote> <local> Here <local> is path of file / folder on your desktop and <remote> is path of file / folder on emulator. example: adb push foo. txt /sdcard/foo. txt foo. txt will be pushed (copied) to emulator. 2. Using DDMS UI: how to work with emulator's file system using DDMS. In Devices tab, select emulator to view file system for. To copy a file from device, locate file in File Explorer and click Pull file button. To copy a file to device, click Push file button on File Explorer tab. I prefer adb pull and adb push commands as can copy multiple files (in single directory) with just one line command, using DDMS can copy only one file at a time (no directory).

A VLAN is Ethernet level concept, a subnet is IP level concept. VLAN splits Ethernet network into multiple logically seperate Ethernet networks. subnet defines which hosts host will try to communicate with directly verses which hosts need to go via a router. It also defines "network" and "broadcast" addresses. common practice to have 1:1 mapping between subnets and VLANs but possible to have multiple subnets on same VLAN. possible to use proxy arp to split a subnet between multiple VLANs or have two VLANs using same IP subnet for different purposes.

no reason not to put multiple subnets on same VLAN, but also probably no reason to do it. Pro: Allows subnets to talk directly without router or firewall Save's VLANs Con: Allows subnets to talk directly without router or firewall It's messy from documentation and troubleshooting perspective More broadcast traffic We generally don't do it because of messiness and lack of security. One VLAN = one subnet is easier to document and easier to troubleshoot usually not good reason to complicate things. only reason of to do it is company mergers or network upgrades for both prefer it to be temporary. Edit to clarify, for hosts on different subnets same VLAN to talk directly need to either make them their own default gateway or add route to "other" subnet that connects it to interface. In gateway case if host IP was 10. 1. 1. 2 then gateway would also be 10. 1. 1. 2. This cause host to ARP for everything on or off it's subnet. allow it to talk to second subnet on VLAN but only way able to talk to anything else is if router/firewall running proxy arp can help it out. In route out interface case add something like "route add -net 192. 56. 76. 0 netmask 255. 255. 255. 0 eth0" to device then 10. 1. 1. 2 will ARP directly on eth0 when it wants to reach 192. 56. 76. *.

only used interchangeably from perspective of each unique vlan at layer 2 should have its own subnet for addressing at layer 3 giving separation and ability to manage broadcast traffic etc. In of scenarios where have a vlan without a subnet only perhaps if using an 'ip unumbered' setup but not too many reasons to want to have to do this. If review best practice models like Cisco's composite network model in of keeping individual subnets and vlans 'local' to switch blocks generally have separate subnet assigned per vlan.

In many implementations IPv4 subnet and a VLAN closely correlated on 1:1 basis. A subnet, is a portion of IPv4 address space from may assign addresses to hosts. differentiated from a "prefix" a term in common parlance or a supernet, may be a larger portion of IP address space comprised of many subnets. reason for correlation is a single VLAN and single subnet both represent a single broadcast domain., these two tend to be overlaid in most implementations. described in earlier answers, a VLAN is a layer 2 entity. All hosts on given VLAN can communicate with each other, but no hosts on one VLAN can communicate to hosts on another without form routing or in rare cases, bridging.

used interchangeably then used incorrectly. Subnet refers to particular IP network, such as 192. 0. 2. 0/28. VLAN refers to 802. 1Q standard, give each port unique MAC address table, separating them from each other. VLAN may transport one or more subnet (but not have to, may be transporting something else than IP entirely). Subnet may be configured for VLAN, but not have to be, could be without 802. 1Q or over different L2 technology than ethernet.

informal way of looking at difference between VLANs and subnets, but not inaccurate (just incomplete). may help networking newcomers get closer to right mental picture. Two different VLANs on a single switch or host are like two physically separate switches. They partition MAC address space, in communications between two parties on single VLAN or on single physical switch don't involve other parties on MAC-level (layer 2) network. VLAN or physical switch limits extent MAC-level message propagation, keeping it as local as possible. In contrast, IP subnets exist at layer 3 and partition IP address space, not MAC address space, but with similar purpose: to limit extent of message propagation. Any partitioning at MAC-level layer 2 network below is transparent to layer 3, VLANs and/or separate physical switches can be treated as one single continuous layer 2 medium from point of IP-level networking. Conversely, switches and VLANs don't see IP addresses nor IP subnetting (with some minor provisos can complicate picture). Everything at layer 3 and higher is just payload to them at layer 2 MAC level. In summary: VLANs and subnets partition different layers of network model. no circumstance in they interchangeable terms.

IPv4 and IPv6 are two separate protocols, with separate, incompatible packet headers and addressing, an IPv4-only host cannot directly communicate with an IPv6-only host. correct way to do this is to dual-stack one or both hosts so they run both IPv4 and IPv6 protocols. Otherwise, you must use kludge to translate between IPv4 and IPv6, but problems and limitations with any of those. For example, more IPv6 addresses than IPv4 addresses, easier to translate IPv4 address into something IPv6-only host understands, than to opposite. In 2017, time has passed there still IPv4-only hosts and networks. Most ISPs support IPv6, if your business has not yet begun to roll out IPv6, it may find itself scrambling to do that in the future.

Welcome to messy world of IPv6 transition. IPv4 and IPv6 are two seperate protocols do not directly interoperate. IPv6 proponents idea was we would move to dual stack, running IPv4 and IPv6 in parallel for a transition period. Then once IPv6 was ubiquitous IPv4 could be turned off. deploying dual stack meant extra cost immediately for benefits at unclear time in future. takeup was slow and IPv4 exhaustion hit without world being dual-stacked. Most IP transit providers provide dual-stack, but with mobile and broadband ISPs picture is often less rosy. anyway back to question of of interoperation. Since clear in real world IPv4 isn't going away soon variety of mechanisms devised to bridge the gap. first and simplest is a point to point tunnel, tunnels can be reliable and with right tunneling technologies can work behind NAT. problem is of tunnel has to terminate somewhere. There exist free tunneling providers but they not without issues in terms of performance and/or restrictions. The next is 6to4. A host or network with non-natted IPv4 only connectivity can generate an IPv6 /48 from public IPv4 IP. Packets from 6to4 clients are encapsulated in IPv4 and can be sent to other 6to4 clients or to a relay anycast address. it doesn't work behind NAT next to is teredo. Teredo tries to provide IPv6 addresses to clients behind NAT using NAT traversal techniques. Unfortunately it is fragile and often fails. due to teredo finds relays it will only work if IPv6 host responds to pings. ISPs mostly don't to have deployed 6to4 and teredo relays in their networks, so 6to4 and teredo traffic ends up via one of a handful of networks who provide relays for internet in.This often ends up limiting performance. Teredo and 6to4 failed to achive increases in ipv6-capable client base. clear while IPv6 deployment is growing, burden of interoperability will to be shouldered by those wanting to run IPv6 only networks. brings to how they can do that. most common approach for clients is NAT64/DNS64. network translates DNS A responses into AAAA responses pointing at range of IPv6 addresses routed to stateful NAT64 boxes. NAT64 boxes translate traffic from IPv6 to IPv4 allowing clients to reach servers on IPv4 internet. extension of this is 464XLAT where client has a stateless NAT46 allowing IPv4 only applications to send requests via NAT64. On server side NAT based approaches can also be possible, but they have problem you still need an IPv4 address for each server defeats most of point of running an IPv6 only network. Another option is reverse proxies can direct traffic based on application layer headers. trying to run services on your cellular modem is likely to be an excercise in frustration. As it doesn't have IPv4 addresses and while it probablly does have public IPv6 address may still find firewalls present and IPv6 address is not very stable. In best approach to administering devices in unknown network situations is to use a VPN. Have a server on public internet (preferablly dual stack) to which all your devices can connect and access devices using VPN IP addresses.

IPv6 link-local addresses are required addresses, cannot be routed. confined to single link, every link has same link-local network. link-local address range is fe80::/10. From RFC 4291, IP Version 6 Addressing Architecture: 2. 5. 6. Link-Local IPv6 Unicast Addresses Link-Local addresses for use on single link. Link-Local addresses have following format: | 10 | | bits | 54 bits | 64 bits | +----------+-------------------------+----------------------------+ |1111111010| 0 | interface ID | +----------+-------------------------+----------------------------+ Link-Local addresses designed to used for addressing on single link for purposes automatic address configuration, neighbor discovery, or when no routers present. Routers must not forward packets with Link-Local source or destination addresses to other links. ULA addresses can be routed (except on public Internet). some rules to ULA addressing. ULA address range is fc00::/7, first half of addresses, fc00::/8, reserved for assignment by global authority. second half of ULA address range, fd00::/8, available for local use, 40-bit Global ID must be randomly chosen. From RFC 4193, Unique Local IPv6 Unicast Addresses: 1. Introduction document defines IPv6 unicast address format globally unique intended for local communications [IPV6]. These addresses called Unique Local IPv6 Unicast Addresses abbreviated as Local IPv6 addresses. not expected to be routable on global Internet. routable inside of more limited area such as site. may also be routed between limited set of sites. Local IPv6 unicast addresses have characteristics: Globally unique prefix (with high probability of uniqueness). Well-known prefix to allow for easy filtering at site boundaries.Allow sites be combined or privately interconnected without creating address conflicts or requiring renumbering of interfaces use these prefixes. Internet Service Provider independent can be used for communications inside site without permanent or intermittent Internet connectivity. If accidentally leaked outside site via routing or DNS, no conflict with other addresses. In practice, applications may treat these addresses like global scoped addresses.

This where PSH flag comes in. socket TCP makes available at session level can be written to by application with option of "pushing" data out immediately, rather than waiting for additional data to enter buffer. When this happens, PSH flag in outgoing TCP packet is set to 1 (on). Upon receiving a packet with PSH flag set, other side of connection knows to immediately forward segment up to application. summarize, TCP's push capability accomplishes two things: • sending application informs TCP that data should be sent immediately. • PSH flag in TCP header informs receiving host data should be pushed up to receiving application immediately. URG flag used to inform receiving station that certain data within segment is urgent and should be prioritized. If URG flag is set, receiving station evaluates urgent pointer, a 16-bit field in TCP header. This pointer indicates how much of data in segment, counting from first byte, is urgent.

Suppose receiving buffer has already some data to be processed by application. A segment with PSH flag set to 1 is sent now. sending buffer will not wait to be filled, instead, it will immediately push data into wire. Now, this data will queue up behind already non-processed data in receiving buffer. After previous data is processed then only data with PSH=1 can be forwarded to application. When URG is set, data can be immediately forwarded to application ignoring already existent data in receiving buffer. -HUP option is signal sent to processes by killall command. It hard to tell, but relevant entry in killall manual is: -SIGNAL Send a different signal instead of default TERM. signal may be specified either as a name (with or without leading SIG), or numerically. difference between default TERM signal killall sends and HUP signal depends on program you're sending signal to. At program end, they receive different interrupt signal value. program can catch interrupts and decide, based on value, if they should do one thing or the other. TERM signal (historically the "terminate signal") is usually sent to a program to request termination (which is a politer version of forcing termination with KILL signal). program is free to catch and ignore TERM signal. It doesn't have to terminate if it doesn't want to and can completely ignore this signal. HUP signal (historically the "hangup signal") is usually sent to program to request it restarts and re-reads all configuration in process. actual behaviour of program depends on program-specific implementation. Not all programs catch HUP and aren't required to by convention or dogma. For example, Apache web server will catch a HUP signal and re-read all configuration files but won't restart any processes. If you want to truly terminate processes and not worry about they to catch and obey signal uses the KILL signal. It cannot be caught or ignored and results in process termination. For good review of available POSIX signals see this Wikipedia article.

This is slower but, much more secure., in to spoof TCP/IP packets, you to catch sequence number and send malicious packet. Without a man in middle, almost impossible! UDP is a "Connetionless" protocol, it just sends data and forgets. no data reliability or integrity, but it's faster and more efficient for some applications.

As others stated, in general pings are ICMP-based have no ports. There is, however, thing as TCP Ping where, instead of typical 3-way TCP handshake, only first 2 steps performed and delay between measured. Once measurement completed, a RST ACK sent to close half-open connection. Then process repeats until counter/duration reached or you terminated process. Using TCP Ping (which I use FREQUENTLY to test for open ports on servers my systems admins work on) you able to specify destination ports to test (to verify server is listening on certain port). source port is just an ephemeral random port. short Youtube Video on how keys work. Given space available for length and number of pins, and operational room for error only so many key combinations possible. Given all different variables involved it's possible for every person on planet to have a unique lock, it's highly impractical. Most vendors distribute key/lock combinations by region. Car companies (or house door lock manufacturers) for example might have 200, 000 possible key/lock pairs but could redistribute same combinations on both east and west coasts since likelihood of 2 people with same key/lock combos meeting and realizing they're the same are extremely low. Generally keys are created using "codes" where a number represents height of peaks on key. given say 5 pins with 10 different height possibilities you're looking at 10^5 unique possibilities. can add another dimension of complexity by putting ridges on sides of keys. A lock could have more pins or more height possibilities depending on manufacturing accuracy and size of lock. If someone to have every possible key combination in one place, NO WAY they would be able to transport it. Let alone go unnoticed. It would take multiple dump trucks to move even a portion of keys.

EMV chips can be cloned, but not with only information on mag stripe. EMVs function as a challenge-response system, EMV authorization is transactionary between ATM/POS and card based on a secret stored on EMV. three stages in process: Card Authentication - card authenticates itself to ATM/POS Cardholder Verification - cardholder authenticates via PIN or signature (the card is not involved in this step) Transaction Authorization - where transaction itself is done Stages one and three present problems to our would-be skimmer. From outset, card has to authenticate itself to machine. It does this by transmitting an RSA signature back to machine over selected records. This signature not to be on the mag stripe. Once's done, transaction needs to be authorized. ATM/POS sends card parameters to transaction (amount, currency, date, etc. ) to card, card returns signed with secret, along with an ATC (a ticker counts transaction number) and an IAD (information specific to card issuer). ATM/POS sends this along to bank for a green light for transaction. By design, secret isn't to be stored on the stripe, and be impossible to store the ATC since changes with each transaction., you could do a preplay attack on chip, or could take chip apart and look at it under an electron microscope, but magnetic stripe isn't to enough to mint new chips.

By default, Nmap scans most common 1, 000 ports for each protocol(tcp, udp). If your port outside it won't scan it hence won't report it. However, can specify ports want to scan with -p option.

You scanning empty space. -Pn option (formerly -PN or -P0) tells Nmap to skip host discovery step (colloquially called "ping scan") assume every target address has a host listening on it. For default TCP scan, means Nmap will scan 1000 different ports on every target address, regardless of replies received. When no reply received for a probe, Nmap will wait a full timeout period (default starts at 1 second) then retry a few times to ensure packet not dropped. Your valuable bandwidth (and time) is wasted sending probes never get response. important part host discovery plays is in giving Nmap baseline for how fast and responsive your network connection is. In doing "ping sweep, " Nmap discovers round-trip time for each target. It can more accurately determine when packet was dropped should be retried, or when sending too many packets at once. Without this information, Nmap has to play it safe, slowing down sending rate making extra retransmissions to make sure no packets are lost. In, -Pn option not usually useful, though one of most commonly used and recommended ones.

'Filtered port' statement from nmap differs according scan method. standard scan (TCP Scan if unprivileged user, or Half-Open scan -sS if superuser) relies on TCP protocol. (named 3-way hanshake) client (you) issues a SYN, if server replies SYN/ACK : it means port is open ! You issue a SYN, if server replies RST : it means port is close ! You issue a SYN, if server not reply, or replies with ICMP error : it means port is filtered. Likely IDS / statefull firewall block request) To figure real status of port, can : use -sV, or -A option (version detection, help to determine status port. use --tcp-flags SYN, FIN to try bypassing fw. use other scan types (http://nmap. org/book/man-port-scanning-techniques. html) "Nmap Network Discovery" book, written by creator Fyodor explains this well. I quote filtered : Nmap cannot determine whether port is open because packet filtering prevents probes from reaching port. filtering could be from dedicated firewall device, router rules, or host-based firewall software. These ports frustrate attackers because provide little information. respond with ICMP error messages as type 3 code 13 (destination unreachable: communication administratively prohibited), but filters that drop probes without responding are more common. This forces Nmap to retry several times in case probe was dropped due to network congestion rather than filtering. This filtering slows scans down dramatically. open|filtered : Nmap places ports in this state when unable to determine whether port is open or filtered. This occurs for scan types in which open ports give no response. lack of response could also mean packet filter dropped probe or response elicited. Nmap does not know for sure whether port is open or filtered.UDP, IP protocol, FIN, NULL, and Xmas scans classify ports this way. closed|filtered : state used when Nmap unable to determine port closed or filtered. only used for IP ID Idle scan discussed in Section 5. 10, "TCP Idle Scan (-sl)

two reasons in favor of using import module rather than from module import function. First is namespace. Importing function into global namespace risks name collisions. Second't relevant to standard modules, but significant for you own modules, especially during development. It's option to reload() a module. Consider: from module import func. reload(module) # func still points to old code On other hand import module. reload(module) # module. func points to new code for speed. importing only function needed rather than import whole module (which contains more useless functions python will waste time importing them) Whether import a module or import function from a module, Python will parse whole module. Either way module is imported. "Importing a function" is nothing more than binding function to a name. In import module less work for interpreter than from module import func.

A python module is a package to encapsulate reusable code. Modules usually, not always, reside in a folder with a __init__. py file. Modules can contain functions also classes. Modules are imported using import keyword. use from imports whenever improves readability. For example, prefer (semicolons to save space here): from collections import defaultdict from foomodule import FooBar, FooBaz from twisted. internet. protocol import Factory defaultdict(); FooBar(); FooBaz(); Factory() instead of import collections import foomodule import twisted. internet. protocol collections. defaultdict(); foomodule. FooBar(); foomodule. FooBaz() twisted. internet. protocol. Factory() latter harder to read (and write) contains redundant information., useful to know ahead of time what parts of module I'm using. prefer regular imports if using lots short names from module: import sys sys. argv; sys. stderr; sys. exit() Or if name generic doesn't make sense outside of namespace: import json json. loads(foo) from json import loads loads(foo) # potentially confusing

Importing module doesn't waste anything; module is always fully imported (into sys. modules mapping), whether you use import sys or from sys import argv makes no odds. only difference between two statements is name is bound; import sys binds name sys to module (so sys -> sys. modules['sys']), from sys import argv binds different name, argv, pointing straight at attribute contained inside of module (so argv -> sys. modules['sys']. argv). rest of sys module is still there, whether you use anything else from module or not. no performance difference between two approaches., sys. argv has to look up two things; to look up sys in global namespace (finds module), then look up attribute argv., by using from sys import argv you can skip attribute lookup, since already have direct reference to attribute. But import statement still has to do that work, looks up same attribute when importing,'ll only need to use argv once. If had to use argv thousands of times in a loop, it could perhaps make a difference, but in this specific case does not., choice between one or the other should be based solely on coding style. In large module, I'd use import sys; code documentation matters, using sys. argv in large module makes it clearer what you referring to than just argv. If only place you use argv is in '__main__' block to call main() function, by use from sys import argv if feel happier about: if __name__ == '__main__': from sys import argv main(argv) I'd still use import sys there myself. All things being equal (and they are, exactly, in terms of performance and number of characters used to write it), that just easier on the eye for me.If importing something else altogether, perhaps performance comes into play. But only if use specific name in a module many times over, in a critical loop for example. creating local name (within function) to faster still: import somemodule def somefunction(): localname = somemodule. somefunctionorother while test: # huge, critical loop foo = localname(bar)

opinion using regular import improves readability. reviewing Python code I like seeing where given function or class comes from right where it is used. saves me from scrolling to top of module to get info. for long module names use as keyword give short aliases: import collections as col import foomodule as foo import twisted. internet. protocol as twip my_dict = col. defaultdict() foo. FooBar() twip_fac = twip. Factory() exception I always use from module import something notation when deal with __future__ module. can't do another way when want all strings to be unicode by default in Python 2, e. g. from __future__ import unicode_literals from __future__ import print_function

TLS not require TCP. For example I use TLS authentication key with OpenVPN my configuration lower goes over TUN interface rides on UDP. TLS can be used on both, and probably on top of other things I not aware of.

You can have SSL/TLS without certificates. This supported in TLS standard: "DH_anon" cipher suites involve no certificate. But to remember unauthenticated TLS is inherently weak against active attackers, cannot prevent client or server impersonation (or both at same time, called a Man-in-the-Middle attack). Most Web browsers deactivate DH_anon cipher suites because of inherent vulnerability to MitM. can have same conceptual effect with self-signed SSL certificate, you can produce yourself without talking to CA. Of, same Web browsers will show "scary warnings", for same reason. From EFF point of view, whose arch-enemy is NSA, generalized DH_anon cipher suites would make sense, since Evil Spy AgenciesTM know to prefer passive eavesdropping (since leaves no incriminating traces). Passive eavesdropping is defeated by DH_anon., for most other people, biggest threat is not governmental intrusiveness, but mundane con-artists that try to separate you from your money, and these do not hesitate to run full MitM attacks, e. g. with fake WiFi access points. Let's Encrypt initiative aims at making certificate issuance free (as in "no money") and automated, while still maintaining a of effort at "verifying" whoever obtains certificate has of control over designated domain. From of, system relies on DNS implies any DNS attack (e. g. DNS spoofing) might be leveraged into rogue certificate issuance, in fully automated way, this initiative would be a weakening of current certificate model. On other, if it convinces more people to use SSL, it contributes to a "safer World", at least from NSA-is-the-Devil point of view, where matters is defeating passive eavesdroppers., without support from Microsoft and Google (i. e. inclusion of Let's Encrypt root CA in IE and Chrome), no way initiative turns into generalized HTTPS. Not a of people would activate SSL on Web site if it means 70% of users will get insulted and scared away by browsers. If Microsoft and Google don't jump in the wagon (and I don't believe they will), Let's Encrypt system will remain a political gesture, but won't be widespread (and ultimately Mozilla will drop it if someone to mount an automated DNS-based attack). another different certificate-less mode for SSL; it called SRP. one is safe, but different from normal Web browsing. SRP ensures mutual client/server authentication with to shared secret, it in a protects shared secret against offline brute force -- it can tolerate use of low entropy shared secret, i. e. a password. TLS-SRP makes of sense for accessing password-protected network resources, involves no certificate at all; yet, it safe against MitM and eavesdropping. Unfortunately, Web browsers don't currently support SRP.

But, if take today's internet usually only have UDP and TCP as transport protocols on top of IP and from these two TCP is only reliable one. means, if only this limited selection of transport protocols available TLS requires TCP because it does not work with UDP. To work with UDP similar protocol DTLS designed to work over unreliable transports.
