SSL/TLS (the underlying protocol for HTTPS) provides two features: Encryption, so nobody passively listen to data. Encryption is done using a key shared between peers. Identification, so you can be sure who you are talking to. usually done with certificates. might have encryption without identification your connection open to active attacks, where instead of expected peer you talk to another party, like a man in middle which can decrypt and manipulate data and forward data to original peer after re-encryption. Without identification not mean only without certificates but also when you trust just any certificate you get, typically self-signed certificates., while TLS could do encryption without certificates, HTTPS requires certificates because this only way for proper identification in this use case.

No, Apple issue SSL/TLS certificates for web hosting purposes. Apple's developer certificates are for code signing only. LetsEncrypt and Caddy Server provide free SSL/TLS certificates for use with web site. ease management web site, consider Caddy for web server. Caddy handles certificate provisioning renewal for. For non-commercial use, StartSSL, offer free certificates.

In practice, SSL and TLS both have issues, but they around Man In the Middle type of attack. For example TLS MITM renegotiation issue see here, this attack requires attacker to be in middle of communication path, which limits threat a little :-)

TLS requires reliable transport. On internet, this leaves only TCP, as UDP does not offer reliability. TLS require reliable transport because (in compliance with layered architecture ISO/OSI reference model) it does not handle transport errors, lost packets or other disturbances occur with IP. TLS designed to offer secure channel on top of reliable transport it does this well. DTLS does (I assume) necessary error handling within protocol. If TLS performed over UDP, connections and handshakes could fail because packet got lost in transit no one noticed. Mitigation of such problems is (according to ISO/OSI reference model) designated task of reliable transport. Any reliable transport works theoretically, yet for all practical purposes of IP networks, usually implies TCP.

Theoretically you can put anything want in a certificate; for instance, this certificate contains a video file as "Subject Alt Name" (surprisingly, Windows has no trouble decoding a 1. 2 MB certificate -- but it does not show the video, alas). However, in practice, certificates "for SSL" just contain intended server name, as specified in RFC 2818. client (Web browser) will verify name from URL appears where it should in certificate. no standard for storing port number in certificate, no client will verify presence of port number, short words: certificates are not port-specific. notion of "identity" certificates manipulate embody does not include notion of "port".

Entirely, in practise. encryption starts with root ssl people (Verisign, Thawte, etc) it's suitable for insecure lines. AFAIK TLS doesn't have problem with man in middle attacks, its only weaker/older handshakes have that problem.

Prefix-list used for route-filtering route redistribution matches on prefixes sent, received or present in routing table or BGP table. They match on bits in prefix but also on prefix-length. ACLs can be used for more features like: traffic filtering, matching traffic for QoS, matching traffic for NAT, VPN, Policy Based Routing, etc. They can also be used for route filters and redistribution but their syntaxes different than used for other purposes.

Not a whole lot. They both provide means to filter on network addresses, but couple key differences: Extended ACL's can filter based on "higher layer" information, ie TCP/UDP port. Prefix lists cannot. Extended/Standard ACL's can use wildcard masks allow for specification of arbitrary addresses or ranges of addresses. Prefix lists can't do this. Prefix lists can match on prefix lengths - minimum or maximum lengths with "ge" and "le" keywords,. For routing policy, folks prefer to use prefix lists because some feel they're more "expressive" but not much to limit using one or other - what situation/requirements call for.

history of how they came into being (and why they are way they are): In early days of Internet, people started asking for packet filters (aka access lists). Cisco implemented simple access lists first (filtering on destination host addresses, augmented by wildcard masks), but they weren't good enough to block (for) SMTP, they created extended access lists, can match on source and destination IP addresses (with wildcards bits on both - these bits allow to match whole prefixes), protocols, port numbers. So: access list = packet filter. Later (but still decades ago) people started running multiple routing protocols on same box wanted to redistribute information between them. Not a problem, but wouldn't want ALL information propagated into other routing protocol - need ROUTE FILTERS. usually case, everything looks like a nail if have hammer, Cisco's engineers implemented route filters with object they already had - access lists.: access list = packet filter (and sometimes route filter) With advent of classless routing (yeah, long ago days Class A, Class B Class C addresses), people wanted to redistribute prefixes of certain size between routing protocols. For example: advertise all /24s from OSPF into BGP, but not the /32s. Impossible to do with access lists. Time for new kludge: use extended access list pretend source IP address in packet filter represents network address (actually prefix address) and destination IP address in same line of packet filter represents subnet mask. far: access lists = packet filters. Simple access lists also serve as route filters (matching only on network addresses) and extended access lists serve as route filters matching addresses and subnet masks.Fortunately someone retained reason started wondering what brilliant minds that decided reusing extended ACLs for route filters makes sense were smoking when they got brilliant idea. End result: Cisco IOS got prefix lists, (almost) identical in functionality to extended access lists as route filters, but displayed in a format a regular human being of understanding. Today: use access lists for packet filters and prefix lists for route filters. You can still use access lists as route filters but don't do it. Makes sense?

You should be fine, you got lucky because you failed your way into saving your disk. I'll first break down your dd command: dd if=/dev/zero of=/dev/rdisk1 Copy everything from zero to /dev/rdisk1 (your main disk, ouch!) bs=1024 Sets size of blocks to be copied. In this case, you coping in 1Kb blocks. more important in next bit. count=1 This argument is saved your entire disk. set count to 1, told dd to only copy 1 block. Since your block size is 1Kb full of zeros, dd command would have zeroed out first kilobyte of your drive. no idea what's in first area on drive, speculate that it holds drive structure information., my recommenced action to is reboot into recovery launch Disk Utility run "Repair Disk" on system drive.

Others explained what they do, so I'll skip that. point in dd having seperate bs and count argument is bs controls how much is written at a time. Specifying large values for bs require large buffer in program, specifying values less than block size of device will be slow because kernel has to build entire block to write to device (in cases like this it can probably buffer writes until complete block, in other cases it might have to read what's already on disc). two commands use different values for bs, leads me to think you might have found them on two different sites. Hard discs used to have block size of 512 bytes, corresponding to bs=512 of latter command, but some (6-8) years ago started making discs with block size of 4096 bytes, making bs=4096 better choice for modern discs.

If you have more complete answer, by means, post. 'dd' is simpler, if you get details right on command line. Disk Utility, may be faster even though you have to partition and restore each partition in turn. This because 'dd' to copy all unused blocks. In my case, with both of on USB 2. 0, if drive hadn't failed, it would have taken sixty hours., if two drives don't have same number of bytes, 'dd' not good. If target is smaller, O. S. will try to use blocks that don't exist (or will fail to copy at all). If target is bigger, extra blocks be inaccessible.

dd doesn't care what data it copies means. Partition tables, partition contents, file fragments, empty filesystem space, it's all bytes. dd if=/dev/sda of=/dev/sdb makes /dev/sdb an exact copy of /dev/sda, provided sdb is at least as large as sda (plus some trailing junk won't be directly accessible if sdb is larger). magic is in sdX block devices. dd is just a tool to copy bytes around. doesn't mean dd is best tool for job. It's somewhat error-prone and typically not fastest. I found cat to be faster when copying between different disks. dd can lose data in unintuitive ways (though modern Linux system is safe in this respect). Using cat has additional advantage less risk of destroying data to typo (like swapping if and of): output specified via familiar shell redirection operator (you can use this syntax for dd too,). cat /dev/sda >/dev/sdb If other disk is larger, can make an image of disk in a file: cat /dev/sda >/path/to/disk. img Such disk image can't be used directly: can't boot off it. But copying it back to disk will yield byte-for-byte copy of original, since whole contents were copied both times. You can also do loopback mount to access files off it. can make loop device with partitions, but Ubuntu only had tools for that in recent versions. If want to preserve data, enough to copy partitions individually, store them in individual files.

wouldn't classify "two-step" as a distinction. It's mechanism of a factor that may or may not still be something you know. For example, if code sent to a cellphone, it's really something you know (password) and something you have (cellphone). If it's sent to e-mail, it's still single factor since both e-mail and account are (most likely) password derived. It's certainly still a mechanism of validation in e-mail sense, but doesn't add more than asking for second password in authentication.

difference is addition versus multiplication. Two-step is additive process: authenticate once with one independent credential (a password), then again with another independent credential (a OTP, delivered via SMS, phone, or generator app). authenticated yourself twice. Two-factor is multiplicative: combining one independent credential (a PIN secret key biomarker) with another (a certificate, or cryptographic token code) to derive stronger single credential than each independent credential. Assigning arbitrary convenient numbers to credential types (1=none, 2=password [any self-defined, OTP,], 3=crypto credential [cert, token code]), demonstrate password stronger than no password (2>1); two-step authentication stronger than single password ((2+2=4)>2) or crypto credential ((2+2=4)>3) independently, but always weaker than any multi-factor scheme ((2+2=4)<(2*3=6)).

Two-factor authentication refers exclusively to authentication mechanisms where two authentication elements fall under different categories "something you have", "something you are", and "something you know". A multi-step authentication scheme requires two physical keys, or two passwords, or two forms of biometric identification is not two-factor, but two steps may be valuable nonetheless. example is two-step authentication required by Gmail. After providing password memorized, required to also provide one-time password displayed on your phone. While the phone may appear to be "something you have", from security perspective it's still "something you know". because the key to authentication isn't the device itself, but rather information stored on device could in be copied by attacker., by copying both your memorized password and OTP configuration, attacker could impersonate you without stealing anything physical. point to multi-factor authentication, for strict distinction, is attacker must pull off two different types of theft to impersonate you: must acquire both your knowledge and your physical device, for example. In case of multi-step (but not multi-factor), attacker needs only to pull off one type of theft, multiple times. for example he needs to steal two pieces of information, but no physical objects. type multi-step authentication provided by Google or Facebook or Twitter is still strong enough to thwart most attackers, but from purist point view, it technically isn't multi-factor authentication.

Others explained what they do, so I'll skip that. point in dd having seperate bs and count argument is bs controls how much is written at a time. Specifying large values for bs require large buffer in program, specifying values less than block size of device will be slow because kernel has to build entire block to write to device (in cases like this it can probably buffer writes until complete block, in other cases it might have to read what's already on disc). two commands use different values for bs, leads me to think you might have found them on two different sites. Hard discs used to have block size of 512 bytes, corresponding to bs=512 of latter command, but some (6-8) years ago started making discs with block size of 4096 bytes, making bs=4096 better choice for modern discs.

help is a bash built-in, providing help for bash commands only man is traditional form of help for almost every command on your system, not only, sometimes also configuration files have own man page. In Linux distros organized in packages, relative text general provided from same package providing command. If have bash-completion can take advantage from TAB to see man pages available. info is alternative system to provide manual pages for commands, based on GNU emacs. provided mainly for GNU commands and utilities. don't widely adopted from others.

help is bash command. uses internal bash structures to store retrieve information about bash commands. man is a macro set for troff (via groff) processor. output of processing single file sent to pager by man command by default. info is text-only viewer for archives in info format output of Texinfo.

help is a built-in command in bash shell (and that shell only) documents builtin commands and keywords of shell.'s an internal documentation system of that shell. Other shells have own documentation system (ksh93 has --help and --man options for builtins, zsh has a run-help helper extracts information from manuals in other formats). Other commands like vim have own embedded documentation system. man is a system-wide documentation system provides short reference manuals (pages) for individual commands, API functions, concepts, configuration file syntax, file formats organised in sections (1 for user commands, 2 for system calls. ).'s traditional Unix documentation system. info is another documentation system originating in GNU project. It's hypertext with links (predates web). info manual is like a digital book with concept of table of contents and (searchable) index helps locating information. overlap between 3. For, bash part of GNU project has both man page and info manual. size of manual makes man system not as appropriate for bash., structure of info manual and index not good in bash makes it not as easy to look information in as in other info manuals like zsh's. zsh manual even bigger is split into several man pages and also has a good info manual with very good index. noted info manual is generated from texinfo format also used to generate HTML and printable (PDF/PS) versions. In case of zsh, texinfo is generated from another format (yodl).

According to Fundamental Concepts of Dependability: A system failure is event occurs when delivered service deviates from correct service. system may fail either because it not comply with specification, or because specification did not adequately describe its function. An error is part of system state may cause subsequent failure: failure occurs when error reaches service interface and alters service. A fault is adjudged or hypothesized cause of error. understand defect as just another name for fault. Bug is confusing and can represent a fault or failure depending on context.

One time error usually means nothing. use it as a warning - keep backups current perhaps test a restore., might check things in a week to sure it's not a sign of hardware errors instead of software error.

io error during fsck / single user mode means inventory backups, perform data recovery if needed, format and erase drive. At point, you will either have stable volume to reinstall OS or continuing hardware errors meaning repair or drive swap. You could buy time by installing OS on to external drive postpone data recovery / backup decision point. failing drives work well for read operations for longer than write operations.

Exception Type, SIGSEGV, is a segment violation -- program tried to access memory other than allocated to it by operating system. Possibly it used uninitialized pointer, or return-address or some other pointer got over-written which could happen if buffer on program stack was over-run. rest of information useless without source code and load-map, i. e., it's of interest to a programmer trying to find out how crash occurred, but not much use to rest of us.

only way filesystem errors like describe could be copied onto different disk (e. g. your Time Machine volume) is if whole disk partition or whole drive copied at block level using dd or like Carbon Copy Cloner. Time Machine doesn't work that way, its stored backups should be free from filesystem errors and files it restores should be free from them.

journaled file system eliminates chances filesystem in inconsistent state after next reboot. But "consistent" is not the same as "correct". Before journaling, filesystem structures could become damaged could lead to more corruption after next boot. journaling limits damage to files written at time of crash. If a file was written at the time of a crash, odds of its contents being incorrect are about 100%. manner of incorrectness would depend on how it was being written at the time. If data was simply appended, last few blocks will probably be truncated off when journal is replayed. But if bits of data were modified throughout file (such as in a database store), its likely to be in a very inconsistent state. Applications write files in that way sometimes have their own consistency checks for purpose. But most files in a typical OS X system get written sequentially. In, many programs write a temporary file and don't move it in to replace old version until new version has committed to disk. This ensures even a forced shutdown in middle of writing a file only loses new version, but preserves the old one. Bottom line: something bad will happen to any data being written at time of a crash, but how bad depends on the application.

question boils down to this: How I know if hard drive is damaged? Your computer would start to fail - as in crash, errors thrown, freeze and perform slowly. When drive gets damaged, it doesn't suddenly read incorrect data or modified data; data is corrupted. Data can't be read will cause (at minimum) error or crash. Can it weaken security? computer wouldn't be functional by time it weakened security. For example, if running File Valut, damaged drive won't decrypt drive; it won't function. Period. If you crash your firewall config, SIP (system integrity protection) will throw errors that system files have changed., how do know if hard drive is damaged? If you start getting crashes or freezes performance problems, things you can do is diagnostic like Apple Hardware Test (AHT). If want to check disks, nice GUI from Clever Files called DiskDrill (free for basic utilities, $$ to activate pro features). This will help you be proactive.

Before journaling, filesystem structures could become damaged could lead to more corruption after next boot. journaling limits damage to files written at time of crash. If a file was written at the time of a crash, odds of its contents being incorrect are about 100%. manner of incorrectness would depend on how it was being written at the time. If data was simply appended, last few blocks will probably be truncated off when journal is replayed. But if bits of data were modified throughout file (such as in a database store), its likely to be in a very inconsistent state. Applications write files in that way sometimes have their own consistency checks for purpose. But most files in a typical OS X system get written sequentially. In, many programs write a temporary file and don't move it in to replace old version until new version has committed to disk. This ensures even a forced shutdown in middle of writing a file only loses new version, but preserves the old one. Bottom line: something bad will happen to any data being written at time of a crash, but how bad depends on the application.

answers seem be all over the place (yes, no, might be, should be), reiterate @waiwai933's answer: it is secure. To specific, you asked: "If malicious user sniffed all my incoming and outgoing packets. Can he calculate same keys and read my encrypted traffic too or send encrypted messages to server in my name?" answer is no and no. With footnote. reason he cannot calculate same keys seems paradoxical, in was major break-through in cryptography when first published by Diffie and Hellman. TLS uses key exchange protocol, like Diffie-Hellman but more sophisticated to protect from man-in-the-middle attacks. protocol lets two people never exchanged information before compute a secret key no one seeing all messages can compute. Once shared secret key, you can use it to encrypt your traffic. malicious user doesn't know key, he can't encrypt traffic that looks like it came from you. footnotes. assuming SSL/TLS protocol is correct. With most involved cryptographic protocols, bugs are found and fixed from time-to-time. SSL/TLS have a recent bug (mentioned in few answers as reason it is not secure), it has been temporarily worked around and now fixed (RFC 5746) and fix is in various stages of deployment. (In your scenario, bug allowed malicious user to send packets in your name but not read your traffic. ) always possible attacker knows how to break TLS/SSL due to unpublished error in protocol. obvious point worth repeating: malicious user could see your request and send his own response using his own certificate. do check the certificate. another obvious point: can only be sure SSL/TLS will be used for future pages if current page is HTTPS.For example, if you are on an HTTP page wants you to log-in, from past experience know clicking log-in button will redirect you to HTTPS connection, this functionality could be stripped out by active malicious user on your network. So only log into pages already HTTPS (unless if you know how to detect if log-in page modified).

With HTTPS, SSL/TLS tunnel is established first, HTTP traffic happens only within that tunnel. Some information still leaks: If client uses a proxy, connection to proxy looks like: CONNECT www. example. com:443 with target server name. Alternatively, client could send target server IP address, but this only marginally less revealing;, to know server IP address, client must do name resolution, using DNS servers provided by company itself. Recent clients will send target server name as part of initial SSL handshake (that's Server Name Indication extension). server responds by sending its certificate back, includes, in plain view and by definition, the server name. From can conclude target server name is not a secret. You may assume your company learns it. rest of communication is encrypted nominally inaccessible from outsiders. However, length of data packets sent and received by client can still be inferred by any eavesdropper (with single byte accuracy if RC4 cipher suite is used), this can also reveal a lot of information, depending on context. If company is serious about security it may have installed more advanced proxy like Blue Coat's ProxySG. Such systems perform Man-in-the-Middle attack by dynamically generating a fake certificate for target server. This gives them access to complete data, as if there was no SSL. Note, such interception is possible only if company could add to trust store of your desktop system root CA certificate proxy uses to issue fake certificates. This is rather intrusive action., if they could do that, why would they stop there ? They may have inserted, easily, handful of spying software will plug in your Web browser, keyboard and your display; everything you do on machine is known to them. Alternatively, if you can make sure your machine is free from interference from your company (e. g. it is your own device and installed no company-provided software on it), MitM-proxy cannot decrypt your SSL connections.simple way to hide your traffic from company is not to use their facilities at all. Bring your own laptop with 3G key (or tethered to smartphone). By paying for your own Internet, you can evade network-based detection spend days roaming Web instead of doing work you paid to do (but, detection of slackers never restricted to only using computerized gizmos).

Let me take a crack at this. I will use Unix and Linux more or less synonymously in. If I referring to something historical predates existence Linux, I will usually write "Unix", and if talking about something more recent, or something specific to Linux flavor of Unix, I will usually write "Linux". Shell only thing in your list a discrete concept no overlap with others is the 'shell'. The shell is a program's purpose is to communicate with a user and carry out operating system operations on their behalf. common shells use a technique called a 'command line' of sending user prompt, waiting for user to type out text command, then carrying out command. But there are menu based shells, and even graphical shells (like Windows File Explorer) no self-respecting Unix person would call such a thing a 'shell'. In Unix, if someone calls something a 'shell' they almost certainly mean form of command line interface as described. odd in Unix world to refer to anything as a 'shell' if it isn't communicating to user using the tty model I describe further on. TTY This is a confusing one because it can refer to a few different kinds of things. In Linux, there is a device called a 'tty'. It is an abstract device expected to be used for bi-directional communication with something either user, or taking input from user in. Sometimes abstract device may correspond directly to physical device. Sometimes it may be a program presenting someone with a window in communication appears and into user can type. But, reason this abstract device exists and reason it is called a 'tty' is that 'tty' is short for 'teletype', was an actual physical device that had a printer printed on paper combined with a keyboard. model abstract 'tty' device presents to programs using it is there is a teletype on the other end. You send it characters and those characters appear on the teletype.When you read characters from it, those characters represent keys typed on a keyboard. old paper-printer based ttys quickly supplanted with video ttys. On those, of, no roll of paper., in, it possible overwrite any character on screen. But, rather than present of abstract 'screen' interface to programs, programs instead expected to send special streams of characters called escape sequences accomplish a variety of tasks. Usually abstract thing called a 'cursor' can be moved around screen, any character sent will replace whatever is at cursor and cursor will move one character further on. Often you can change color of character's about to be printed with escape sequences as. 'glass ttys' do not follow this model handled poorly in Unix world. IBM 3270 family of video terminals fall into this category. What Linux/Unix people typically call a 'shell window' is emulation of a glass tty using graphical user interface. Internally, programs running inside of shell window are talking to a virtual tty device sometimes called a pseudo-tty or pseudo-terminal (aka a pty). Terminal A terminal is just a place where computer and human supposed to interface. Terminals may be completely graphical and not follow tty model in way, even though program may use their capabilities to emulate this. All actual physical ttys (glass or otherwise) are terminals. Console A console is a special kind of terminal generally supposed to be attached in direct secure way to hardware operating system is running on. In Linux, console is virtualized in small way allows to use special keystroke to switch between virtual consoles. But this virtualization is done with real piece of hardware by software in kernel.ways to use Linux through a 'serial console' is a console's attached to computer through a serial port like a USB port (or, on some very small and/or old computers, an RS-232 port of kind) and follows old teletype model in a fairly strict way., idea is this console is connected in a direct physical way to computer instead of through some of network that might allow anybody to connect.

help is a built-in command in bash shell (and that shell only) documents builtin commands and keywords of shell.'s an internal documentation system of that shell. In case of zsh, texinfo is generated from another format (yodl).

Scroll to All apps then scroll down to “Google Play Services” app. Open app details and: tap on “Force stop” (see "Force stop is disabled" below) button tap on "Disable" button tap on three dots at top right select: "Uninstall updates" once uninstallation completed, tap on "Enable" button Solution 4 – Clear Google Services Framework cache. As you noted, rights are you have granted to you; permissions are resources you need configured to require. But not uncommon to hear people confuse the two, saying like "I will grant you permission to access my resource. " distinction matters more when start using Role Based Access Control model. For example I would never intentionally grant a user permission to access my system. Instead, I would tell user to request membership in an access group has rights. I already think in terms of rights vs. permissions. Once concepts split lines, I've found myself less likely to interchange two terms. But bottom line is distinction is not important. If you want to grant permission to access your folder, go right ahead. :-)

I don't think there really, good reason for distinction. It's just way it wound up in Windows. In everyday language rights/permissions/privileges are somewhat synonymous anyway. Re. "User rights" term "User rights" on Windows usually refers to something granted to user. Microsoft seem unsure about terms. painful bit from Wikipedia: https://en. wikipedia. org/wiki/Privilege_(computing)#Nomenclature names used in Windows source code end in either "Privilege" or "LogonRight". This led to confusion about what full set of "Rights" and "Privileges" should be called. Microsoft currently uses term "User Rights". In past other terms also been used by Microsoft, as "Privilege Rights", "logon user rights" and "NT-Rights".

rsync -a preserves permissions your current computer/account is concerned. Accessing files from different user/different account is controlled by parameters outside of rsync's influence (mainly by access protocoll and its options used when mounting the drive).

man chmod for what command does. Basically it sets access permissions on files and folders, with three digits standing for user, group other permissions. first digit defines permissions for user owning file, second for group owning file, third for anybody else. In case chmod 777 gives everybody read, write execute rights for most problems is too much chmod 760 gives all rights to owner, read and write to group owning file no rights to users neither own file nor part of owning group Granting too many rights might be a security problem, depending on whether other people can access your computer and/or computer is accessible from outside. To resolve apache/PHP issues, granting 777 seems to be rather broad. I would go with 664 (or even 660) first.

Clicking lock icon will prompt you for admin password. After you provide it, system allow you to change permissions for file or folder in "Sharing & Permissions" pane at bottom of Get Info window. This is feature of underlying Unix operating system allows different privileges for user, group, and others. Note you always allowed to change permissions (whether icon locked or unlocked) when you (your user) is owner of file -- e. g. most of files in your own user folder such as your Desktop and Documents folders. But when you not owner, you'll have to unlock this option to change permissions.'s reason this feature is "locked" against casual access.'s not something you want to touch if you're not sure what you're doing. Messing with permissions can cause access problems, security problems, or both. For more details, check out Wikipedia article: http://en. wikipedia. org/wiki/Filesystem_permissions#Traditional_Unix_permissions

permission command chmod 644 working! permission of your file Owner. conf is -rw-r--r--. chmod command works by specifying (1) permissions for file owner - in this case root, (2) permissions for anyone in same group as file owner - in this case group is wheel, and (3) permissions for everybody else (global permissions). For each of three above groups of users, possible permissions are read, write, and execute. Full permissions look like this: -rwxrwxrwx. permissions specified using binary notation. 1 means permission should be set, 0 means should not be., setting chmod 644 sets permissions 6 - or 110 in binary - for file owner, and 4 - or 100 in binary - for group and for everybody else. creates permission string -110100100. translates to: -rw-r--r--. Note in question above, username. conf and Owner. conf both have permissions of 644.

ACLs are extending normal permissions system used to control access to file/folder. Ordinarily permissions system works by explicitly allowing read, write or execute permissions against owner, members of same group, and other people. ACL allows to extend by providing exceptions and additions to these normal operations, so file might be writable by owner, readable by members of same group (say Users), but not accessible to anyone else. you could drop ACL in that allowed user Bob write access, even though standard permissions should only allow him read access through his User grown membership.

As noted in Mac Technology overview: App Sandbox Introduced in OS X v10. 7, App Sandbox provides last line of defense against stolen, corrupted, or deleted user data if malicious code exploits your app. App Sandbox minimizes damage from coding errors. strategy is twofold: App Sandbox enables you to describe how your app interacts with system. system grants your app only access it needs to get job done, no more. App Sandbox allows user to transparently grant app additional access by using Open and Save dialogs, drag and drop, other familiar user interactions. developer can implement following entitlement as noted in Enabling App Sandbox, this is exactly what you described in your question, probably entitlement A/V program developer had utilized to obtain just read and write access. com. apple. security. files. user-selected. read-write Read/write access to files user has selected using Open or Save dialog not the same as true administrator user, since program would not be granted execute privilege.

Physical cores are, physical cores within CPU. Logical cores are abilities of a single core to do 2 or more things simultaneously. grew out of early Pentium 4 CPUs ability to Hyper Threading (HTT). It was a a game played where sub components of core weren't used for certain instructions while, another long running instruction might have executed. CPU could work on 2 things simultaneously. Newer cores are more full-fledged CPUs're working on multiple things simultaneously, but aren't true CPUs as physical cores are. read more about limitations of hyperthreading functionality vs. physical capabilities of core on tomshardware in article titled: Intel Core i5 And Core i7: Intel’s Mainstream Magnum Opus. see breakdown of box using lscpu command: $ lscpu Architecture: x86_64 CPU op-mode(s): 32-bit, 64-bit CPU(s): 4 Thread(s) per core: 2 Core(s) per socket: 2 CPU socket(s): 1 NUMA node(s): 1 Vendor ID: GenuineIntel CPU family: 6 Model: 37 Stepping: 5 CPU MHz: 2667. 000 Virtualization: VT-x L1d cache: 32K L1i cache: 32K L2 cache: 256K L3 cache: 3072K NUMA node0 CPU(s): 0-3 In my Intel i5 laptop has 4 "CPUs" in total CPU(s): 4 2 physical cores (1 socket × 2 cores/socket = 2 cores) Core(s) per socket: 2 CPU socket(s): 1 each can run up to 2 threads Thread(s) per core: 2 at the same time. Your computer has 2 cores, but 4 logical processors. seeing is Intel's hyper-threading technology. This technology puts multiple logical processors on single core, so each core can run multiple threads at once. difference between this and multiple cores is hyper-threading only duplicates parts of processor control current state, not actual execution unit, but multiple cores duplicate everything. This means computer will run like it has four cores only if threads on each core using different parts of execution unit, but if exact same thing was running on both threads in single core, it wouldn't be faster than two-core system without hyper-threading.

As an OS designer I agree with result of measurements. amount bullshit produced elsewhere about subject matter is unbelievable. See number of logical cores as number parallel threads/processes can be executed by HW. achieved by duplicating e. g. registers and instruction pointers of CPU core. CPU core itself decides which thread (instruction pointer) to use. It will decide to use other thread as instruction of current thread not available in cache and need to be fetched from e. g. memory or L3 cache. This mechanism create 10%-30% potential improvement in instructions/seconds or CPU performance. If run single application with one thread, you not able to reap this benefit, but if run two high load applications on e. g. old HT Pentium, you will be able to reap benefits. same true of for applications, have more then one thread. My Linux system has 200 threads, some benefits dependent on actual load are always present. All remarks apply without virtualization. Virtualbox only limits number of threads can run in parallel for each virtual machine (VM), but host process scheduler will change logical processor(s) and physical processor(s), on which VM processes run dynamically. If run high load applications on VM, additional logical cores will give you same benefit of 10%-30%. load can be single multi-threaded application or set of different applications. On modern systems with VT-x or AMD-V no performance penalty for maxing out number of logical cores, since also no noticeable performance penalty for running more virtual machines at same time. Your limit is performance of your CPU chip, so can't render videos on 3 VMs at same time without slowing down each VM, because they to share same physical CPU. Your host system might become irresponsive, if you render a video on a VM with all logical cores present, but have almost same problem, if you run that rendering app on your host.least in VM you have a choice could solve it by limiting max CPU load to 80%-90% or reducing number of cores for this reason.

Ramesh indicated by default UID and GID are equal for ordinary users. However this not always the case so you must not make such assumption as this may wreak havoc to your system. Assigning file/folder permissions to wrong group is somewhat messy, isn't it?, short answer: no, UID not always equal to GID. Still, /etc/passwd contains both UID and GID of default group on same line's easy to extract them.

From this link, I see below information. A user ID (UID) is a unique positive integer assigned by Unix-like operating system to each user. Each user identified to system by UID, and user names generally used only as interface for humans. UIDs stored, along with corresponding user names and other user-specific information, in /etc/passwd file, can be read with cat command: cat /etc/passwd third field contains UID, and fourth field contains group ID (GID), by default is equal to UID for all ordinary users. EDIT, as @Karlson points out not true UID equal to GID by default. statement is true only if no ordinary groups are added separately and no groups explicitly specified on user creation. By default gid for next added user = max(gid) + 1. no correlation between UID and GID required by *NIX system they just happen to coincide in some cases. More references http://www. thegeekstuff. com/2009/06/useradd-adduser-newuser-how-to-create-linux-users

user private group idiom often used in modern Linux systems, *nix not require unique primary group for each user, possible for several user accounts to share a common primary group such as users or staff. Even in cases UPG idiom enforced, no particular reason that numeric GID of a particular UPG should be equal to owner's UID, although most account-creation tools will try to assign UIDs and GIDs in order, if available. IDs can easily get out of step if users and/or groups need to be consistent across multiple systems (for example to accommodate pre-existing NFS shares).

Ultimately, proper solution is to use a directory service (like NIS or LDAP) to provide consistent UID/GID mapping for all users., this is very heavy solution for a smaller/or home network. easiest thing to is simply make UIDs/GIDs consistent on all hosts involved.

Given length of UID, suspect value is a cryptographic hash value. Hashes often used to avoid collisions can be recreated if original input is known. SHA1 is 40 characters when hex encoded. can rule out OS X uuid and Window's GUID as lengths too short. values returned by uuid on same hardware include identical segments – unlike a hash.

Are you guys mapping UID's to different attributes? In past've seen this in OS X / MacOS it's because we mapped UID's to universal ID internally (it same across UNIX and AD) and it barfed when trying to translation. Users lost permissions to home directories showed symptoms're seeing in Finder, etc. In Directory Utility can see "Map UID to attribute:" in Mappings tab under Active Directory.

finally 10. 10 provides correct "launchctl bsexec" implementation can use: sudo /bin/launchctl bsexec PID chroot -u UID -g GID / open /Applications/TextWrangler. app man says This executes given command in similar execution context possible to target PID. as PID param use pid of appropriate loginwindow process. UID is user id of user owns loginwindow and GID is it's primary group. works fine for any command and for launchd jobs (f. e. launchagents) at last like: /bin/launchctl bsexec 104 chroot -u 501 -g 20 / /bin/launchctl load -S Aqua /Library/LaunchAgents/com. youragent. plist 2>&1

Diffie-Hellman used in SSL/TLS, as "ephemeral Diffie-Hellman" (the cipher suites with "DHE" in name; see standard). rarely encountered is "static Diffie-Hellman" (cipher suites with "DH" in name, but neither "DHE" or "DH_anon"): these cipher suites require server owns a certificate with DH public key in, rarely supported for a historical and economical reasons, main one is availability of free standard for RSA (PKCS#1) while corresponding standard for Diffie-Hellman (x9. 42) costs a hundred bucks, not much, but sufficient to deter most amateur developers. Diffie-Hellman is a key agreement protocol, if two parties (say, SSL client and SSL server) run this protocol, they end up with shared secret K., neither client or server gets to choose value of K; from their points of, K looks randomly generated. It is secret (only them know K; eavesdroppers on line do not) and shared (they both get same value K), but not chosen. This is not encryption. shared secret K is good enough, to process terabytes of data with symmetric encryption algorithm (same K to encrypt on one side and decrypt on other), that is what happens in SSL. There well-known asymmetric encryption algorithm called RSA,. With RSA, sender can encrypt message M with recipient's public key, and recipient can decrypt it and recover M using his private key. This time, sender can choose contents of M. question might be: in an RSA world, why do we bother with AES at? answer lies in points: constraints on M. If recipient's public key has size n (in bytes,. n = 256 for a 2048-bit RSA key), maximum size of M is n-11 bytes.to encrypt longer message, we have to split it into small blocks, include reassembly mechanism. Nobody knows how to do that securely. good reasons to believe RSA on single message is safe, but subtle weaknesses can lurk in any split-and-reassemble system we not comfortable with that. It already bad enough with symmetric ciphers, where mathematical situation is simpler, Even if we could handle splitting-and-reassembly, there would be size expansion. With 2048-bit RSA key, internal message chunk has size of at most 245 bytes, but when encrypted, it yields to be a 256-byte sequence. This wastes life energy, i. e. network bandwidth. Symmetric encryption incurs only bounded overhead (well, SSL adds slight overhead proportional to data size, but much smaller than with RSA-only protocol), Compared to AES, RSA is slow as hell, We like to option of using key agreement protocols like DH instead of RSA. In older times (before 2001), RSA was patented but DH was not, so US government was recommending DH. Nowadays, we want to be able to switch algorithms in case one becomes broken. In to support key agreement protocols, need symmetric encryption, may use it with RSA. It simplifies implementation and protocol analysis. See this answer for detailed description of how SSL works.

answers seem be all over the place (yes, no, might be, should be), reiterate @waiwai933's answer: it is secure. To specific, you asked: "If malicious user sniffed all my incoming and outgoing packets. Can he calculate same keys and read my encrypted traffic too or send encrypted messages to server in my name?" answer is no and no. With footnote. reason he cannot calculate same keys seems paradoxical, in was major break-through in cryptography when first published by Diffie and Hellman. TLS uses key exchange protocol, like Diffie-Hellman but more sophisticated to protect from man-in-the-middle attacks. protocol lets two people never exchanged information before compute a secret key no one seeing all messages can compute. Once shared secret key, you can use it to encrypt your traffic. malicious user doesn't know key, he can't encrypt traffic that looks like it came from you. footnotes. assuming SSL/TLS protocol is correct. With most involved cryptographic protocols, bugs are found and fixed from time-to-time. SSL/TLS have a recent bug (mentioned in few answers as reason it is not secure), it has been temporarily worked around and now fixed (RFC 5746) and fix is in various stages of deployment. (In your scenario, bug allowed malicious user to send packets in your name but not read your traffic. ) always possible attacker knows how to break TLS/SSL due to unpublished error in protocol. obvious point worth repeating: malicious user could see your request and send his own response using his own certificate. do check the certificate. another obvious point: can only be sure SSL/TLS will be used for future pages if current page is HTTPS.For example, if you are on an HTTP page wants you to log-in, from past experience know clicking log-in button will redirect you to HTTPS connection, this functionality could be stripped out by active malicious user on your network. So only log into pages already HTTPS (unless if you know how to detect if log-in page modified).

TLS does not require TCP, it only requires a reliable transport. even standard for TLS over SCTP is another reliable transport protocol. But, if take today's internet usually only have UDP and TCP as transport protocols on top of IP and from these two TCP is only reliable one. means, if only this limited selection of transport protocols available TLS requires TCP because it does not work with UDP. To work with UDP similar protocol DTLS designed to work over unreliable transports.

TLS requires reliable transport. On internet, this leaves only TCP, as UDP does not offer reliability. TLS require reliable transport because (in compliance with layered architecture ISO/OSI reference model) it does not handle transport errors, lost packets or other disturbances occur with IP. TLS designed to offer secure channel on top of reliable transport it does this well. DTLS does (I assume) necessary error handling within protocol. If TLS performed over UDP, connections and handshakes could fail because packet got lost in transit no one noticed. Mitigation of such problems is (according to ISO/OSI reference model) designated task of reliable transport. Any reliable transport works theoretically, yet for all practical purposes of IP networks, usually implies TCP.

Connecting to port 389 isn't wrong. It's actually "standards compliant". See RFC 4511 4. 14 StartTLS Operation. From Wikipedia page: "Servers often support non-standard "LDAPS" ("Secure LDAP", commonly known as "LDAP over SSL") protocol on separate port, by default 636. LDAPS differs from LDAP in two ways: 1) upon connect, client and server establish TLS before LDAP messages are transferred (without StartTLS operation) and 2) LDAPS connection must be closed upon TLS closure. LDAPS was used with LDAPv2, because StartTLS operation had not yet defined. use of LDAPS is deprecated, modern software should only use StartTLS. " iOS 6 account setup sends starttls extended request on port 389 to indicated server. Upon success response client (iOS in case) initiates tls handshake and if completes regular bind, etc. proceeds after that., server must be able to handle both tls and non-tls connections on port 389. Setup on various servers left as exercise to readers ;-), iOS 5 and below used LDAPS connection to port 686 but iOS 6 is now "modern software"., think startTLS operation is superfluous. Why bother announcing to world over open channel what you to doing inside secure connection?

Yes. Follow this guide or any other after getting song from ~/Music/iTunes/iTunes Music. Select and edit a song first thing need to choose a song in iTunes to use as a ringtone. Open up iTunes on your Mac or PC click on My Music tab. Choose a song on your hard drive then right click on it, choose Get Info, then click Options tab. Within main panel see settings for Start and Stop. A ringtone can only be thirty seconds long, use these settings to isolate part of song you want then click OK. You won't be deleting anything on actual track itself, don't worry. highlight the song, go up to File at top of screen select Create New Version>Create AAC version. iTunes will duplicate track, but look closely see new version is only thirty seconds long. That's one we'll use for our ringtone. Remember to go back to original track now untick Start and Stop options, otherwise track will only play that short section. Change file type Highlight short version of song, right click and select Show in Finder. Now'll see two versions of song. duplicate should have a 1 at end of name to differentiate it, of file size will be smaller. To use it as a ringtone need to convert file type from. m4a to. m4r, involves clicking on name once to highlight it, then once again to edit name can change last three letters. Finder will ask if sure you want to use new file type? Choose 'Use. m4r' in pop up box to confirm. Leave Finder window open for now, we'll use it again in a moment. Delete the shorter track Return to iTunes and delete the short version of track, remembering to check length carefully before do so. When prompted choose Keep File, as we want to remove track from our music library but not our computer entirely.Import track to iTunes as a ringtone Go back to Finder window double click shorter file. disconcertingly it will disappear from box, but start playing in background. Don't worry, it isn't really gone. Return to iTunes, go to row of icons in top left corner click on three dots. This brings up more options, one of is Tones. Click this and'll see short version of song is now a ringtone. Sync ringtone with your iPhone Connect iPhone to iTunes click on little phone icon to right of three dots. This will bring up iTunes panel for your phone, from want to select Tones in left hand column. Once inside click Sync Tones>Selected tones>then the track you've created. Finally go to bottom right hand corner and click Apply. Set new ringtone All remains to be done now is to go to Settings on iPhone, then Sounds, and'll find new ringtone at top of list. Tap on it to select it as your general tone.

best chance of recovering deleted files if you scan your Mac immediately after realizing deleted files you need. otherwise your files are gone. in your case, unix(Darwin in yourcase) filesystem has already written over significant portions of those files. http://www. faqs. org/faqs/unix-faq/faq/part3/section-6. html "For intents purposes, when you delete a file with "rm" it is gone. Once you "rm" a file, system forgets which blocks scattered around disk were part of your file. worse, blocks from file you just deleted are to be first ones taken and scribbled upon when system needs more disk space. However, never say never. theoretically possible if shut down system immediately after "rm" to recover portions of data. However, had better have very wizardly type person at hand with hours or days to spare to get it all back. " in this case, finder trashing equals "rm" How To Recover Accidentally Deleted Files: If attempting to recover files from Trash, note following: If've emptied Trash or deleted files with rm (remove) command, your files and data is recoverable IF you STOP using Mac right now. This particularly true if currently running low on disk space. Mac OS X overwrites this free space quickly with temp files. Next, can try to recover deleted Trash files on Mac using good recovery program. best 2 are Data Rescue 3 and Stellar Mac Data Recovery - (free download). for doing with this app follow this tutorial.

Although this Question solved few years old, want to mention testdisk utility. to recover files with testdisk explained well in this tutorial. To recover files run testdisk /dev/sdX select your partition table type. After, select [ Advanced ] Filesystem Utils, then choose your partition select [Undelete]. Now can browse and select deleted files copy them to another location in filesystem.

OS X maintains deleted files in local time machine storage area if you enabled (or system enabled) local store. tmutil snapshot If you can make a snapshot, you can enter Time Machine and recover these files. If get error like **Local snapshots not enabled. ** then you don't have ability to recover files from OS level. no other undelete mechanism in filesystem, you have good survey of recovery tools (I use Data Rescue exclusively) only third option to locate a viable backup of system or files in question. I make habit of enabling local store and forcing a snapshot before doing anything as root or anything I might regret from terminal. Having made mistakes like this over years, I've learned to have "premonition" to check backup and double check syntax. In, I try to make a list of files to delete and save it to a file have pause and second script does removal rather than piping them together. It's not going to help, but it's my experience and way to mitigate when can't ensure good backup. sudo tmutil enablelocal sleep 8 && tmutil snapshot

Unfortunately no way to recover from that, aside from restoring from backup. Command line utilities don't have undo command (and don't typically delete to Trash). lost+found wouldn't help either, since only used when filesystem recovery utility has found filesystem corruption.

Assuming files are gone two potential solutions I can think of, neither of necessarily rely on Terminal (which allow to see invisible files, but not deleted files). first of requires using Time Machine. If Time Machine connected to your backup drive yesterday after imported files, it would create new backup every hour including any files new to system since previous backup. Simply open Time Machine, navigate to folder where your files were previously, and go back to time when they were still there. Highlight file(s) click Recover button. second solution requires third party software. When files are "deleted" they usually only removed from "catalog" or "index" of file system. This means according to index space where file X used to take up is now empty and available to be overwritten at any point in future when it needs to save new files. Data recovery software ignores this index and scans actual blocks of space on drive to see if any data there. I don't endorse any data recovery software in particular however, as been years since I've used any. Searching web will find various titles, both commercial and open source,'ll likely need external HDD to recover found files onto. Best of luck.

null byte is byte with value zero, i. e. 0x00 in hex. security vulnerabilities related to null bytes. occur because C uses null bytes as string terminator. Other languages (Java, PHP, etc. ) don't have string terminator; they store length of every string separately., consider a Java web application accepts file uploads. Perhaps want to let users upload. jpg files, nothing else., if user can upload a. jsp file, this be a serious security vulnerability. hacker might try is to upload hack. jsp<NUL>. jpg. think about how this will be processed. First, Java will look at file name, see it ends in. jpg allow upload. It then calls operating system library, written in C. C sees <NUL> character as string terminator, saves file as hack. jsp. Many languages fix this by explicitly disallowing <NUL> bytes in file names. know Python and PHP do this., if your language does not do this for you, you must do it yourself. More information - OWASP: Null-Byte Injection don't know how exactly "serialised instances" related to this, but gives some idea what's going on.

general answer is Java's pattern of memory usage differs from other apps as it uses garbage collection in fixed size memory thus getting all memory it might use up front rather than getting it when needed. start is JVM allocating memory, then its garbage collection tends to access memory often or else you allocated large Java dataset only accessing part of it. 11G of memory is accessed but not often enough to be marked as active. A C based program won't have background thread looking at all pages of memory so pages can be inactive long enough to be swapped out. From experience on other OSs Java slows down if memory is swapped and you adjust size of VM so it does not. If need more memory then get more RAM or alter algorithm to use less.

why Java can be slower:- JVM needs to interpret pseudo machine code, C++ blindly executes native machine code. JVM manages memory, C++ its up to programmer to manage memory more efficient but more error prone. JVM needs to start up, then load and interpret various classes; with C++ program load is basically copying instructions from disk to memory, in many cases (with DLL,., shared libraries etc. ) program will already been loaded and sitting in memory ready to go. This is biggest performance hit with Java makes language unsuitable for short running independent executions. While java may be up to three times slower it often almost as fast as C++. to ask if this matters when running on a 3ghz processor spending most of time waiting for memory to be loaded (or worse disk IO). other side of equation (highly subjective, but, backed by years of experience) is Java programs can be developed up to three times faster. toolsets are more functional, vast selection of good libraries to choose from, limited number of gotchas to look out for (no if (a = b), no mixing up pointers with pointed to). Personally where I feel need for speed I code in plain C. Its language I know well performance constrained parts of system tend to be small and well defined. its C for speed. Java for production code. Groovy or Python for everything else!

core of many important languages written in C, but things changing: reference implementation of Python (CPython) is written in C (but other implementations written in other languages, e. g. Jython / Java, PyPy / Python, IronPython / C#. ) PHP Zend Engine written in C first Java compiler developed by Sun Microsystems was written in C, but now class libraries always written in Java (since intended to be run using Java VM). Certain libraries using JNI (Java Native Interface) may be partially written in variety of other languages, intended to used OUTSIDE JVM. Sun/Oracle VM written in C++. BEA/Weblogic/Oracle VM written in C. But JVM written in Java, Lisp, SmallTalk (IBM). Perl implemented as core interpreter, written in C, together with large collection of modules, written in Perl and C (but Pugs, a compiler and interpreter for Perl 6 programming language, written in Haskell) official Ruby interpreter, referred to as Matz's Ruby Interpreter or MRI, written in C uses its own Ruby-specific virtual machine (but JRuby, a Java implementation runs on Java virtual machine; Rubinius, a C++ bytecode virtual machine uses LLVM to compile to machine code at runtime. ) about 50% of R written in C and, of, C is (was) written in C! (but first C compiler, targeted to PDP-11, was a mix of B and assembler). many reasons why C often chosen: performance, portability, experience. last most important: Python started in 1991, PHP in 1994/1995, Perl in 1988, Ruby in 1995. standard is 100m (~333. 33 ft; 1m = 3 1/3 ft) before attenuation makes signal unusable, but direct answer to question is yes, long cable can slow your connection. Attenuation is caused by internal resistance of copper humans perceive as lag/slow down of network connectivity. If cable is under 100m, slow down is relatively unnoticeable. It can cause issues if close to 100m mark though. keep in mind 100m length is measured from point cable plugs into port on computer to point it plugs into device that regenerates signal, like a switch or router. For all practical purposes, no effect on speed of your connection. insignificant amount of delay due to long cables. This won't affect maximum speed of your connection, but would cause some latency. pjc50 points out it's about a nanosecond for every foot of cable length, a good rule of thumb used by many engineers when developing systems dependent on latencies on timescales. In reality, you will never notice a difference. "fast" ping time on Internet is 10 ms, which is 10, 000, 000 ns. Adding even a few hundred feet of cable isn't to have noticeable effect at point. In fact, nearly every step of way involves delays more extreme than those seen from signal propagation. For example, most consumer grade routers will wait for last byte of incoming packet to be received and check it for errors before sending first byte of packet on way. This delay will be on order of 5, 000 ns! maximum length of cable can run (per Ethernet spec) is 300 ft, cable length could never cause more than 300 ns of delay due to cable!

terminal is at end of electric wire, shell is home of turtle, tty is strange abbreviation and console is kind of cabinet., etymologically speaking, anyway. In unix terminology, short answer is terminal = tty = text input/output environment console = physical terminal shell = command line interpreter Console, terminal and tty are closely related. Originally, they meant piece of equipment through which interact with computer: in early days of unix, meant teleprinter-style device resembling typewriter, sometimes called teletypewriter, or “tty” in shorthand. name “terminal” came from electronic point of view, and name “console” from furniture point of view. early in unix history, electronic keyboards and displays became norm for terminals. In unix terminology, tty is particular kind of device file implements number of additional commands (ioctls) beyond read and write. In most common meaning, terminal is synonymous with tty. Some ttys provided by kernel on behalf of hardware device, for example with input from keyboard and output to text mode screen, or with input and output transmitted over serial line. Other ttys, sometimes called pseudo-ttys, are provided (through thin kernel layer) by programs called terminal emulators, such as Xterm (running in X Window System), Screen (which provides layer of isolation between program and another terminal), Ssh (which connects terminal on one machine with programs on another machine), Expect (for scripting terminal interactions), etc. word terminal can also have more traditional meaning of device through which one interacts with computer, typically with keyboard and display. For example X terminal is kind of thin client, special-purpose computer only purpose is to drive keyboard, display, mouse and occasionally other human interaction peripherals, with actual applications running on another, more powerful computer. console is generally a terminal in physical sense is by some definition primary terminal directly connected to machine.console appears to operating system as a (kernel-implemented) tty. On some systems, Linux and FreeBSD, console appears as several ttys (special key combinations switch between these ttys); to confuse, name given to each tty can be “console”, ”virtual console”, ”virtual terminal”, and other variations. See also Why is a Virtual Terminal “virtual”, and what/why/where is the “real” Terminal?. shell is primary interface users see when log in, primary purpose is to start other programs. (I don't know whether original metaphor is shell is home environment for user, or shell is what other programs running in. In unix circles, shell specialized to mean command-line shell, centered around entering name of application wants to start, followed by names of files or other objects application should act on, pressing Enter key. Other types of environments don't use word “shell”; for, window systems involve “window managers” and “desktop environments”, not a “shell”. many different unix shells. Popular shells for interactive use include Bash default on most Linux installations, zsh power and customizability) and fish simplicity). Command-line shells include flow control constructs to combine commands. In addition to typing commands at interactive prompt, users can write scripts. most common shells have common syntax based on Bourne_shell. When discussing “shell programming”, shell is almost always implied to be a Bourne-style shell. Some shells often used for scripting but lack advanced interactive features include Korn shell (ksh) and many ash variants. any Unix-like system has a Bourne-style shell installed as /bin/sh, usually ash, ksh or bash. In unix system administration, user's shell is program invoked when they log in.Normal user accounts have a command-line shell, but users with restricted access may have restricted shell or other specific command (e. g. for file-transfer-only accounts). division of labor between terminal and shell not obvious. their main tasks. Input: terminal converts keys into control sequences (e. g. Left → \e[D). shell converts control sequences into commands (e. g. \e[D → backward-char). Line editing, input history and completion are provided by shell. terminal may provide its own line editing, history and completion instead, only send a line to shell when ready to be executed. only common terminal operates in this way is M-x shell in Emacs. Output: shell emits instructions as “display foo”, “switch foreground color to green”, “move cursor to next line”,. terminal acts on these instructions. prompt is purely a shell concept. shell never sees output of commands it runs (unless redirected). Output history (scrollback) is purely a terminal concept. Inter-application copy-paste provided by terminal (usually with mouse or key sequences Ctrl+Shift+V or Shift+Insert). shell may have its own internal copy-paste mechanism (e. Meta+W and Ctrl+Y). Job control (launching programs in background and managing them) mostly performed by shell., it terminal handles key combinations like Ctrl+C to kill foreground job and Ctrl+Z to suspend it.

Let me take a crack at this. I will use Unix and Linux more or less synonymously in. If I referring to something historical predates existence Linux, I will usually write "Unix", and if talking about something more recent, or something specific to Linux flavor of Unix, I will usually write "Linux". Shell only thing in your list a discrete concept no overlap with others is the 'shell'. The shell is a program's purpose is to communicate with a user and carry out operating system operations on their behalf. common shells use a technique called a 'command line' of sending user prompt, waiting for user to type out text command, then carrying out command. But there are menu based shells, and even graphical shells (like Windows File Explorer) no self-respecting Unix person would call such a thing a 'shell'. In Unix, if someone calls something a 'shell' they almost certainly mean form of command line interface as described. odd in Unix world to refer to anything as a 'shell' if it isn't communicating to user using the tty model I describe further on. TTY This is a confusing one because it can refer to a few different kinds of things. In Linux, there is a device called a 'tty'. It is an abstract device expected to be used for bi-directional communication with something either user, or taking input from user in. Sometimes abstract device may correspond directly to physical device. Sometimes it may be a program presenting someone with a window in communication appears and into user can type. But, reason this abstract device exists and reason it is called a 'tty' is that 'tty' is short for 'teletype', was an actual physical device that had a printer printed on paper combined with a keyboard. model abstract 'tty' device presents to programs using it is there is a teletype on the other end. You send it characters and those characters appear on the teletype.When you read characters from it, those characters represent keys typed on a keyboard. old paper-printer based ttys quickly supplanted with video ttys. On those, of, no roll of paper., in, it possible overwrite any character on screen. But, rather than present of abstract 'screen' interface to programs, programs instead expected to send special streams of characters called escape sequences accomplish a variety of tasks. Usually abstract thing called a 'cursor' can be moved around screen, any character sent will replace whatever is at cursor and cursor will move one character further on. Often you can change color of character's about to be printed with escape sequences as. 'glass ttys' do not follow this model handled poorly in Unix world. IBM 3270 family of video terminals fall into this category. What Linux/Unix people typically call a 'shell window' is emulation of a glass tty using graphical user interface. Internally, programs running inside of shell window are talking to a virtual tty device sometimes called a pseudo-tty or pseudo-terminal (aka a pty). Terminal A terminal is just a place where computer and human supposed to interface. Terminals may be completely graphical and not follow tty model in way, even though program may use their capabilities to emulate this. All actual physical ttys (glass or otherwise) are terminals. Console A console is a special kind of terminal generally supposed to be attached in direct secure way to hardware operating system is running on. In Linux, console is virtualized in small way allows to use special keystroke to switch between virtual consoles. But this virtualization is done with real piece of hardware by software in kernel.ways to use Linux through a 'serial console' is a console's attached to computer through a serial port like a USB port (or, on some very small and/or old computers, an RS-232 port of kind) and follows old teletype model in a fairly strict way., idea is this console is connected in a direct physical way to computer instead of through some of network that might allow anybody to connect.

Setting ibase means need set obase in same base. examples show this: echo "ibase=F;obase=A;C0" | bc set bc to consider input numbers represented in base 15 with "ibase=F". "obase=A" sets output numbers to base 10, default. bc reads C0 as base 15 number: C = 12. 12*15 = 180. echo "ibase=F;obase=10;C0" | bc, set input to base 15, and output to 10 - in base 15, so output base is 15. C0 input in base 15 is C0 output in base 15. echo "ibase=16;obase=A;C0" | bc Set input to base 16, output to base 10 (A in base 16 is 10 in base 10). C0 converted to base 10 is: 12*16 = 192 personal rule is to set obase first, use base 10. Then set ibase, also using base 10. bc ironic exception: ibase=A and obase=A always sets input and output to base 10. From bc man page: Single digit numbers always have value of digit regardless of value of ibase. behavior enshrined in specification of bc: From 2004 OpenGroup bc specification: When either ibase or obase assigned a single digit value from list in 'Lexical Conventions in bc', value assumed in hexadecimal. (For example, ibase=A sets to base ten, regardless of current ibase value. ) Otherwise, behavior is undefined when digits greater than or equal to value of ibase appear in input. ibase=F setting changed input base to base 15, recommended to always set base using base 10. Avoid confusing.

iBGP isn't used for internal routing, it is used by all eBGP routers to share routes. Ex: If you peering with 3 other network, you want all eBGP routers to know routes received by other ones so they can propagate information to peers if necessary/needed (opening possibility of peer using transit through you)

using iBGP, router must have full mesh, or must use a mitigation. Route reflectors are one mitigation. another mitigation similar to you suggest, called confederations. It breaks your AS in sub-ASes uses eBGP between sub-ASes. can search for BGP confederations, find documents, such as IP Routing: BGP Configuration Guide: BGP Routing Domain Confederation One way to reduce internal BGP (iBGP) mesh is to divide autonomous system into multiple subautonomous systems and group them into single confederation. To outside world, confederation looks like a single autonomous system. Each autonomous system is fully meshed within itself has few connections to other autonomous systems in same confederation. Even though peers in different autonomous systems have external BGP (eBGP) sessions, they exchange routing information as if they were iBGP peers. Specifically, next hop, Multi Exit Discriminator (MED) attribute, and local preference information are preserved. This feature allows to retain single Interior Gateway Protocol (IGP) for all autonomous systems. To configure BGP confederation, must specify confederation identifier. To outside world, group of autonomous systems will look like single autonomous system with confederation identifier as autonomous system number. Route reflectors are simpler to configure, easy to screw up confederation design and configurations. If large AS, buying many AS numbers can be problematic, confederations can internally use private AS numbers because do not advertise them outside your AS. Some people like router reflectors, and some people like confederations. Having multiple, real ASes isn't practical.

numbers interpreted by GNU bc as current input base in effect for statement number appears in. When use a digit outside current input interpret them as highest digit available in base (9 in decimal) when part of a multiple digit number, or as their normal values when used as a single digit number (A == 10 in decimal). From GNU bc manual: Single digit numbers always have value of the digit regardless of value of ibase. (i. e. A = 10. ) For multi-digit numbers, bc changes all input digits greater or equal to ibase to value of ibase-1. This makes number FFF always be the largest 3 digit number of input base., aware POSIX standard only defines this behavior for assignments to ibase and obase, not in any other context. From SUS specification on bc: When either ibase or obase is assigned a single digit value from list in Lexical Conventions in bc, value be assumed in hexadecimal. (For example, ibase=A sets to base ten, regardless of current ibase value. ) Otherwise, behavior is undefined when digits greater than or equal to value of ibase appear in input. Both ibase and obase have initial values of 10. key factor missing is that F is not in fact sixteen, but is actually fifteen, setting ibase=F setting input base to fifteen., to portably set ibase to hexadecimal from unknown state, need to use two statements: ibase=A; ibase=16., in beginning of program can rely on it being decimal and simply use ibase=16.

you want to say is: $ echo "ibase=16; C0" | bc 192 for hex-to-decimal, and: $ echo "obase=16; 192" | bc C0 for decimal-to-hex. don't need to give both ibase and obase for any conversion involving decimal numbers, since these settings default to 10. need to give both for conversions as binary-to-hex. In, easiest to make sense if give obase first: $ echo "obase=16; ibase=2; 11000000" | bc C0 If give ibase first instead, it changes interpretation of following obase setting, command has to be: $ echo "ibase=2; obase=10000; 11000000" | bc C0 This because in this order, obase value is interpreted as a binary number, need to give 100002=16 to get output in hex. That's clumsy. let’s work out why your three examples behave as they do. echo "ibase=F;obase=A;C0" | bc 180 sets input base to 15 and output base to 10, since single-digit value is interpreted in hex, according to POSIX. This asks bc to tell you what C015 is in base A15=10, it correctly answering 18010, not the question you meant to ask. echo "ibase=F;obase=10;C0" | bc C0 This is null conversion in base 15. Why?, because single F digit is interpreted in hex, pointed out in previous example. now set it to base 15, following output base setting is interpreted that way, and 1015=15, have null conversion from C015 to C015., output isn't in hex as assuming, it's in base 15! can prove this to by trying to convert F0 instead of C0.no F digit in base 15, bc clamps it to E0, gives E0 as output. echo "ibase=16; obase=A; C0" 192 This only one of your three examples likely has any practical use. It is changing input base to hex first, so no longer need to dig into POSIX spec to understand why A is interpreted as hex, 10 in this case. only problem with it is redundant to set output base to A16=10, since that's its default value.
