Someone might encourage developer to push malicious code. For paranoid, these issues could be mitigated by: Only logging in to sensitive sites (ie banking) using Incognito mode (where extensions are disabled by default). Disabling automatic extension updates, but you lose lot of convenience. it intellectually dishonest to say, "no, there is no risk, " risk is overblown by GMX. Just as I trust Google to give browser that does not steal my personal data, I trust AdBlock developer to give me extension that does not steal my data. risk of extension being updated with malicious code is small enough I don't worry about it, if slightest concern,'s easy enough to disable the extension.

tcp6 means TCP protocol over IP v6. tcp6 0 0 dmz. local. net:www 5. 140. 235. 6%14631:49964 ESTABLISHED 21393/apache2 from netstat manual: tcp6: protocol used. Here it is TCP over IPv6 0: count of bytes not copied by user program connected to this socket. 0: count of bytes not acknowledged by remote host. Local Address dmz. local. net:www: Address and port number of local end of socket. Unless (-n) option specified, socket address is resolved to canonical host name (FQDN), port number translated into corresponding service name. 5. 140. 235. 6%14631:49964: Address and port number of remote end of socket. ESTABLISHED: state of socket. state ESTABLISHED means socket has established connection. 21393/apache2: Slash-separated pair of process id (PID) and process name of process that owns socket. your local apache2 process (pid= 21393), listening on standard www port (80) has established TCP (over IPv6) connection with remote host 5. 140. 235. 6%14631 on port 49964 (unresolved IPv6 address is link-local IPv6 address: address computer assigns itself to facilitate local communications). For more about IPv6: wikipedia IPv6 address notation this superuser thread about % in IPv6, Scope ID.

Is TCP more secure than UDP? Yes, but we to be clear about what we are talking about talking about "security" not generalize this statement to upper layer protocols. Currently, security is often associated to CIA triad: Confidentiality. Integrity. Availability. version 4 of IP protocol, still most commonly used now, is a very old beast developed during 70's and 80's. At that time, confidentiality was not really a subject targeted was to achieve integrity and availability (the Arpanet network, ancestor of Internet gave birth to IP protocol, designed to ensure continuity of service even in of nuclear war, not to protect in-transit data). In this optic, two transport protocols developed over IP layer: TCP and UDP. TCP was one designed to ensure both integrity and availability properties. It includes at advanced techniques as three-way handshake, parameters negotiation, various connection state handling, transparent packet reordering, acknowledgement windows and retry mechanisms. This brings good guaranties to sender that data it sent has received in complete an uncorrupted form (ie. no missing, altered or unordered parts). Remind this protocol was targeting was technical disaster, not malicious tampering of data in transit. Such issue out-of-scope at that time. UDP on contrary was designed to be a fast protocol. It has none of above mentioned feature, and therefore none of their overhead too. In, when sender sends some data using UDP, data received may be incomplete, unordered or not received at all: UDP protocol by does not provide any mechanism to prevent or detect this neither on sender or receiver sides. In, when focusing on data integrity and availability properties of security, TCP is indeed more secure than UDP. Is application protocol relying on TCP more secure than one relying on UDP? Certainly not.means people developing application protocol relying on UDP will have more work since they may to implement in application protocol workarounds for features missing in UDP protocol. They to take into account data sent may not be necessarily received, data received may not be in right order, etc. These all well-known problems. OpenVPN for, supports TCP mostly for compatibility with restrictive firewalls, runs by default runs best over UDP. Switching it to TCP is possible but not increase its security as difference between two transport layer protocol UDP and TCP is fully handled by OpenVPN. Switching it to TCP will only add TCP overhead to OpenVPN protocol, reducing its performance. Is TCP better than UDP? No, this is entirely an application protocol design choice. UDP is a more raw protocol. When used correctly and carefully it may achieve better performances than TCP at price of more difficult development and maintenance of application protocol. When application is not time sensitive, TCP imposes itself as natural choice no need to reinvent the wheel. When application is time sensitive, discussion must occur on which to choose knowing each will with drawback: potential performance penalty with TCP against more complex application with UDP. Most protocols are not time sensitive TCP is most widely used protocol., when you load a web page or receive email, no difference if you receive it 10 milliseconds sooner or later. Two classical examples of protocols using UDP, in to OpenVPN cited, are media streaming and DNS. With media streaming, you don't care if one video frame or few milliseconds of video or audio is missing, as long as video or audio is playing smoothly and synchronously. In case, you don't want to induce repetitive pauses because TCP detected missing packet and asked sender to resend content of last acknowledgement window.With DNS, requests and answers usually short you want name resolution process to fast as possible (note longer and less time-sensitive answers such as DNS zone transfers usually still occur on TCP). faster to resend name resolution request to DNS server on very few times request or answer gets lost than processing full-fledged three-way handshake for every request. What about confidentiality and malicious sniffing/tampering (and IPv6)? All cared about until now was, in spirit of old IPv4, balance between transmission speed and data integrity + availability. Now, if want to add confidentiality on top of this, we can do this but it will have to be done at application layer as, as stated before, IPv4 not concerned by confidentiality issues. modern, full-fledged implementation of security can be implemented at application layer rely on either TCP or UDP (or both) protocols without impact on application protocol security (see example of OpenVPN above). However, as stated in beginning, IPv4 comes from another computing age. got successor by name if IPv6, natively supports IPSec at IP layer, providing more modern security services below transport protocols such as UDP and TCP. This allows to delegate in-transit data encryption from application to network layer, allows both UDP and TCP to provide same security guaranties. However, in most scenarios UDP performance gain will counterbalanced by IPSec overhead, not sure advantage in using UDP instead TCP as long as IPv6 IPSec is being used.

This where PSH flag comes in. socket TCP makes available at session level can be written to by application with option of "pushing" data out immediately, rather than waiting for additional data to enter buffer. When this happens, PSH flag in outgoing TCP packet is set to 1 (on). Upon receiving a packet with PSH flag set, other side of connection knows to immediately forward segment up to application. summarize, TCP's push capability accomplishes two things: • sending application informs TCP that data should be sent immediately. • PSH flag in TCP header informs receiving host data should be pushed up to receiving application immediately. URG flag used to inform receiving station that certain data within segment is urgent and should be prioritized. If URG flag is set, receiving station evaluates urgent pointer, a 16-bit field in TCP header. This pointer indicates how much of data in segment, counting from first byte, is urgent.

They to take into account data sent may not be necessarily received, data received may not be in right order, etc. These all well-known problems. OpenVPN for, supports TCP mostly for compatibility with restrictive firewalls, runs by default runs best over UDP. Switching it to TCP is possible but not increase its security as difference between two transport layer protocol UDP and TCP is fully handled by OpenVPN. Switching it to TCP will only add TCP overhead to OpenVPN protocol, reducing its performance. Is TCP better than UDP? No, this is entirely an application protocol design choice. UDP is a more raw protocol. When used correctly and carefully it may achieve better performances than TCP at price of more difficult development and maintenance of application protocol. When application is not time sensitive, TCP imposes itself as natural choice no need to reinvent the wheel. When application is time sensitive, discussion must occur on which to choose knowing each will with drawback: potential performance penalty with TCP against more complex application with UDP. Most protocols are not time sensitive TCP is most widely used protocol., when you load a web page or receive email, no difference if you receive it 10 milliseconds sooner or later. Two classical examples of protocols using UDP, in to OpenVPN cited, are media streaming and DNS. With media streaming, you don't care if one video frame or few milliseconds of video or audio is missing, as long as video or audio is playing smoothly and synchronously. In case, you don't want to induce repetitive pauses because TCP detected missing packet and asked sender to resend content of last acknowledgement window.With DNS, requests and answers usually short you want name resolution process to fast as possible (note longer and less time-sensitive answers such as DNS zone transfers usually still occur on TCP). faster to resend name resolution request to DNS server on very few times request or answer gets lost than processing full-fledged three-way handshake for every request. What about confidentiality and malicious sniffing/tampering (and IPv6)? All cared about until now was, in spirit of old IPv4, balance between transmission speed and data integrity + availability. Now, if want to add confidentiality on top of this, we can do this but it will have to be done at application layer as, as stated before, IPv4 not concerned by confidentiality issues. modern, full-fledged implementation of security can be implemented at application layer rely on either TCP or UDP (or both) protocols without impact on application protocol security (see example of OpenVPN above). However, as stated in beginning, IPv4 comes from another computing age. got successor by name if IPv6, natively supports IPSec at IP layer, providing more modern security services below transport protocols such as UDP and TCP. This allows to delegate in-transit data encryption from application to network layer, allows both UDP and TCP to provide same security guaranties. However, in most scenarios UDP performance gain will counterbalanced by IPSec overhead, not sure advantage in using UDP instead TCP as long as IPv6 IPSec is being used.

When this happens, PSH flag in outgoing TCP packet is set to 1 (on). Upon receiving a packet with PSH flag set, other side of connection knows to immediately forward segment up to application. summarize, TCP's push capability accomplishes two things: • sending application informs TCP that data should be sent immediately. • PSH flag in TCP header informs receiving host data should be pushed up to receiving application immediately. In practice, TCP easier to police in a firewalled network: Traffic pertaining to externally vs internally established connections, client vs server roles, can be clearly distinguished handled by separate policy. Physical cores are number of, actual hardware components. Logical cores are number of physical cores times number of threads run on each core through hyperthreading. for example, my 4-core processor runs two threads per core, so I have 8 logical processors.

Hyperthreading technology allows single physical processor core to behave like two logical processors. single processor core can execute two independent threads simultaneously. Intel refers to physical processor as a socket. Hyperthreading makes Physical Processor to behave like two Physical Processors, called Logical Processor. why? hyperthreading not double performance system, it can increase performance by better utilizing idle resources leading to greater throughput for certain important workload types. application running on one logical processor of busy core can expect slightly more than half of throughput it obtains while running alone on non-hyperthreaded processor. As an OS designer I agree with result of measurements. amount bullshit produced elsewhere about subject matter is unbelievable. See number of logical cores as number parallel threads/processes can be executed by HW. achieved by duplicating e. g. registers and instruction pointers of CPU core. CPU core itself decides which thread (instruction pointer) to use. It will decide to use other thread as instruction of current thread not available in cache and need to be fetched from e. g. memory or L3 cache. This mechanism create 10%-30% potential improvement in instructions/seconds or CPU performance. If run single application with one thread, you not able to reap this benefit, but if run two high load applications on e. g. old HT Pentium, you will be able to reap benefits. same true of for applications, have more then one thread. My Linux system has 200 threads, some benefits dependent on actual load are always present. All remarks apply without virtualization. Virtualbox only limits number of threads can run in parallel for each virtual machine (VM), but host process scheduler will change logical processor(s) and physical processor(s), on which VM processes run dynamically. If run high load applications on VM, additional logical cores will give you same benefit of 10%-30%. load can be single multi-threaded application or set of different applications. On modern systems with VT-x or AMD-V no performance penalty for maxing out number of logical cores, since also no noticeable performance penalty for running more virtual machines at same time. Your limit is performance of your CPU chip, so can't render videos on 3 VMs at same time without slowing down each VM, because they to share same physical CPU. Your host system might become irresponsive, if you render a video on a VM with all logical cores present, but have almost same problem, if you run that rendering app on your host.least in VM you have a choice could solve it by limiting max CPU load to 80%-90% or reducing number of cores for this reason.

neither a stream cipher nor block cipher. Both use same key to encrypt and decrypt (symmetric encryption). RSA is asymmetric meaning you encrypt with different key than decrypt with. advantage is encryption key can be made public, people can only use it to encrypt no one can decrypt if you keep decryption key to yourself. Unlike) block and stream ciphers, RSA based directly on mathematics.

wikipedia definitions, both stream and block ciphers require symmetric keys. RSA has asymmetric key not one of these. If you drop symmetric key requirement (I don't see relevant for term "block" versus "stream") then it would be a block cipher.

RSA is a block cipher can use variable-length block sizes. it not symmetric not mean it can not be a block or stream cipher., it not intended to be used as a block cipher, it is nonetheless a block cipher. Confused yet? :) RSA typically meant to only encrypt small pieces of data, typically hashes and symmetric key used to encrypt majority of data., RSA encryption/decryption works on blocks of data, usually 64 or 128 bits at a time. size of blocks determined at run time. requisite data can often be en(de)crypted in single use, it often mistakenly assumed it not a block cipher because data is single block, than several. This does not change fact it indeed work in a block cipher manner.

Rsync can be slower than cp in some situations. For example when destination exists rsync doing expensive comparisons for each block, does not find equal blocks copies complete source file. Also when destination files don't exist, rsync not provide advantage above cp.
As long your device received info before block happened, then answer is yes.

, private key using on my machine was old one. key did not contain encryption information added to private key file if generate new one: -----BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY----- Proc-Type: 4, ENCRYPTED DEK-Info: AES-. To solve problem, I decrypted key with openssl: $ cd ~/. ssh $ cp id_rsa id_rsa. bck $ openssl rsa -in id_rsa -out id_rsa. then re-encrypted it: $ openssl rsa -in id_rsa -aes256 -out id_rsa $ chmod 0600 id_rsa, regenerate public key: $ ssh-keygen -y -f id_rsa > id_rsa. pub
Another interesting finding is if you copy & paste content of PEM file, you might have ending missing dash. remember to add final line as, -----END RSA PRIVATE KEY-----

I can not repair your battery, but try to provide with information to decide if battery is EOL. 3 conditions reported. Replace Soon: battery is functioning normally but holds less charge than when new. Replace Now: battery is functioning normally but holds significantly less charge than when new. can continue to use battery until you replace it without harming your computer. Service Battery: battery isn’t functioning normally, you may or may not notice change in its behavior or amount of charge it holds. Take computer in for service. can continue to use battery before it’s checked without harming computer. In About This Mac-- more info look for battery information as: Charge Information: Charge Remaining (mAh): 2147 (it shows at 40% remaining based on current consumption) Fully Charged: No Charging: No Full Charge Capacity (mAh): 4829 (this indicates age, or capacity of Battery)---> on new and healthy battery for my MBA should be in range of 7500 mAh, lost some over 2 Years of use. Health Information: Cycle Count: 480 (this is my battery on MBA 2012) Condition: Service Battery :( Battery Installed: Yes Amperage (mA): -1458 (this is current consumption) Voltage (mV): 7612 (this also a indicator of battery health in how well can it keep Voltage at load) circuit mounted on/in battery, not part of your computer but part of battery, reports battery information to your computer. information used to present with battery conditions. If circuit is faulty, you have to replace battery, even if battery self is still in good condition. no way to reset or repair circuit.

two reasons in favor of using import module rather than from module import function. First is namespace. Importing function into global namespace risks name collisions. Second't relevant to standard modules, but significant for you own modules, especially during development. It's option to reload() a module. Consider: from module import func. reload(module) # func still points to old code On other hand import module. reload(module) # module. func points to new code for speed. importing only function needed rather than import whole module (which contains more useless functions python will waste time importing them) Whether import a module or import function from a module, Python will parse whole module. Either way module is imported. "Importing a function" is nothing more than binding function to a name. In import module less work for interpreter than from module import func.

use from imports whenever improves readability. For example, prefer (semicolons to save space here): from collections import defaultdict from foomodule import FooBar, FooBaz from twisted. internet. protocol import Factory defaultdict(); FooBar(); FooBaz(); Factory() instead of import collections import foomodule import twisted. internet. protocol collections. defaultdict(); foomodule. FooBar(); foomodule. FooBaz() twisted. internet. protocol. Factory() latter harder to read (and write) contains redundant information., useful to know ahead of time what parts of module I'm using. prefer regular imports if using lots short names from module: import sys sys. argv; sys. stderr; sys. exit() Or if name generic doesn't make sense outside of namespace: import json json. loads(foo) from json import loads loads(foo) # potentially confusing

A python module is a package to encapsulate reusable code. Modules usually, not always, reside in a folder with a __init__. py file. Modules can contain functions also classes. Modules are imported using import keyword. Python put definitions in a file use them in script or interactive instance of interpreter. a file is called a module; definitions from module can be imported into other modules or main module. Learn more about Python modules at links: https://docs. python. org/2/tutorial/modules. html (Python 2) https://docs. python. org/3/tutorial/modules. html (Python 3) Classes, can be defined in your main application code or inside modules imported by application. Classes are code of Object Oriented Programming can contain properties and methods. Importing module doesn't waste anything; module is always fully imported (into sys. modules mapping), whether you use import sys or from sys import argv makes no odds. only difference between two statements is name is bound; import sys binds name sys to module (so sys -> sys. modules['sys']), from sys import argv binds different name, argv, pointing straight at attribute contained inside of module (so argv -> sys. modules['sys']. argv). rest of sys module is still there, whether you use anything else from module or not. no performance difference between two approaches., sys. argv has to look up two things; to look up sys in global namespace (finds module), then look up attribute argv., by using from sys import argv you can skip attribute lookup, since already have direct reference to attribute. But import statement still has to do that work, looks up same attribute when importing,'ll only need to use argv once. If had to use argv thousands of times in a loop, it could perhaps make a difference, but in this specific case does not., choice between one or the other should be based solely on coding style. In large module, I'd use import sys; code documentation matters, using sys. argv in large module makes it clearer what you referring to than just argv. If only place you use argv is in '__main__' block to call main() function, by use from sys import argv if feel happier about: if __name__ == '__main__': from sys import argv main(argv) I'd still use import sys there myself. All things being equal (and they are, exactly, in terms of performance and number of characters used to write it), that just easier on the eye for me.If importing something else altogether, perhaps performance comes into play. But only if use specific name in a module many times over, in a critical loop for example. creating local name (within function) to faster still: import somemodule def somefunction(): localname = somemodule. somefunctionorother while test: # huge, critical loop foo = localname(bar)

opinion using regular import improves readability. reviewing Python code I like seeing where given function or class comes from right where it is used. saves me from scrolling to top of module to get info. for long module names use as keyword give short aliases: import collections as col import foomodule as foo import twisted. internet. protocol as twip my_dict = col. defaultdict() foo. FooBar() twip_fac = twip. Factory() exception I always use from module import something notation when deal with __future__ module. can't do another way when want all strings to be unicode by default in Python 2, e. g. from __future__ import unicode_literals from __future__ import print_function

Devices in different subnets can communicate. purpose of a router. Routers route packets between different networks. Even if devices in different networks on same layer-2 broadcast domain, you need a router to let devices communicate at layer-3. because each host will compare destination layer-3 address and its own layer-3 address and mask to see if they on same network. If destination host is on different network, host will send packets in layer-2 frames to its configured gateway (router). host must assume destination network could be across world from its network, gateway is the host on network that knows how to forward packets toward destination network.

Communication between different subnets packet reach router or layer3 devices to process packet. If another networks directly connected forwards packets on basis of ARP table. If destination on another networks forwards packet to next hops on basis route entry Configured on network. layer2 device understand IP address. Only same subnets traffic handle by layer2 device, traffic forwarded based on mac-address table

A VLAN is Ethernet level concept, a subnet is IP level concept. VLAN splits Ethernet network into multiple logically seperate Ethernet networks. subnet defines which hosts host will try to communicate with directly verses which hosts need to go via a router. It also defines "network" and "broadcast" addresses. common practice to have 1:1 mapping between subnets and VLANs but possible to have multiple subnets on same VLAN. possible to use proxy arp to split a subnet between multiple VLANs or have two VLANs using same IP subnet for different purposes.

In many implementations IPv4 subnet and a VLAN closely correlated on 1:1 basis. A subnet, is a portion of IPv4 address space from may assign addresses to hosts. differentiated from a "prefix" a term in common parlance or a supernet, may be a larger portion of IP address space comprised of many subnets. reason for correlation is a single VLAN and single subnet both represent a single broadcast domain., these two tend to be overlaid in most implementations. described in earlier answers, a VLAN is a layer 2 entity. All hosts on given VLAN can communicate with each other, but no hosts on one VLAN can communicate to hosts on another without form routing or in rare cases, bridging.

no reason not to put multiple subnets on same VLAN, but also probably no reason to do it. Pro: Allows subnets to talk directly without router or firewall Save's VLANs Con: Allows subnets to talk directly without router or firewall It's messy from documentation and troubleshooting perspective More broadcast traffic We generally don't do it because of messiness and lack of security. One VLAN = one subnet is easier to document and easier to troubleshoot usually not good reason to complicate things. only reason of to do it is company mergers or network upgrades for both prefer it to be temporary. Edit to clarify, for hosts on different subnets same VLAN to talk directly need to either make them their own default gateway or add route to "other" subnet that connects it to interface. In gateway case if host IP was 10. 1. 1. 2 then gateway would also be 10. 1. 1. 2. This cause host to ARP for everything on or off it's subnet. allow it to talk to second subnet on VLAN but only way able to talk to anything else is if router/firewall running proxy arp can help it out. In route out interface case add something like "route add -net 192. 56. 76. 0 netmask 255. 255. 255. 0 eth0" to device then 10. 1. 1. 2 will ARP directly on eth0 when it wants to reach 192. 56. 76. *.

In other words, any cases for having a VLAN without Subnet, still have IP (L3) communication? These need to be in same L2 domain but not in same IP subnet, since IP is not required. In case may be practical to use VLANS without considering IP/Subnetting of.

informal way of looking at difference between VLANs and subnets, but not inaccurate (just incomplete). may help networking newcomers get closer to right mental picture. Two different VLANs on a single switch or host are like two physically separate switches. They partition MAC address space, in communications between two parties on single VLAN or on single physical switch don't involve other parties on MAC-level (layer 2) network. VLAN or physical switch limits extent MAC-level message propagation, keeping it as local as possible. In contrast, IP subnets exist at layer 3 and partition IP address space, not MAC address space, but with similar purpose: to limit extent of message propagation. Any partitioning at MAC-level layer 2 network below is transparent to layer 3, VLANs and/or separate physical switches can be treated as one single continuous layer 2 medium from point of IP-level networking. Conversely, switches and VLANs don't see IP addresses nor IP subnetting (with some minor provisos can complicate picture). Everything at layer 3 and higher is just payload to them at layer 2 MAC level. In summary: VLANs and subnets partition different layers of network model. no circumstance in they interchangeable terms.

In computing, a Job is a unit of work or unit of execution (that performs said work). A component of job unit of work) is called a task or a step (if sequential, as in a job stream). As unit of execution, a job may be identified with a single process, may have subprocesses (child processes; process corresponding to job parent process) perform tasks or steps comprise work of job; or with a process group; or with abstract reference to process or process group, as in Unix job control. process is any running program with its own address space. A job is a concept used by shell - any program you interactively start that doesn't detach (ie, not a daemon) is a job. If running interactive program, can press CtrlZ to suspend it. Then start it back in foreground (using fg) or in background (using bg). While program is suspended or running in background, can start another program - have two jobs running. can also start a program running in background by appending an "&" like this: program &. That program become a background job. To list all jobs running, use jobs. For more information on jobs, see this section of bash man page.

UNIX has separate concepts "process", "process group", "session". Each shell at login becomes leader of own new session and process group, sets controlling process group of terminal to itself. shell creates process group within current session for each "job" it launches, places each process starts into appropriate process group. For example, ls | head is a pipeline of two processes, shell considers a single job, belong to single, new process group. A process is a (collection of thread of execution and other context, address space file descriptor table. A process may start other processes; these new processes belong to same process group as parent unless other action is taken. Each process may also have a "controlling terminal", starts off same as parent. shell has concept of "foreground" jobs and "background" jobs. Foreground jobs are process groups with control of terminal, background jobs are process groups without control of terminal. Each terminal has a foreground process group. When bringing a job to foreground, shell sets it as terminal's foreground process group; when putting job to background, shell sets terminal's foreground process group to another process group or itself. Processes may read from and write to their controlling terminal if in foreground process group. Otherwise they receive SIGTTIN and SIGTTOU signals on attempts to read from and write to terminal. By default these signals suspend process, most shells mask SIGTTOU so background job can write to terminal uninterrupted.

standard way approaching these terms is an "application" is a specific, static program on storage. It's piece of code stored on a hard drive, CD-ROM or elsewhere. A "process" is a specific instance of a running program. it is registered by operating system as executing or able to execute whenever operating system feels like it. If take for example Calculator. app, it is a single application. you can have multiple Calculator processes if you start program multiple times. As chananelb wrote, also possible to have processes not "just" ordinary applications started up. could be for example kernel processes, or ordinary processes spawning up subprocesses to do specific tasks. Regarding services, chananelb's answer leads you in wrong direction. His answer tells you about what is called a "Service" in Mac OS X. but you asked about what a "Service" in Windows. counterpart to Windows Service is a Daemon on Mac OS X (and other Unix-derived systems). Daemons are normally categorized by running in "background",. without direct user interaction through graphical or non-graphical user interface. distinction is blurry though, as a Daemon might for example have a web interface for user interaction. Daemons on Mac OS X are controlled by launchd program, responsible for for example starting up daemons on boot, and letting user start and stop daemons at request.
Another point: ps - (Process Status) reports snapshot of current processes. top (Table Of Processes) - task manager program displays information about CPU memory utilization.

I was taught, clear difference between two. A software process model is abstract representation of process methodology. Waterfall1 is a process model. Iterative methodologies are process models. They don't specify how to do things, but outline types of things done and sequencing for things. For, Waterfall identifies phases project through - requirements, design, implementation/unit testing, integration testing, system testing, deployment - without saying what artifacts to produce or tools to use (although output of code is implied). Agile defines core values in Manifesto for Agile Software Development, time-boxed iterations, continuous response to change, but doesn't say how long iterations should be or how responding to change. Spiral model is a third software process model. software process methodology is a specific way of conducting software project. things like Rational Unified Process and Scrum. They define exactly what, when, and/or how various artifacts are produced. They might not be entirely explicit with - for, Scrum doesn't identify what documents to produce or not to produce, focus is on delivering value to customer - but they define, in, actions members of project team must deliver. However, in actuality, point is often moot. Many times, process methodologies are presented as frameworks tailor to needs of customer and development team, based on requirements and resources., organizations might deal with regulatory or legal guidelines that dictate certain aspects of what must be produced or how to performing certain tasks (especially related to verification and validation activities). frequently becomes more important to discuss each team or organization's process in terms of plan-driven versus agile or amount of formality and ceremony. in theory one can write BIOS in any language, modern reality is most BIOS is written using Assembly, C, or a combination of the two. BIOS must be written in a language that can compile to machine code, understood by physical hardware-machine. This eliminates directly or intermediate-ly interpreted languages (Perl, Python, PHP, Ruby, Java, C#, JavaScript, etc) as appropriate for writing BIOS. (Though, in theory, one could implement one of these languages to either compile directly to static machine code or embed the interpreter in BIOS., for-example, the abandonware GCJ project for Java. ) Most OEMs implement BIOS by extending proprietary, generic BIOS implementations by companies like American Megatrends and Phoenix Techologies. (You seen one those companies displayed on first boot screen computer before. ) source code for these implementations is not publicly available, but some of it has leaked. not want to link to directly to C and assembly source code, but places on Internet where this source code is discussed for those peek. Some hardware manufacturers, like targeting high-performance and gaming markets, saturate BIOS implementations with customization features, statistics, and attractive user interfaces designed for their exact implementations. Many these features go beyond in generic products produced by American Megatrends and others., these companies often see release of source code as a security risk, little is known about these high-end implementations because little is shared about them. One could find ways to access and de-compile such BIOS implementations but may be difficult and possibly illegal. back to original question, because of need to produce native machine code, a BIOS would have to be implemented in a programming language supported by a native machine code compiler. many such languages over last few decades, several languages used in experimentation, every open BIOS implementation to find specifically relies on combination of C and/or assembly.open-sourced BIOS implementations I looked at to form this conclusion include OpenBIOS, tinyBIOS, coreboot, Intel BIOS, and Libreboot. I also looked at old BIOS implementations not relevant today but also followed C and/or assembly rule. it's also relevant to look at other software built to interact directly with hardware. know, for example, Linux Kernel, OS X kernel, Windows kernel are largely C with some assembly and some higher level languages for specific tasks. know hardware drivers on Linux and hardware drivers on Windows are written largely in C. back to BIOS, important to consider economics of programming language chosen. BIOS is generally written as a necessity to complement hardware sales. Modern BIOS systems are known to be largely written in C and/or assembly. move to other tool would add significant costs to to commodity products could adversely affect sales. Without into Economics 101, can assure it's probably not worth it to an OEM to deviate from tried-and-true tools proven over decades. Of there are will be hobbyist projects to write BIOS as well. actual BIOS for a computer written in language (probably C or assembly) compiled to architecture dependent binary code; this code can't run on any other architecture (and arguably doesn't need to, it already very specific to machine with it shipped). possibly thinking about Option ROMs (which sometimes called BIOSes, as in "Video BIOS" for a GPU option ROM)? For actual, legacy BIOS compatible option ROMs, they probably be ISA dependent executable code (again generated by any language can be compiled to target desired architecture); PCI allows including code for multiple ISAs and allows host to select appropriate binary image during boot process. For UEFI compatible option ROMs, also architecture-independent byte code format can be run on different architectures, but ISA-dependent code can also still be used.

BIOSes used to be written exclusively in assembly language, but transition was made long time ago to write majority of code in higher level language, leave written in assembly few portions of as possible, preferably only bootstrapper, (the first few hundreds of instructions CPU jumps to after start / reset, ) and routines deal with specific quirks of underlying architecture. BIOSes were already written primarily in C as early as early nineties. (I wrote a BIOS in 90% C, 10% assembly in early nineties. ) helped in this direction is: C libraries that target specific architecture and include functions for dealing with peculiarities of that architecture, for example, functions for reading/writing bytes to/from I/O ports of x86 architecture. Microsoft C has always offered library functions for that kind of stuff. C compilers not only target specific CPU architecture but offer extensions to C language can use in to write code makes use of special CPU features. For example, x86 architecture supports known interrupts, invoke routines known as interrupt handlers, requires to special entry/exit instruction sequences. From early days, Microsoft C supported special keywords use to mark a function as an interrupt handler, so it could be invoked directly by CPU interrupt, did not have to write any assembly for it. Nowadays assume most of BIOS is written in C++, if not in any higher level language. vast majority of code makes up a BIOS is specific to underlying hardware, so it does not really need to be portable: it is guaranteed it will always run on same type of CPU. CPU may evolve, but as long as it maintains backwards compatibility with previous versions, it can still run the BIOS unmodified. Plus, you can always recompile parts of BIOS written in C to run natively on any new CPU up, if need arises.reason why we write BIOSes in languages higher level than assembly is because easier to write this way, not because they really need to be portable.

used to own an Apple ][. It had floating-point BASIC installed in upper 16kb of memory. "Booting" took maybe 1 second - flip switch -> Beep -> it's ready. If bought a disk drive, boot loader was in 256 byte (bytes, singles, no M or k) ROM on interface card. Apple DOS written onto every floppy disk took up about 10kb of RAM. trivia for project: Apple ]['s documentation included fold-out circuit diagram of computer's electronics. in case needed to repair it. documentation also included complete source code (6502 Assembler) of operating system. Maybe 30 pages. Assembler at time was 1:1 representation of machine code. wrote Apple (on paper - no internet back then) asking for Integer BASIC source code for comparison. They wrote back said would happy to send it, but don't have copy. Wozniak wrote Integer BASIC himself, compiled it with pencil and Motorola 6502 data sheet, typed in resulting hexadecimal opcodes by hand. All bow to Greatness of The Woz.

ssh provides a connected stream from local system running rsync to another instance running on remote server. local rsync starts it as part of ssh connection process - not the same instance of rsync might running as a daemon on remote server. What is an ssh stream? ssh stream is what you use when you ssh to a remote system. You might prefer to call it an ssh session. fine. As example, ssh snow@grumpy. example. net would connect you to remote system and give interactive session. Anything typed locally received and actioned remotely, anything generated remotely presented locally. Similarly, ssh -t snow@doc. example. net vi /etc/hosts would set up connection to run vi /etc/hosts on remote system as if you using it locally. (The -t flag tells ssh to ensure remote command, vi, is run on a pseudo-terminal; otherwise it would skip layer of complexity. ), for rsync, connection is set up by local instance with something like ssh snow@bashful. example. net rsync --server -nlogDtpre. iLsf {local_path} {remote_path}. This allows local rsync to talk with remote rsync over a connection just like you to access same remote server. remote instance of rsync knows it's a server because of flags provided when started by local instance. can see how rsync called remotely by running something like ssh snow@dopey. example. net 'ps -ef| grep [r]sync' while rsync is in progress. Why not just have rsync talk directly without ssh? advantage of using ssh is twofold It is a well known protocol and mechanisms for authentication and logging in to remote system are well understood (by) and trusted It provides secure and encrypted channel over sensitive data can be safely passed.Without this layer rsync either implement own encryption or ignore issue. Both are hazardous in today's Internet connected world.

It works well, but can be pain to setup. In testing, seen it run 2x-3x faster than rsync.

You didn't do wrong, but point with rsync is after initial backup/copy, subsequent rsync runs clever to only copy/backup stuff's changed. say you do your 300GB backup, then a week later want to backup again, if you've only made 5GB of changes on your disk, rsync will only try to edit/backup this 5GB, rather than to copy over full 300GB again. This is time saving you benefit from when using rsync, only get it when running regular backups of same disk. answer to your question is no, for one off copy operation, rsync and finder likely to be exactly the same -, may be finder is slightly faster. Rsync is for keeping/maintaining up-to-date backup of working disk, time savings are in long-run, not taking initial backup. To get benefits from rsync, you should take a copy of your rsync command, store it in way you can run it again in future (for example, might embed it in a batch/script file can run periodically in future). next time you run same backup, it might take 5 minutes, since's unlikely you have changed that much on your disk. for example, here's content of script file I use to keep up-to-date backup of my music folder on my mac - set to run every 24 hours: #!/bin/bash rsync -ariv /Users/myuser/Music /Volumes/data/media/myuser first time I ran this it took ages, but now, when I run it again, it just backs up what's changed in my Music folder, might take a minute or two. Meanwhile, I know I've got a 100% up-to-date copy of my music folder in my backup drive I can go to should my primary drive fail.

If want to preserve file attributes, symbolic links, recursive structure, rsync should suffice: rsync -a ~/somefolder /Volumes/SomeUSB/ -a (archive) flag is shortcut for following rsync options: --recursive recurse into directories --links copy symlinks as symlinks --perms preserve permissions --times preserve times --group sets group of destination file to same as source file --owner sets owner of destination file to same as source file (if copying to remote system, remote SSH user need to have superuser status for this) --devices rsync will transfer character and block device files to remote system.

Strictly speaking yes, you can always use rsync. From man rsync (emphasis mine): Rsync is a fast extraordinarily versatile file copying tool. It can copy locally, to/from another host over any remote shell, or to/from remote rsync daemon. offers large number of options control every aspect of its behavior permit flexible specification of set of files to be copied. famous for its delta-transfer algo‐ rithm, reduces amount data sent over network by sending only differences between source files and existing files in destina‐ tion. Rsync widely used for backups mirroring as improved copy command for everyday use. Now, sometimes not worth typing few extra characters just to use a tank to kill a fly., rsync often not installed by default so cp is nice to have.

add itemised "-i" or "--itemize-changes" option to command rsync will tell you why it transferring files. For each file you'll see strings looks like ">f. t. ". format of string is "YXcstpoguax". Y is direction of transfer. X is type of object being transferred (for example 'f'ile, 'd'irectory). rest of string documents changes. c for checksum s for size t for modification time p for permissions o for owner g for group u is currently reserved for future use a for ACL permissions x for extended attributes in example above it transferred file because modification time was different. This should help identify why files are still being transferred.

short answer is via iCloud Drive. WhatsApp backup(s) stored in hidden folder of iCloud Drive on your MacBook (if signed into iCloud and turned on iCloud Drive). To find WhatsApp backup(s): Launch Terminal (in /Applications/Utilities folder) Type following commands cd ~/Library/Mobile\ Documents/ find *whatsapp* You should see all files related to WhatsApp backup(s). If don’t see anything, make sure iCloud drive is turned on. If only see *. icloud files, turn off “optimize mac storage” in icloud system preferences. knowledge, can’t access directly messages as stored in encrypted SQLite database. documents, pictures and videos stored in separate, unencrypted archives: Document. tar (PDFs and other attachments) Media. tar (pictures) Video. tar (videos) To extract in there, copy files to desktop via terminal command: cp *whatsapp*/Accounts/*/backup/*. tar ~/Desktop Then, double-click on. tar files to extract folder structure containing files organised by conversation. Note: If multiple WhatsApp accounts backed up to same iCloud account, need to replace ‘*’ between “Accounts/” and “/backup” by desired phone number. Hope this helps!

It possible, but requires setup. Here is how it is done, and how you can tell. On corporate computer, where software updates pushed from central location, possible to send to your computer a "trusted" certificate stored next to trusted certificate of say, Verising or Entrust. Your company's proxy hold private key of certificate. When you visite HTTPS web site, like https://mybank. com/, proxy will put itself in middle. establish HTTPS connection with your browser generating on fly a certificate for mybank. com. It will replay (and possibly monitor or log) all traffic on new connexion, from proxy to mybank. com. You can tell if this is case by looking at padlock icon. If see certificate for mybank. com was issued by acmesprockets. com (the name of your company), you know they can see your "encrypted" traffic. you company can force your computer to trust any certificate, they could create certificate using well known name, like "Entrust. net Secure Server Certification Authority" (even if probably illegal under trademark law). how can you tell? After connecting to website, look at certificate. Details vary for each browser, but clicking on padlock icon next to https is usually place to start. From certificate, find certificate thumbprint and look it up online. Better yet, do same thing with certificate authority. If you don't find certificate thumbpring online (but you can when at home or on phone), chances are your HTTPS traffic is decrypted along the way.

sender on email not be used to determine if email is legitimate, only can be used to determine when email is not. email claiming to be from Paypal and coming from gmail. com address is obviously fake. email claiming to from Microsoft sent from microsoft. com address could or not be real. How to tell difference? The body of email. If email contains links point to any service not linked to Microsoft, or shortened links, or links with IP addresses, email is a phishing attempt. If email contains writing errors, usually it is false. If email is about any service you don't signed for, it's fake too. If email contains this line and link text points to Microsoft service and underlined link points to same address, usually email is real. If email telling you about something wrong on account, log in on account and check, without clicking in link on email. Type address by hand. If something wrong, you will see on site.

not "safe" in meaning of "no risk at all" to install any of software on same device you use for online banking since you don't know what software is actually doing. not matter if this is open source or closed source software. But, also not "safe" in same "no risk" meaning to use online banking at all or to use a laptop, because you cannot fully trust online banking, browser use, operating system or hardware and firmware of laptop. Additionally cannot fully trust your internet provider, vendor of router etc. This means, no such thing as "safe" in meaning of "no risk". There is always some risk and question is if this risk can be accepted. In case of installing widely used software from well known source and keeping software up-to-date risk is probably acceptable. But, if you got software on an USB stick from a suspicious person I would probably not trust it even if person claims this is well known and widely used software you can also download., if download was not done from original site I would be suspicious too. But, even if download done from official site it still might be malicious in case download site was infected., risk is not zero., this true not only for open source software but also for closed source. In: risk is never zero and more software you install your on system the larger attack surface gets. You have to decide yourself if risk is acceptable or not based on various factors. Closed source vs open source software might be such a factor but more relevant ones, like download source or reputation of vendor or author of software.
. swp files created by Vim, they should be automatically deleted when you close file exit editor.

. swp files are nothing but a lock file you editor, generally vim, creates to indicate file is being edited. This if you open file in another vim instance of if someone in network did, they'll see a warning file is being edited. You need not to delete them manually. You editor will remove swap file once you close file in editor.

. swp file is not a swap file in OS sense. It is a state file. It keeps your changes since last save (except last 200 characters), buffers you saved, unsaved macros and undo structure. can read more in VIM's help: vim +help\ swap-file. If a crash (power failure, OS crash, etc. ), you can recover your changes using this swap-file. After saving changes from swap file to original file, need to exit vim and remove swap file yourself.

Set immutable flag on file(s) to prevent changes*: sudo chflags hidden, uchg /path/to/file What's an immutable flag? "Immutable flags, also known as immutable bits, are file system attributes that, when enabled, prohibit changes to files or folders (objects), i. e lock them. Enabled, immutable flags supersede permissions: you cannot modify object whose immutable flags enabled despite Read & Write permissions on object. " Note*: This will ensure file remains hidden, but may prevent application from running properly if RW access is needed. This is tradeoff., to unset flag, run: sudo chflags nouchg /path/to/file If this case, I advise contact developer of application since it need not automatically make hidden file visible in order to to RW to file. That's a bug in application itself, period.

A script is a file: is human-readable (at least to reasonably trained human,. file consists of printable characters); understood by interpreter as instructions describing behavior of a program. A shell script is a script whose interpreter is a shell. In unix world, “shell” refers to family of shells resemble Bourne shell; modern shells (ash, bash, ksh, zsh, ...) conform to POSIX shell standard. generally, word “shell” can include other command interpreters as csh, tcsh, fish, ... An executable is any file that can be executed. In to be effectively executable, file needs to have two properties: user must have permission to execute it. seen with command ls -l: x character must be present in permission column. format of file must be one system recognizes as executable. Executable formats can be divided into several categories: Native executables, of machine code organized according to operating system's binary executable layout. Most modern unix systems use ELF format for native executables. Scripts. An executable script is a file begins with a shebang line, of two characters #! followed by a path to a file. To execute such file, kernel executes interpreter program and passes it path to script as an argument. Possibly other formats depending on system. For example, Linux can register arbitrary file formats through binfmt_misc facility. allows Java bytecode files to be executed through registered JVM, Windows executables to be executed through Wine,. Note executable is dependent on system. For example, amd64 Linux binary is executable on amd64 Linux system but not on 32-bit system. A binary for Android is not executable on normal Linux installation. Windows executable is only executable on Linux if Wine is present.script begins with #!/usr/local/bin/ruby only executable if program located at /usr/local/bin/ruby. shell script usually is executable. But can be non-executable, if you not have permission to execute it. can still have it interpreted by passing it explicitly to interpreter (e. g. bash /path/to/script) — “have it interpreted” is fancy way of saying “execute”.

function returns value, but procedure does not. method is similar to a function, but is internal to part of class. term method is used almost exclusively in object-oriented programming.

A function is takes inputs returns one or more values. If returned values entirely determined by inputs, function doesn't have side effects (logging, perhaps, or causing state changes outside itself), then it's called a pure function. A procedure is a function that doesn't return a value., this means procedure can only cause side effects. (That might include mutating input parameter!) A method is function that closes over a set of variables, a closure. It takes zero or more input parameters, has access to set variables, returns zero or more values. In OO languages methods are attached to objects or classes. In most mainstream OO languages, closed-over variables are called member fields, or instance variables, of an object. A method can be a pure function, impure function or a procedure. latter definition leads to object = struct + closures correspondence.

I'm going with different answer here: practically speaking, no difference, with slight exception that "method" usually refers to a subroutine associated with object in OO languages. terms "procedure, function, subroutine, subprogram, and method" all mean same thing: a callable sub-program within a larger program. difficult to come with definition that captures all variant usages of these terms, because they not used consistently across programming languages or paradigms. You might say a function returns a value., following C function doesn't return a value: void f() { return; }. but doubt you'd find anyone would call it a procedure., in Pascal, procedures don't return values and functions return values, but merely a reflection of how Pascal designed. In Fortran, function returns a value, and subroutine returns multiple values. none of this allows us to "universal" definition for these terms. In, term "procedural programming" refers to whole class of languages, including C, Fortran and Pascal, only one of uses term "procedure" to mean anything. none of this is really consistent. only exception is probably "method", to used almost entirely with OO languages, referring to a function associated with object., this not always consistent. C++, for example, usually uses term "member function" rather than method, (even though term "method" has crept into C++ vernacular among programmers. ) point is, none of this is really consistent. It simply reflects terminology employed by whatever languages are en vogue at the time.

good detailed answers above; short story is they'll all flavors of subroutines; what meant by each term vary according to programming language context in, functions return a value, but don't have to methods are generic OOP terms present in SQL, stored procedures have outputs typically only return error code, user-defined functions must return a value (which may be result-set), precise difference between these terms depends on who you're talking to!

Is TCP more secure than UDP? Yes, but we to be clear about what we are talking about talking about "security" not generalize this statement to upper layer protocols. Currently, security is often associated to CIA triad: Confidentiality. Integrity. Availability. version 4 of IP protocol, still most commonly used now, is a very old beast developed during 70's and 80's. At that time, confidentiality was not really a subject targeted was to achieve integrity and availability (the Arpanet network, ancestor of Internet gave birth to IP protocol, designed to ensure continuity of service even in of nuclear war, not to protect in-transit data). In this optic, two transport protocols developed over IP layer: TCP and UDP. TCP was one designed to ensure both integrity and availability properties. It includes at advanced techniques as three-way handshake, parameters negotiation, various connection state handling, transparent packet reordering, acknowledgement windows and retry mechanisms. This brings good guaranties to sender that data it sent has received in complete an uncorrupted form (ie. no missing, altered or unordered parts). Remind this protocol was targeting was technical disaster, not malicious tampering of data in transit. Such issue out-of-scope at that time. UDP on contrary was designed to be a fast protocol. It has none of above mentioned feature, and therefore none of their overhead too. In, when sender sends some data using UDP, data received may be incomplete, unordered or not received at all: UDP protocol by does not provide any mechanism to prevent or detect this neither on sender or receiver sides. In, when focusing on data integrity and availability properties of security, TCP is indeed more secure than UDP. Is application protocol relying on TCP more secure than one relying on UDP? Certainly not.means people developing application protocol relying on UDP will have more work since they may to implement in application protocol workarounds for features missing in UDP protocol. They to take into account data sent may not be necessarily received, data received may not be in right order, etc. These all well-known problems. OpenVPN for, supports TCP mostly for compatibility with restrictive firewalls, runs by default runs best over UDP. Switching it to TCP is possible but not increase its security as difference between two transport layer protocol UDP and TCP is fully handled by OpenVPN. Switching it to TCP will only add TCP overhead to OpenVPN protocol, reducing its performance. Is TCP better than UDP? No, this is entirely an application protocol design choice. UDP is a more raw protocol. When used correctly and carefully it may achieve better performances than TCP at price of more difficult development and maintenance of application protocol. When application is not time sensitive, TCP imposes itself as natural choice no need to reinvent the wheel. When application is time sensitive, discussion must occur on which to choose knowing each will with drawback: potential performance penalty with TCP against more complex application with UDP. Most protocols are not time sensitive TCP is most widely used protocol., when you load a web page or receive email, no difference if you receive it 10 milliseconds sooner or later. Two classical examples of protocols using UDP, in to OpenVPN cited, are media streaming and DNS. With media streaming, you don't care if one video frame or few milliseconds of video or audio is missing, as long as video or audio is playing smoothly and synchronously. In case, you don't want to induce repetitive pauses because TCP detected missing packet and asked sender to resend content of last acknowledgement window.With DNS, requests and answers usually short you want name resolution process to fast as possible (note longer and less time-sensitive answers such as DNS zone transfers usually still occur on TCP). faster to resend name resolution request to DNS server on very few times request or answer gets lost than processing full-fledged three-way handshake for every request. What about confidentiality and malicious sniffing/tampering (and IPv6)? All cared about until now was, in spirit of old IPv4, balance between transmission speed and data integrity + availability. Now, if want to add confidentiality on top of this, we can do this but it will have to be done at application layer as, as stated before, IPv4 not concerned by confidentiality issues. modern, full-fledged implementation of security can be implemented at application layer rely on either TCP or UDP (or both) protocols without impact on application protocol security (see example of OpenVPN above). However, as stated in beginning, IPv4 comes from another computing age. got successor by name if IPv6, natively supports IPSec at IP layer, providing more modern security services below transport protocols such as UDP and TCP. This allows to delegate in-transit data encryption from application to network layer, allows both UDP and TCP to provide same security guaranties. However, in most scenarios UDP performance gain will counterbalanced by IPSec overhead, not sure advantage in using UDP instead TCP as long as IPv6 IPSec is being used.

TCP is "Connection-Based" means it has reliability built in, in form of sequence numbers., for example, I send you an image over TCP but, 1/4 of packets get dropped. Since we connection based protocol with sequence numbers, your computer will know you missing data and request data from me in to have data integrity. This is slower but, much more secure., in to spoof TCP/IP packets, you to catch sequence number and send malicious packet. Without a man in middle, almost impossible! UDP is a "Connetionless" protocol, it just sends data and forgets. no data reliability or integrity, but it's faster and more efficient for some applications.

should take less than a millisecond to ping a host on same physical network. In reality, networks get busy hosts get slow - might take 5 milliseconds. Like UDP, no guarantee you'll receive reply at all.

TCP isn’t more secure than UDP, it more “reliable” as stateful requires acknowledgment of each segment. UDP is stateless sends segments without knowing client gets them or not. Neither have bespoke security features other doesn’t, differences are mealy down to different requirements of each protocol, perceived security benefits are by-products of protocols functionally rather than deliberate security feature. EDIT: UDP and TCP have specific uses, none these uses relates to security. Both protocols rely on other protocols to provide security. TCP may have slightly smaller attack surface, inconsequential as to secure either you require a security orientated protocol. Protocol such as DTLS or googles QUIC. Choosing to implement TCP for use case better suited for UDP, rather than securing UDP correctly (TCP would also require securing in most use cases), like using a 9 iron for putting because you think 9 iron better weapon to defend yourself with in fight. when you have a gun in your pocket.

As others stated, in general pings are ICMP-based have no ports. There is, however, thing as TCP Ping where, instead of typical 3-way TCP handshake, only first 2 steps performed and delay between measured. Once measurement completed, a RST ACK sent to close half-open connection. Then process repeats until counter/duration reached or you terminated process. Using TCP Ping (which I use FREQUENTLY to test for open ports on servers my systems admins work on) you able to specify destination ports to test (to verify server is listening on certain port). source port is just an ephemeral random port. If to see example of TCP Ping utility (the one I use on Windows systems), here you go: TCPing. Also, NMAP comes with utility called NPING has flag to allow it to perform TCP based pings too. note, some network equipment also has this capability, such as Cisco ASAs using newer operating system versions. command is: ping tcp <destination IP> <destination port>

Ping on Windows & Linux systems by default use ICMP. ping Request Type 8 & Code 0 ping Reply Type 0 & Code 0 other utilities can use to run ping like test for TCP/UDP. common quick test for seeing if TCP port is open is using telnet client on Windows. Is TCP more secure than UDP? Yes, but we to be clear about what we are talking about talking about "security" not generalize this statement to upper layer protocols. Currently, security is often associated to CIA triad: Confidentiality. Integrity. Availability. version 4 of IP protocol, still most commonly used now, is a very old beast developed during 70's and 80's. At that time, confidentiality was not really a subject targeted was to achieve integrity and availability (the Arpanet network, ancestor of Internet gave birth to IP protocol, designed to ensure continuity of service even in of nuclear war, not to protect in-transit data). In this optic, two transport protocols developed over IP layer: TCP and UDP. TCP was one designed to ensure both integrity and availability properties. It includes at advanced techniques as three-way handshake, parameters negotiation, various connection state handling, transparent packet reordering, acknowledgement windows and retry mechanisms. This brings good guaranties to sender that data it sent has received in complete an uncorrupted form (ie. no missing, altered or unordered parts). Remind this protocol was targeting was technical disaster, not malicious tampering of data in transit. Such issue out-of-scope at that time. UDP on contrary was designed to be a fast protocol. It has none of above mentioned feature, and therefore none of their overhead too. In, when sender sends some data using UDP, data received may be incomplete, unordered or not received at all: UDP protocol by does not provide any mechanism to prevent or detect this neither on sender or receiver sides. In, when focusing on data integrity and availability properties of security, TCP is indeed more secure than UDP. Is application protocol relying on TCP more secure than one relying on UDP? Certainly not.means people developing application protocol relying on UDP will have more work since they may to implement in application protocol workarounds for features missing in UDP protocol. They to take into account data sent may not be necessarily received, data received may not be in right order, etc. These all well-known problems. OpenVPN for, supports TCP mostly for compatibility with restrictive firewalls, runs by default runs best over UDP. Switching it to TCP is possible but not increase its security as difference between two transport layer protocol UDP and TCP is fully handled by OpenVPN. Switching it to TCP will only add TCP overhead to OpenVPN protocol, reducing its performance. Is TCP better than UDP? No, this is entirely an application protocol design choice. UDP is a more raw protocol. When used correctly and carefully it may achieve better performances than TCP at price of more difficult development and maintenance of application protocol. When application is not time sensitive, TCP imposes itself as natural choice no need to reinvent the wheel. When application is time sensitive, discussion must occur on which to choose knowing each will with drawback: potential performance penalty with TCP against more complex application with UDP. Most protocols are not time sensitive TCP is most widely used protocol., when you load a web page or receive email, no difference if you receive it 10 milliseconds sooner or later. Two classical examples of protocols using UDP, in to OpenVPN cited, are media streaming and DNS. With media streaming, you don't care if one video frame or few milliseconds of video or audio is missing, as long as video or audio is playing smoothly and synchronously. In case, you don't want to induce repetitive pauses because TCP detected missing packet and asked sender to resend content of last acknowledgement window.With DNS, requests and answers usually short you want name resolution process to fast as possible (note longer and less time-sensitive answers such as DNS zone transfers usually still occur on TCP). faster to resend name resolution request to DNS server on very few times request or answer gets lost than processing full-fledged three-way handshake for every request. What about confidentiality and malicious sniffing/tampering (and IPv6)? All cared about until now was, in spirit of old IPv4, balance between transmission speed and data integrity + availability. Now, if want to add confidentiality on top of this, we can do this but it will have to be done at application layer as, as stated before, IPv4 not concerned by confidentiality issues. modern, full-fledged implementation of security can be implemented at application layer rely on either TCP or UDP (or both) protocols without impact on application protocol security (see example of OpenVPN above). However, as stated in beginning, IPv4 comes from another computing age. got successor by name if IPv6, natively supports IPSec at IP layer, providing more modern security services below transport protocols such as UDP and TCP. This allows to delegate in-transit data encryption from application to network layer, allows both UDP and TCP to provide same security guaranties. However, in most scenarios UDP performance gain will counterbalanced by IPSec overhead, not sure advantage in using UDP instead TCP as long as IPv6 IPSec is being used.

TCP isn’t more secure than UDP, it more “reliable” as stateful requires acknowledgment of each segment. UDP is stateless sends segments without knowing client gets them or not. Neither have bespoke security features other doesn’t, differences are mealy down to different requirements of each protocol, perceived security benefits are by-products of protocols functionally rather than deliberate security feature. TCP may have slightly smaller attack surface, inconsequential as to secure either you require a security orientated protocol. Protocol such as DTLS or googles QUIC. Choosing to implement TCP for use case better suited for UDP, rather than securing UDP correctly (TCP would also require securing in most use cases), like using a 9 iron for putting because you think 9 iron better weapon to defend yourself with in fight. when you have a gun in your pocket.

As others stated, in general pings are ICMP-based have no ports. There is, however, thing as TCP Ping where, instead of typical 3-way TCP handshake, only first 2 steps performed and delay between measured. Once measurement completed, a RST ACK sent to close half-open connection. Then process repeats until counter/duration reached or you terminated process. Using TCP Ping (which I use FREQUENTLY to test for open ports on servers my systems admins work on) you able to specify destination ports to test (to verify server is listening on certain port). source port is just an ephemeral random port. If to see example of TCP Ping utility (the one I use on Windows systems), here you go: TCPing. Also, NMAP comes with utility called NPING has flag to allow it to perform TCP based pings too. note, some network equipment also has this capability, such as Cisco ASAs using newer operating system versions. command is: ping tcp <destination IP> <destination port>

shell path (i. PATH) for user in OSX is variable defining set of locations in file system user can use certain applications, commands and shell scripts without need to specify full path to command or program in Terminal. If enter abc in Terminal first occurrence of abc in one of paths defined in PATH will be executed. To access or print variable PATH use $PATH. Example: echo $PATH variable PATH has general and user specific part. 1. General part: part is defined by (superior) file /etc/paths and (inferior) content of folder /etc/paths. d. default content of file /etc/paths (in OS X) is: /usr/bin /bin /usr/sbin /sbin /usr/local/bin default folder /etc/paths. d is empty. On older systems with X11 installation folder contains file named 50-X11 with content /usr/X11/bin adds additional path (/usr/X11/bin) to PATH. prepended number- defines load order. /etc/paths. d folder contains following files: /etc/paths. d/40-mysql #file content: /usr/local/mysql/bin /etc/paths. d/50-X11 #file content: /usr/X11/bin /etc/paths. d/60-testdisk #file content: /usr/local/testdisk /etc/paths. d/70-git #file content: /usr/local/git/bin resulting PATH is echo PATH$ /usr/bin:/bin:/usr/sbin:/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/local/mysql/bin:/usr/X11/bin:/usr/local/testdisk:/usr/local/git/bin 2. User-specific part: user-specific part is defined by file ~/. bash_profile.If created folder bin in user folder installed apps in add following line in ~/. bash_profile export PATH="/Users/username/bin:$PATH" or export PATH="$PATH:/Users/username/bin" first entry preferably executes command abc found in /bin folder of user, second one command abc found in general path before executing identical named one in ~/bin folder. This part of PATH defined by. bash_profile only effective for respective user. To add path entered in. bash_profile to current PATH immediately to source file once: source ~/. bash_profile 3. Temporary paths By issuing export PATH="/Users/username/bin:$PATH" or export PATH="$PATH:/Users/username/bin" in Terminal can add path temporarily. This part of PATH lost after closing Terminal window, logging out or rebooting Mac. Examples (using general part from above): file ~/. bash_profile contains export PATH="/Users/username/bin:$PATH" you issue in Terminal export PATH="/Users/username/bin2:$PATH" then resulting PATH is: /Users/username/bin2:/Users/username/bin:/usr/bin:/bin:/usr/sbin:/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/local/mysql/bin:/usr/X11/bin:/usr/local/testdisk:/usr/local/git/bin \____temp. path_____/ The file ~/.bash_profile contains export PATH="$PATH:/Users/username/bin" issue in Terminal export PATH="/Users/username/bin2:$PATH" resulting PATH is: /Users/username/bin2:/usr/bin:/bin/usr/sbin:/sbin/usr/local/bin:/usr/local/mysql/bin:/usr/X11/bin:/usr/local/testdisk:/usr/local/git/bin:/Users/username/bin \____temp. path_____ Summary PATH (or $PATH) defined by files: /etc/paths, files in /etc/paths. d and ~/. bash_profile adding temporary path by additional RAM content.
