You can control your idevice (not only view it's screen) given you have a mac / PC paired with it (that, you had them connected in past using USB cable, pressed "Trust" button on iPhone's screen alert). few UI automation tools capable of doing that. Try evaluation version of SeeTest Automation for instance. You required to generate Apple's provision profile unique for your iPhone (in automatic, free of charge process) allow viewing and controlling phone, managing applications etc. EDIT (or How To Trust a Device with Broken Screen) need: Siri turned on / triple tap on home to activate VoiceOver bluetooth keyboard. Lightning to USB adapter. simple USB keyboard. If device not previously trusted by computer, cannot tap "Trust this computer" on broken screen, you might be able to use VoiceOver with USB and Bluetooth keyboards to virtually tap trust (and to control device) even with broken screen. trick is to bring up trust alert by connecting lightning port to computer running iTunes (or Xcode), then tap "Trust" button using Space / Enter key on VoiceOver and bluetooth keyboard (this must be a bluetooth keyboard since USB connection cannot be used for communicating with computer AND with keyboard simultaneously). If have bluetooth keyboard paired with Apple device, great. connect device to computer, open iTunes hit Space (not sure, maybe Enter. ). If have problems with that, or not sure whether alert is displayed, read further and turn on VoiceOver. Turn on VoiceOver: To do, use Siri (assuming it configured). Just Say "Hi Siri, turn on VoiceOver". If Siri is off, some iOS versions configured by default to turn VoiceOver on/off using triple tap on home button. If have a paired bluetooth keyboard, skip to step 6.Now VoiceOver turned on, you need a USB keyboard to navigate to Bluetooth settings (of, if screen still responds to touch not need keyboard, just listen to instructions and tap): Connect USB keyboard to device using Lightning to USB adapter (it meant for camera, but also work with standard keyboards). Navigate to Settings app using VoiceOver (this tricky part, controlling VoiceOver is a mastery. ). Left / Right arrow keys used for navigation of UI items, Left + Right keys for "Quick Nav On" and Up + Down keys to activate an item. In Settings app, go to Bluetooth settings and pair keyboard. Once have bluetooth keyboard paired, connect device to computer, control VoiceOver with keyboard to trust it. Now can proceed to using any viewing tool you like. P. S. You might also be able to see screen without trusting device (and using Quicktime) by using Lightning AV Adapter. But I've never given it a try.

Terms like "smart switch" and "managed switch" are terms invented by vendors. exact meaning may vary from vendor to vendor. In general "managed" switches aimed at large proffesionally managed networks where people prepared to pay substantial money for advanced management features/or perceived reliability. They typicaly have a serial console port allowing recovery from misconfigurations with minimal downtime. other extreme "unmanaged" switches offer no management capability and are dirt cheap. "smart" switches fill a middle ground. They have some management facilities support VLANS but often lacking stuff compared to conventional managed switch, for example: They usually lack a serial console port. if screw up configuration or forget password only option is reset to factory defaults. Some of have no ability to configure VLAN for management interface may do strange things regarding management port and VLANS (I seen reports of some where management IP can be reached from native VLAN on any port). Some can only be configured by web interface. Some only configured with vendor-provided client application. They unlikely to support features for automatically pushing configuration to multiple switches in network. Some vendors divide smart switches into multiple teirs, for example TP-link have "websmart/easysmart" line seem like total crap and their "smart" line seems fairly decent. Before buying any of networking gear suggest downloading and reading the manual. This will tell you whether it suffers from brain damage like no VLAN setting for management port and whether it supports features you need.

differences in features and application scenarios among various serial switches? L2/L3 managed Switch, Smart Switch, Easy Smart Switch and Unmanaged Switch in TP-LINK official website, this article brief account about features and application scenarios of respective switch. Unmanaged Switch not able to configure unmanaged switch because it doesn’t support configuration interface or options. It is plug-and-play, only need to connect computer or other network devices to unmanaged switch directly., if not need L2 features, only need to extend number of Ethernet ports, unmanaged switch is right switch for you. Easy Smart Switch use Utility or Web interface (Web only for TL-SG1016DE and TL-SG1024DE) to manage easy smart switch configure basic settings, VLAN, QoS few L2 features like LAG, IGMP Snooping and Port Mirroring. If no advanced applications needed, easy smart switch should be best choice for. Normally, easy smart switch be found in home, SOHO or small business. Smart Switch Smart switch can be managed by Web interface, Telnet, SSH and SNMP. supports more L2 features better QoS than easy smart switch, smart switch supports more advanced functions like ACL and Spanning Tree protocol, if to support solution for small company or colleague with lower price, Smart switch is indispensable device. L2 Managed Switch L2 managed switch has console port for CLI (Command Line Interface), has all managing ways and advanced features that smart switch has, besides, L2 managed switch has abundant VLAN and Multicast features cluster for logical stacking and Network Security features including 802. 1X and IP-MAC binding. can use L2 managed switch to build resiliency and availability network or build up small ISP Access Network. L3 Managed Switch L2 switch only work in Layer 2--Data Link Layer of OSI model.Layer 3 switch has L3 functions like traditional router--static routing, routing protocol like OSPF ECMP, multicast routing protocol DHCP relay. Compared with traditional router, L3 switch has lower cost better performance in packet routing speed because layer 3 switch routes packets by hardware--ASIC instead of CPU, once it learned IP address, forward packets by switching performance. mainly used in core layer of middle sized business network, providing better hardware switching performance in routing. source: TP-LINK

S. M. A. R. T is a monitoring system for HDD and SSD implemented in firmware of drive using two standards: ATA and SCSI. SMART data is usually written to a special service part of platter/flash storage unit. All modern interface standards and underlying protocols (SCSI, FireWire, USB – with USB-(S)ATA-Bridges, eSATA, Thunderbolt, SAS) capable of transmitting SMART-data. SMART data not actively transmitted to hosts, but to queried by host-OS, applications or drivers. Depending on OS, SMART application, drivers build-in hardware success of queries may vary broadly. to retrieve SMART data from external USB/FireWire-drives attached to Macs use this kext driver (compatibility list). Target Disk Mode doesn't 'bypass' SMART, because SMART is implemented in hard disk. hard to say in if operating systems (or application and drivers) locking out failing disks based on SMART data. doubt that because SMART isn't reliable implemented attributes varies between manufacturers and hard drive models meanings and interpretations of attributes values varies between manufacturers i don't know of any such OS or application. It's rather the OS in conjunction with firmware and (failing) hard disk itself which 'lockout' a device.

Restore Backup restores contents of iPhone backup performed in past. Restore iPhone wipes iPhone of all data & apps reinstalls iOS, leaving iPhone reset to factory settings. iPhone left with just latest iOS and Apple default apps. In to successfully copy files in first place, need read access to files at original location. To can read them, can either change their permissions with sudo chmod -R o+rx /drag/your/original/folder/from/Finder/here or as suggested in comments of question have ownership of drive ignored for time-being, which leaves original files unchanged. To copy files over, use following command: cp -R /drag/your/original/folder/from/Finder/here /drag/your/target/folder/from/Finder/here/ For more information during copy process, use following command: cp -Rv /drag/your/original/folder/from/Finder/here /drag/your/target/folder/from/Finder/here/ Mind slash at end of target folder or target folder will be overwritten by contents. Understanding permissions when moving/copying files in UNIX/BSD (Mac OS X's underlying system is based on BSD): When moving a file from A to B on same partition/volume, ownership of files will not change When moving a file from A to B between different partitions/volumes, ownership of files will change to user moving them (applying sudo to copy command will have target files ownership set to root) When copying a file from A to B regardless of location will apply ownership of target files to user copying them (applying sudo to copy command will target files ownership set to root) With number 1 only file descriptors will change internally, but no file be physically moved. With 2 and 3 files are physically copied over to new location with step 2 doing second step and deleting them from original location after each copy. UPDATE (to address comment): If you copied over files using sudo, can modify permissions of target files using chown and chmod.Commands: sudo chown -R <user>[:group] /drag/your/target/folder/from/Finder/here <user> is account name of your user (not full name) :group is group, by default for any user is staff and any admin is admin. not required, can omit to leave it as is (hence square brackets) sudo chmod -R 770 /drag/your/target/folder/from/Finder/here This give you primary group r/w and execution/traversal rights on files.

OS X prevents copying files and folders to root directory or "Macintosh HD". It prefers write files only in user directory to prevent accidental file deletions, overwrites,. However, if you have a file or folder on Desktop, and you are an administrator on computer, you can copy file using super user privileges. open Terminal application. use Spotlight to search for it or go to Applications folder, then Utilities folder. Once in Terminal,'ll be faced with a prompt. Run command below to put file or folder in root directory. Put name of file or folder in place of "FILE". sudo cp -p Desktop/FILE / Press return key. You'll be prompted for password. sudo is command to provide super user privileges. cp is copy. -p means to preserve file owner and permissions. If required to change owner or permissions of file, can run command like chown change owner or chgrp change group or chmod change file permissions.

iBGP isn't used for internal routing, it is used by all eBGP routers to share routes. Ex: If you peering with 3 other network, you want all eBGP routers to know routes received by other ones so they can propagate information to peers if necessary/needed (opening possibility of peer using transit through you)

iBGP requires full mesh or use of mitigation like confederations or route reflectors, BGP doesn't converge with like speed of OSPF, etc. Each OSPF router would full understanding of all routes in area in it resides without needing full mesh, it converges very, quickly. Using IGP is recommended with iBGP. Without IGP, iBGP must neighbor on external-facing interfaces, with an IGP, iBGP can neighbor on loopback interfaces never go down, can have multiple paths to reach. seen iBGP-only for local routing, but it more difficult and fragile.

anyone explain need of IBGP communication for routes, when we have IGP protocols (OSPF, RIP) for internal communication? Scalability1: Imagine you receiving 500, 000 EBGP routes in more than one location2, need to influence per route exit point in your AS. BGP can handle more routes than IGP protocols., iBGP required unless you willing to redistribute all routes learned via eBGP Enforce boundaries of trust / control: BGP has more ways to filter peers than IGPs (for controlling what you advertise and receive). Flexible data structures (somewhat related to previous bullet): BGP communities, BGP Extended communities, local-pref, etc. these make BGP attractive way to implement custom routing policies within own autonomous system (by using iBGP). with everything trade offs; scalability, control, flexibility from iBGP means it's slower converging protocol than IGPs (in general). End Notes: 1 Scalability: use BGP because don't want to carry entire internet routing table in your IGP (i. e. in case, OSPF). OSPF not designed to handle many thousands of routes in internet BGP tables. if try to use OSPF for this purpose, it will break your network. Using example of OSPF, LSA processing / flooding requirements from 500, 000 routes uses too many resources in routers. Name any other IGP (EIGRP, RIPv1/2, IS-IS, IGRP) same story is true. notorious instances where Tier-1 ISP accidentally redistributed BGP table into IGP (even internet table small fraction of current size) caused major outages. Countermeasures now implemented in IGP protocols (like this one for OSPF in IOS) to prevent redistribution from BGP into OSPF from causing major outage.2 iBGP routing example understand want iBGP, consider routing entry to 4. 2. 2. 2. R2>sh ip bgp 4. 2. 2. 2 BGP routing table entry for 4. 0. 0. 0/9, version 3146 Paths: (32 available, best #7, table Default-IP-Routing-Table).! extra BGP RIB entries deleted 7660 2516 3356, (aggregated by 3356 4. 69. 130. 4) 203. 181. 168 from 203. 181. 168 (203. 181. 248. 168) Origin IGP, localpref 100, valid, internal atomic-aggregate Community: 2516:1030 3356, (aggregated by 3356 4. 69. 130. 6) 4. 69. 184. 193 from 4. 69. 184. 193 (4. 69. 184. 193) Origin IGP, metric 0, localpref 100, valid, atomic-aggregate, Community: 3356:0 3356:3 3356:100 3356:123 3356:575 3356:2012.! extra BGP RIB entries deleted 32 paths to consider., BGP chose to go to 4. 0. 0. 0/9 via 4. 69. 184. 193 (notice best under RIB entry)., BGP chose route shortest AS Path list., not all routes preferred via AS3356 (attached to R1). Some preferred out R3 (via AS7660). iBGP ability to know (at R2) way take shortest BGP path. using iBGP, router must have full mesh, or must use a mitigation. Route reflectors are one mitigation. another mitigation similar to you suggest, called confederations. It breaks your AS in sub-ASes uses eBGP between sub-ASes. can search for BGP confederations, find documents, such as IP Routing: BGP Configuration Guide: BGP Routing Domain Confederation One way to reduce internal BGP (iBGP) mesh is to divide autonomous system into multiple subautonomous systems and group them into single confederation. To outside world, confederation looks like a single autonomous system. Each autonomous system is fully meshed within itself has few connections to other autonomous systems in same confederation. Commonly deployed in DMVPNS. EIGRP is less confusing than OSPF not have different network types and EIGRP easier to deploy in hub and spoke scenarios. EIGRP uses flat network without areas, this can both be an advantage and disadvantage. OSPF is an open standard's logical choice if multiple vendors. Network administrators usually be more comfortable with OSPF because it's more commonly deployed. Both protocols have advantages and disadvantages. But common answer that EIGRP should be discarded because being proprietary is not entirely true any longer.

remember models like OSI are just, models. theoretical. real world doesn't fall neatly into these models. For most part, routing is a layer-3 function, but, pointed out, BGP uses layer-4 protocol to communicate with other BGP speakers to do normally considered a layer-3 function. Many network protocols fall into gray area, or are considered in one layer while using another layer. Take ARP for instance. It resolves layer-3 addresses to layer-2 addresses. Which layer should it be considered to in? Understanding models is useful, but models are not mandated by organization, you free to create protocols and functions that do not follow any model.

Link local addresses are local to a link*. Packets to/from link local addresses cannot cross any router. to use a link local address requires knowing what interface it relates to. trouble is interface IDs are a machine local concept not nessacerally stable. These restrictions limit utility of link local addresses. Unique local addresses are akin to RFC1918 addresses of IPv4. They can be routed within a site or group of cooperating sites but can't be advertised on the Internet. They treated like global scope addresses by applications, none of interface ID BS. problem with RFC1918 addresses was when interconnection needed to established between two private networks not previously connected. a substatial chance two networks would use overlapping RFC1918 space interconnection would be difficult. ULAs were designed to mitigate this problem. ULA block was split into two parts, lower half (FC00::/8) intended to be allocated by a registry body gave gaurantee of uniqueness. this never happened** these addresses are considered reserved. upper half (FD00::/8) was allocated to probabalistically unique addresses. Sites supposed to pick a /48 prefix pesudo-randomly (an algorithm suggested but not mandated in standard) from FD00::/8. probablity of address collision in a group of n sites is roughly n2/(2*240). guess is confusion comes from a home/small buisness perspective on networking. In home/small buisness network rare for to be more than one "link" within a private network. On in larger organisations more common for to complex private networks with many "link"s and routing between those links. * a Link being a group of machines connected by a protocol at lower level than IP. For example a single Ethernet VLAN (or single ethernet network without VLANs) ** concerns about blurring line between private addresses and provider independent global addresses.

Apple is generating IPv6 addresses unrelated to MAC address in to prevent tracking of users based on MAC addresses assigned to Apple. link-local address is generated once and does not change (since less privacy concern in local-only communication), non-temporary address will change when connecting to new network.

IPv6 link-local addresses are required addresses, cannot be routed. confined to single link, every link has same link-local network. link-local address range is fe80::/10. From RFC 4291, IP Version 6 Addressing Architecture: 2. 5. 6. Link-Local IPv6 Unicast Addresses Link-Local addresses for use on single link. Link-Local addresses have following format: | 10 | | bits | 54 bits | 64 bits | +----------+-------------------------+----------------------------+ |1111111010| 0 | interface ID | +----------+-------------------------+----------------------------+ Link-Local addresses designed to used for addressing on single link for purposes automatic address configuration, neighbor discovery, or when no routers present. Routers must not forward packets with Link-Local source or destination addresses to other links. ULA addresses can be routed (except on public Internet). some rules to ULA addressing. ULA address range is fc00::/7, first half of addresses, fc00::/8, reserved for assignment by global authority. second half of ULA address range, fd00::/8, available for local use, 40-bit Global ID must be randomly chosen. From RFC 4193, Unique Local IPv6 Unicast Addresses: 1. Introduction document defines IPv6 unicast address format globally unique intended for local communications [IPV6]. These addresses called Unique Local IPv6 Unicast Addresses abbreviated as Local IPv6 addresses. not expected to be routable on global Internet. routable inside of more limited area such as site. may also be routed between limited set of sites. Local IPv6 unicast addresses have characteristics: Globally unique prefix (with high probability of uniqueness). Well-known prefix to allow for easy filtering at site boundaries.Allow sites be combined or privately interconnected without creating address conflicts or requiring renumbering of interfaces use these prefixes. Internet Service Provider independent can be used for communications inside site without permanent or intermittent Internet connectivity. If accidentally leaked outside site via routing or DNS, no conflict with other addresses. In practice, applications may treat these addresses like global scoped addresses.

An alias contains two pieces information: unique identifier of file it links to, and path and file name of file it links to. If you rename or move a file, then create a new file with path and file name file originally had, then any alias linked to original file now links to new file. However, if you rename or move a file without replacing it, and then invoke an alias, alias is updated to point to new path and file name, making use of unique identifier to. A symbolic link, on, does not contain unique identifier to file, appear as broken if file is renamed or moved and not replaced with file of same path and file name. Your choice should depend on which scenario suits you best.

Both hard links and symbolic links link a path to destination, substantial difference should be aware of: Hard links link a path to a file. This means if you rename/move destination file, hard link follows. Symbolic links link a path to a path. This means if you rename/move destination file, link is broken., later replacing file with different one will make link work again. Links of both types are made with ln tool. Hard links made without options, whereas symlinks made with -s option. For more information on constructing command, see: How can I create a symbolic link in Terminal?

Both hard links and symbolic links link a path to destination, substantial difference should be aware of: Hard links link a path to a file. This means if you rename/move destination file, hard link follows. Symbolic links link a path to a path. This means if you rename/move destination file, link is broken., later replacing file with different one will make link work again. Links of both types are made with ln tool. Hard links made without options, whereas symlinks made with -s option. For more information on constructing command, see: How can I create a symbolic link in Terminal?

explain to boss difference between "zero" and "null": "Zero" is a value. It is unique, known quantity of zero, meaningful in arithmetic and other math. "Null" is a non-value. For example, in comments: "What is your yearly income?" is question requiring numeric answer. "0" is valid answer for someone not work has no investment income. If user not enter value at all, they don't necessarily make no money; just didn't want to tell software how much (or little) they make. It's an unknown, not specified;, to allow software to continue, specify "null" placeholder for data field within software. That's technically valid from a data perspective; whether valid at business level depends on whether actual numeric value (even zero) is required in to perform mathematical operation (such calculation of taxes, or comparison with thresholds determining benefits). Others addressed issue in C, strings are largely what you make of them. confusion in your question w. r. t. the terminator itself, from one perspective, this could be what someone in your position is worried about. C strings are null-terminated., they terminated by null character, NUL. not terminated by null pointer NULL, a completely different kind of value with different purpose. NUL is guaranteed to have integer value zero. Within string, it will also have size of underlying character type, usually be 1. NULL not guaranteed to have an integer type at all. NULL is intended for use in a pointer context, is generally expected to have a pointer type, shouldn't convert to a character or integer if your compiler is good. definition of NULL involves glyph 0, it not guaranteed to actually have that value[1], unless your compiler implements constant as a one-character #define (many don't, NULL shouldn't be meaningful in non-pointer context), expanded code is not guaranteed to involve a zero value (even though it confusingly involve zero glyph). If NULL is typed, it unlikely to have a size of 1 (or another character size). This may cause additional problems, actual character constants don't have character size for most part. most people will see this and think, "null pointer as anything other than all-zero-bits? what nonsense" - but assumptions like that only safe on common platforms like x86. Since you've explicitly mentioned interest in targeting other platforms, you need to take this issue into account, as you explicitly separated your code from assumptions about nature of relationship between pointers and integers., while C strings are null-terminated, they aren't terminated by NULL, but by NUL (usually written '\0').Code explicitly uses NULL as a string terminator will work on platforms with straightforward address structure, will even compile with many compilers, but it's not correct C. [1] actual null pointer value is inserted by compiler when it reads a 0 token in context where it be converted to a pointer type. not a conversion from integer value 0, not guaranteed to hold if anything other than token 0 itself is used, such as a dynamic value from a variable; conversion also not reversible, null pointer doesn't have to yield value 0 when converted to integer.

I've deleted my original answer because initially misunderstood how +48 numbers were added, sorry about that. Instead of using AppleScript, I'm to offer different solution because while could modify original AppleScript code to delete entire number had +48 prefix, nonetheless errors stopped script from executing completely during testing phase. opting for different solution over debugging AppleScript code. This solution requires exporting entire contents of Contacts. app to vCard file (. vcf), modifying it using RegEx in sed, then importing modified vCard file (. vcf) back into Contacts. Note this method will replace all existing contacts with updated new allcontacts. vcf file should not be an issue as's only removing information you stated you wanted removed, just in roundabout way. NOTE: directions tested under OS X 10. 11. 5 with Contacts. app using default preferences. Open Contacts. Backup Contacts, click: File > Export > Contacts Archive... Now Contacts backed up, do following. Select first contact then press commandA to select all contacts. Click: File > Export > Export vCard... In Save As dialog box will show as, name of first contact and n others, change it to: allcontacts Copy and paste following command into Terminal, then press Space bar to add space afterwards. sed -i. bak -E '/^TEL. *\+48. *$/d' From Finder, drag and drop allcontacts. vcf file onto Terminal window. Note in Finder,. vcf extension may be hidden and it will show in Terminal. Example: sed -i. bak -E '/^TEL. *\+48. *$/d' /Users/me/Documents/allcontacts. vcf Now press enter to modify allcontacts. vcf file. backup of original is created as: allcontacts. vcf. bak Now import updated allcontacts. vcf file into Contacts.File > Import select allcontacts. vcf file, click Open. On "Are you sure you want to import n cards?" sheet click: Review Duplicates... On ensuing sheet select Keep New check Apply to All checkbox click Import. Contacts telephone entries containing numbers with +48 prefix removed. target lines in allcontacts. vcf file have following pattern note example below not only way it can present need to use RegEx aside from phone numbers different as value for type= can vary too. Example line in vCard file: TEL;type=CELL;type=VOICE:+48 697 107 394 RegEx is: ^TEL. *\+48. *$ Explanation: ^ assert position at start of string. TEL matches characters TEL literally (case sensitive). * matches any character (except newline). Quantifier: * Between zero and unlimited times, as many times as possible, giving back as needed [greedy]. \+ matches character + literally. 48 matches characters 48 literally. * matches any character (except newline). Quantifier: * Between zero and unlimited times, as many times as possible, giving back as needed [greedy]. $ assert position at end of string., sed command, sed -i. bak -E '/^TEL. *\+48. *$/d' file backups file (-i. bak) deletes any line starting with TEL that contains +48. based on how lines stored in vCard will just remove lines needed to accomplish task as lines starting with TEL that have +48 in them can only be lines you want removed. NOTE: assumes you did not previously have any numbers with +48 prefix before updated Contacts with original vCard file contained numbers with +48 prefix.

Unfortunately,'s highly unlikely you will able to send contacts back to your phone. iPhone (iPhone 4 and newer) supports Bluetooth Phone Book Access Profile (PBAP) process is typically only one-way. two roles in PBAP profile: Phone Book Server Equipment (PSE) role - this role is for device contains source phone-book objects; for example, a mobile phone. Phone Book Client Equipment (PCE) role - this role is for device that retrieves phone-book objects from PSE device; for example, a portable navigation device (PND). Your iPhone acts as server and car radio acts as client. Phone Book Download Feature This feature used to download entire content of phone book object. especially designed for devices with large storage capacity typically attempting to download and locally store entire phone book. Note this feature is very basic. In, phone book entries are delivered in ascending index order only. No sorting possible. M = mandatory In Bluetooth specification for Phone Book Access Profile (where info sourced), no "push" function; only "pull. " This means for iPhone to receive Phone Book, it must change roles to being a client and car radio to becoming a server. can't find documentation indicates iPhone supports this role or Kia radios becoming a server.

According to Apple, closest supported Bluetooth profile is Phone Book Access Profile (PBAP), mainly used with car kits to: Allow car kit to display name of incoming caller Allow car kit to download the phone book so user can initiate a call from car display no mention of sending contacts to iPhone. You might be to find something on Cydia with a Jailbroken phone, though. For example, iBluetooth app adds file syncing capabilities., it doesn't mention about contact syncing.

Backup means copying personal data from your phone to computer. includes application settings, text messages, voicemails, etc. Sync means copying new apps, music, video, or books from iTunes to your phone, or from your phone to iTunes. think: backup saves copy of stuff you've created, sync copies media downloaded via iTunes Store. Backup copies everything, but Sync only copies what you choose through iTunes. By default, it copies everything, but you can fine tune it all you want. might want to stop movies from syncing to phone if you never use it to watch movies, for example. Unless changed settings, when connect iPhone to computer, iTunes always performs backup first, then sync. When connect new iPhone to computer, iTunes will to reconfigure it using latest backup it has. if connect your old iPhone, let it backup/sync, then connect your new iPhone, it should transfer everything so new phone is just like old one, but faster!

When iPhone is backing up to iCloud, iTunes doesn't automatically do backup of phone when it syncs. You can, however, manually tell iTunes to back up iPhone. When you connect iPhone to iTunes, click on it and it opens to summary page (where it tells you name of phone, gives option to restore it and see home much space on it is used), a Backup button in right side of page. Check out Apple's "HT5262: Choosing an iOS backup method" on Apple Knowledgebase. It talks about benefits of iCloud backup, benefits of iTunes backup, talks about how to do both together.

Apart from answer Shaggy D gave, it doesn't overwrite anything unless specifically instructed, just merges two "branches" of library (including pointing out and creating separate files in instances of for example notes modified on both locations creating a conflict) sync is also when phone contents aren't part of iTunes library get backed up, if you're backing up to a computer instead of iCloud. for example your sms convos, preference files etc. part of it is one-way process, from phone to computer. reverse is when you click "restore from backup". to note if want backup to truly mirror your device need to turn on encryption or it will skip sensitive data, health. Everything about this is muddled these days as you can choose to backup to iCloud instead of computer, most probably have contacts, notes etc already mirrored through either iCloud or Google/Exchange accounts - that stuff isn't touched in sync as it's already in cloud. last tip about library - generally it will transfer App Store purchases made on phone to computer, which can take up a lot of space and files are of no use to computer. Still, if they're not on computer they won't be put back on device in event of restore. If in need of space on main drive either move your entire iTunes library to different drive, or symlink Mobile Applications folder and move. ipa files, works perfectly well.
doesnt back up everytime you charge it. Wireless syncing means you dont need data transfer cable, you can do it "over the air", week old back ups are legit ones

Apple Support article provides quick summary of what syncing does. Basically, as XAlexOwnZX mentions, a sync copies applications, music, other information between your iTunes account and iDevice. This process backs up content (apps, etc. ) on your computer. advantage of syncing is if iPhone gets corrupted, you'll able to restore it (or replacement) to working condition, with all purchased content installed. disadvantage is syncing takes time - however, with iOS 5, you can choose to sync over WiFi and don't need to tether iPhone to computer.

I agree Qt is a nice framework to work with. Still, a number of issues I have with it: It is written in C++, a low level language. fact it is C++ will make every Qt programmer less productive compared to Frameworks written in other languages. main beef with C++ as a GUI development language is it has next to no notion of automatic memory management, makes development process more prone to errors. not introspective, makes debugging difficult. Most other major GUI toolkits have some notion of automatic memory management and introspection. Every cross-platform toolkit suffers from problem it only can implement least common denominator of all supported platforms. That, and different UI guidelines on different platforms questions desirability of cross-platform GUIs at whole. Qt is centered on coding up all your UI. Even can use QtDesigner to build some parts of UI, it lacking in comparison to, (Cocoa/Obj-C) Interface Builder or. Net tools. Even Qt include lot of low-level application functionality, it can not compare to framework hand-tailored for a certain platform. native operating system libraries for both Windows and OSX are more powerful than Qt's implementations. (Think audio frameworks, low level file system access etc. ), I love using PyQt for rapid application prototyping or in-house applications. Using Python to do all coding alleviates concerns with C++ and makes Qt a pleasant place. Edit, in response to comments: When wrote about Qt being written in C++, not much complaining about Qt itself, but more about the environment it lives in. true Qt manages its own resources well, but all your GUI-related-but-not-Qt code has to be written in C++, too. Even there, Qt provides many nice tools, but ultimately, you have to deal with C++ at that level. Qt makes C++ bearable, but it is still C++.As for introspection, I mean is this: hardest cases to debug are when you have a pointer to object that not behave the way you think it should. With C++, your debugger might to look inside object bit (if it happens to have type information at thwt point), but even that not always work. Take, on other hand, Cocoa in same situation. In Cocoa/Obj-C, you able to send messages ('call functions') to object right within debugger. You can change objects state, can query it for its attributes, ask it for its type and function names. This can make debugging more convenient. Qt/C++ has nothing close to that.

had same problem solved it by noticing wrong (corrupted or) qlgenerator used to generate quicklook preview of plain-text files. To do this, can type, in terminal, qlmanage -m plugins search for public. plain-textstring (e. g. using grep), should get something similar to qlmanage -m plugins | grep public. plain-text public. plain-text -> /Library/QuickLook/QLMultiMarkdown. qlgenerator (1. 2. 1 - loaded) means in my case QLMultiMarkdown responsible for generating corrupted quicklook for plain-text extension (. txt). must be way to force quicklook to point to another qlgenerator for public. plain-text., didn't try because don't need QLMultiMarkdown. Instead, moved QLMultiMarkdown. qlgenerator to backup subfolder (/Library/QuickLook/bak/) reloaded qlmanage with qlmanage -r can now try to preview any. txt files with quicklook by hitting spacebar. hope it works for you! for own info, to verify which qlgenerator is in use now, re-type qlmanage -m plugins | grep public. plain-text outputs public. plain-text -> /Library/QuickLook/QLColorCode. qlgenerator (2. 0. 1 - loaded) in my case. (Note QLColorCode is handy extension for syntax highlighting of source code but useless for simple text files. However it works won't complain about it. )

Functional specification is a design document - describes functionality of system. John Bode suggest is something else, system specification in OP's context means specification of software system, done by business analyst. System requirements specification describes functionality system as wanted by users.

Basically, yes. Software Requirements Specification states business users want system to do, Functional specification describes actual functions of system, usually linked to business requirements. E. g: Business requirement (User): I want to see number of trades and exposures Functional spec: grid displaying in one column Trade with its ID and other column exposure. exposure taken from table TRADE_EXPOSURES. design should be separated from requirements. FS is lower level of SRS. FS is used for test case derivation in functional testing, SRS usually for acceptance testing. SRS also used as base for system testing, where implenentation is validated against it (does it fit what customer wanted?)

IME, system specs define hardware and software environment new application will operate in, functional specs define what application will do (my experience may not be typical,). Design documents are different animal. They define structure of application, breaking it into components, specifying implementation of each component, interfaces between components, order in which components perform operations, etc. ("component" is meant to be high-level, abstract term here; it could correspond to classes, modules, or individual functions or methods). Design documents often have a "traceability matrix" showing requirements satisfied by particular elements of design. For simple example: System specification: application will run on Linux as command-line app in bash shell. Functional specification: application will print text "Hello, World" to console then terminate. Design document: application will be implemented as single C program consisting of function main, taking no arguments. Upon entry, it will call standard library function printf with string literal "Hello, World\n" as its sole argument. After printf call, application will return a 0 to execution environment. "design document" isn't usually so detailed as to specify individual lines of code, but you should get idea.

Features are what your program can do. Features direct result of user requirements, and business objectives. a program's features exist mainly to meet user demands. Functionality, on other hand, is how features are implemented.

For a PM, "Function" is purpose and "Feature" is product behavior user can interact with. people often get two backwards (which is case in your question). Getting me from place A to place B is a key function of a car. Its reason (purpose) it exists. steering wheel is a feature, as is gear stick. driver interacts with multiple features to achieve function of getting somewhere. "Function" not be confused with programming language function (method) talks about implementation of feature software. most likely not what a PM would talking about when refer to "Features and Functions". not a nice hierarchy to functions and features, one feature may be used to support multiple product functions.

V-model is an extension of Waterfall model, don't expect it to be hugely different. Basically, you follow V-model from left to right, just like in Waterfall model. In Waterfall, you do requirements, design, implementation, verification and finally maintenance. In same way, in V-model, you do requirements, design, implementation, verification and maintenance: same steps in both cases. major differences with Waterfall are way it presented and emphasis on testing. Representing flow as V-shape helps making difference between everything prior to coding (requirements, architecture and design) and everything follows coding (essentially testing). While tests are just one of five steps in Waterfall, looks like practically half of process in V-model. diagram in question is more complicated. tries to show, for example, system design step leads not only to system design document, like Waterfall model suggest, but also system tests design, will later help writing system tests. diagram puts more emphasis on testing., doing system test design helps in architecture design (it be awkward to do architecture design regardless system test design). Searching other explanations on internet, can't avoid quoting following article by Bhakti Satalkar: main difference between waterfall model and V model is in waterfall model, testing activities are carried out after development activities are over. On in V model, testing activities start with first stage itself. In, waterfall model is a continuous process, while V model is a simultaneous process. As compared to software made using waterfall model, number of defects in software made using V model are less. due to fact, testing activities, carried out simultaneously in V model. Therefore, waterfall model is used, when requirements of user are fixed. If requirements of user are uncertain and keep changing, then V model is better alternative. This explanation is misleading. true only if you replace “V-model” in quote by any Agile method.Unlike article states, in V-model, testing done after coding; for example, see Wikipedia: common practical criticism of V-Model is it leads to testing squeezed into tight windows at end of development when earlier stages overrun but implementation date remains fixed., in V-model, system test design follows system design without waiting until product implementation done, doesn't mean tests performed before coding. author confounds V-model with Agile approaches like Test Driven Development (TDD) in Extreme Programming (XP).

For a PM, "Function" is purpose and "Feature" is product behavior user can interact with. people often get two backwards (which is case in your question). Getting me from place A to place B is a key function of a car. Its reason (purpose) it exists. steering wheel is a feature, as is gear stick. driver interacts with multiple features to achieve function of getting somewhere. "Function" not be confused with programming language function (method) talks about implementation of feature software. most likely not what a PM would talking about when refer to "Features and Functions". not a nice hierarchy to functions and features, one feature may be used to support multiple product functions.

Features are what your program can do. Features direct result of user requirements, and business objectives. a program's features exist mainly to meet user demands. Functionality, on other hand, is how features are implemented.
Features are what sales people sell. Functions programmers develop.

Functions don't fit into context user story are mostly transparent to user. They may be a backend process or unique or common application functionality enables other features or possibly other functions to implemented appropriately. Tasks are individual units of work must be completed to deliver either a feature or function. In my projects I not to differentiate between a Feature and a Function I write user stories for features add functions or refactoring efforts as Tasks to complete a single feature. This sometimes makes certain features look bloated on project plan but this is okay, because if I need Functions 1 and 2 and Function 3 to be refactored to deliver Feature 1 perhaps my only deliverable for sprint will be Feature 1, or possibly no deliverables at all. As long by end of sprint I still have working software then my project is Agile.

A function is takes inputs returns one or more values. If returned values entirely determined by inputs, function doesn't have side effects (logging, perhaps, or causing state changes outside itself), then it's called a pure function. A procedure is a function that doesn't return a value., this means procedure can only cause side effects. (That might include mutating input parameter!) A method is function that closes over a set of variables, a closure. It takes zero or more input parameters, has access to set variables, returns zero or more values. In OO languages methods are attached to objects or classes. In most mainstream OO languages, closed-over variables are called member fields, or instance variables, of an object. A method can be a pure function, impure function or a procedure. latter definition leads to object = struct + closures correspondence.

good detailed answers above; short story is they'll all flavors of subroutines; what meant by each term vary according to programming language context in, functions return a value, but don't have to methods are generic OOP terms present in SQL, stored procedures have outputs typically only return error code, user-defined functions must return a value (which may be result-set), precise difference between these terms depends on who you're talking to!
function returns value, but procedure does not. method is similar to a function, but is internal to part of class. term method is used almost exclusively in object-oriented programming.

I'm going with different answer here: practically speaking, no difference, with slight exception that "method" usually refers to a subroutine associated with object in OO languages. terms "procedure, function, subroutine, subprogram, and method" all mean same thing: a callable sub-program within a larger program. difficult to come with definition that captures all variant usages of these terms, because they not used consistently across programming languages or paradigms. You might say a function returns a value., following C function doesn't return a value: void f() { return; }. but doubt you'd find anyone would call it a procedure., in Pascal, procedures don't return values and functions return values, but merely a reflection of how Pascal designed. In Fortran, function returns a value, and subroutine returns multiple values. none of this allows us to "universal" definition for these terms. In, term "procedural programming" refers to whole class of languages, including C, Fortran and Pascal, only one of uses term "procedure" to mean anything. none of this is really consistent. only exception is probably "method", to used almost entirely with OO languages, referring to a function associated with object., this not always consistent. C++, for example, usually uses term "member function" rather than method, (even though term "method" has crept into C++ vernacular among programmers. ) point is, none of this is really consistent. It simply reflects terminology employed by whatever languages are en vogue at the time.

IME, system specs define hardware and software environment new application will operate in, functional specs define what application will do (my experience may not be typical,). Design documents are different animal. They define structure of application, breaking it into components, specifying implementation of each component, interfaces between components, order in which components perform operations, etc. ("component" is meant to be high-level, abstract term here; it could correspond to classes, modules, or individual functions or methods). Design documents often have a "traceability matrix" showing requirements satisfied by particular elements of design. For simple example: System specification: application will run on Linux as command-line app in bash shell. Functional specification: application will print text "Hello, World" to console then terminate. Design document: application will be implemented as single C program consisting of function main, taking no arguments. Upon entry, it will call standard library function printf with string literal "Hello, World\n" as its sole argument. After printf call, application will return a 0 to execution environment. "design document" isn't usually so detailed as to specify individual lines of code, but you should get idea.

iBGP requires full mesh or use of mitigation like confederations or route reflectors, BGP doesn't converge with like speed of OSPF, etc. Each OSPF router would full understanding of all routes in area in it resides without needing full mesh, it converges very, quickly. Using IGP is recommended with iBGP. Without IGP, iBGP must neighbor on external-facing interfaces, with an IGP, iBGP can neighbor on loopback interfaces never go down, can have multiple paths to reach. seen iBGP-only for local routing, but it more difficult and fragile.

anyone explain need of IBGP communication for routes, when we have IGP protocols (OSPF, RIP) for internal communication? Scalability1: Imagine you receiving 500, 000 EBGP routes in more than one location2, need to influence per route exit point in your AS. BGP can handle more routes than IGP protocols., iBGP required unless you willing to redistribute all routes learned via eBGP Enforce boundaries of trust / control: BGP has more ways to filter peers than IGPs (for controlling what you advertise and receive). Flexible data structures (somewhat related to previous bullet): BGP communities, BGP Extended communities, local-pref, etc. these make BGP attractive way to implement custom routing policies within own autonomous system (by using iBGP). with everything trade offs; scalability, control, flexibility from iBGP means it's slower converging protocol than IGPs (in general). End Notes: 1 Scalability: use BGP because don't want to carry entire internet routing table in your IGP (i. e. in case, OSPF). OSPF not designed to handle many thousands of routes in internet BGP tables. if try to use OSPF for this purpose, it will break your network. Using example of OSPF, LSA processing / flooding requirements from 500, 000 routes uses too many resources in routers. Name any other IGP (EIGRP, RIPv1/2, IS-IS, IGRP) same story is true. notorious instances where Tier-1 ISP accidentally redistributed BGP table into IGP (even internet table small fraction of current size) caused major outages. Countermeasures now implemented in IGP protocols (like this one for OSPF in IOS) to prevent redistribution from BGP into OSPF from causing major outage.2 iBGP routing example understand want iBGP, consider routing entry to 4. 2. 2. 2. One reason I've seen often is clarity: all routes carried within one routing protocol (BGP), IS-IS, OSPF or RIP only used for adjacency. no need to redistribute routes from one routing protocol to another.

iBGP isn't used for internal routing, it is used by all eBGP routers to share routes. Ex: If you peering with 3 other network, you want all eBGP routers to know routes received by other ones so they can propagate information to peers if necessary/needed (opening possibility of peer using transit through you)

suggest right answer is depends on topology of network. OSPF requires area boundaries to do summarization, if you doing green field network or topology condusive to drawing areas out use it. If network requires spokes to connect to multiple hubs, OSPF is harder to do, when I had this requirement on my frame relay network I migrated remote sites to BGP. wanted to use EIGRP and stub routers but cisco mentioned more resources spent on BGP-OSPF interoperability vs EIGRP-OSPF interoperability so I went BGP on basis. Another way to put it is EIGRP with stub routers and ability to summarize wherever you want will scale better in 'messy' topology.

using iBGP, router must have full mesh, or must use a mitigation. Route reflectors are one mitigation. another mitigation similar to you suggest, called confederations. It breaks your AS in sub-ASes uses eBGP between sub-ASes. can search for BGP confederations, find documents, such as IP Routing: BGP Configuration Guide: BGP Routing Domain Confederation One way to reduce internal BGP (iBGP) mesh is to divide autonomous system into multiple subautonomous systems and group them into single confederation. To outside world, confederation looks like a single autonomous system. Each autonomous system is fully meshed within itself has few connections to other autonomous systems in same confederation. Even though peers in different autonomous systems have external BGP (eBGP) sessions, they exchange routing information as if they were iBGP peers. Specifically, next hop, Multi Exit Discriminator (MED) attribute, and local preference information are preserved. This feature allows to retain single Interior Gateway Protocol (IGP) for all autonomous systems. To configure BGP confederation, must specify confederation identifier. To outside world, group of autonomous systems will look like single autonomous system with confederation identifier as autonomous system number. Route reflectors are simpler to configure, easy to screw up confederation design and configurations. If large AS, buying many AS numbers can be problematic, confederations can internally use private AS numbers because do not advertise them outside your AS. Some people like router reflectors, and some people like confederations. Having multiple, real ASes isn't practical.

IGP usually is OSPF or ISIS are link-state based, gives us all information of network, everyone knows network from everyone's point-of-view, allows for interesting convergence options and traffic engineering options. BGP is essentially distance-vector, knows limited view on network at whole. BGP handles well filtering and modifying routing information. Link-state protocol is expensive compared to distance-vector, problematic to scale to INET DFZ size. reason why we have both, is because inside one specific network, sufficiently low-complexity to handle with link-state protocol, allows to gain advantages of high degree of knowledge of network. But does not scale to Internet size, need other network to connect these many link-state islands. You could inside your own network carry all prefixes (including customer) in IGP, but will negatively impact IGP performance, all convergence and TE advantages can be gained by just carrying loopback addresses of core routers. Adding customer prefixes to IGP hurts network performance by making IGP unnecessarily complex.

You can read about finer workings of these protocols for yourself, they thoroughly documented on Internet it's a doddle to find information on them. From practicle perspective in case of EIGRP vs OSPF, OSPF always wins for following reasons: Convergence Speed: Everyone mentioned EIGRP faster than OSPF using default settings. If deploy either protocol without reading about them and use their default settings, you clearly don't know what you are doing in my opinion. Why deploy default settings without knowing what they are, when realise what they are realise OSPF supports BFD becomes lightening quick (as does ISIS). Traffic Engineering: OSPF like ISIS is based on TLV values, been extended quite a lot. It support for extensions like MPLS-TE and GMPLS. Continual Expansion As mentioned, OSPF and ISIS extended quite a lot extension drafts written regularly will continue to be. EIGRP doesn't have many of advanced options these two do. Scalability OSPF scales better than EIGRP with its use of areas however, don't think this really matters (like convergence time aregument, due to BFD). Not many people running 10k routes in one area in OSPF. Typically I would use IGP for fast routing within given part of network, but ultimately iBGP carries all internal routes. Every single router doesn't need every internal route in its RIB sourced via OSPF if you have hundreds or thousands or routers, some of far away (topologically speaking) it's worthless knowing about them. Interoperability Lastly reason EIGRP is/was a Cisco proprietary technology. this recently submitted into draft for other software vendors to start incorporating, it's too late (I believe).No currently running network to waste huge sums money switching from other IGP to EIGRP, I don't know why new network would consider it (if mixing Cisco equipment with non-Cisco). Simply because non-Cisco equipment supports OSPF has been doing so for years. code is tried and test, many bugs fixed, oodles of information on line etc. It will take years for EIGRP to catch up (if't too late already!).

, I dispute assertion some others made OSPF converges faster than BGP, more on later. To answer OP question first. You want both. iBGP designed to run between loopback interfaces on routers doesn't (at least without tweaking and turning knobs) change attributes (which includes next-hop) of routes it's advertising. what implications of that? Let's call your border routers router A, and router B and your for-argument's-sake three access routers router 1, router 2, and router 3. Router's A and B get full Internet feeds from upstreams, with next-hop set to upstream's interface address on interconnecting link. EIGRP is now an IETF draft no longer proprietary. Commonly deployed in DMVPNS. EIGRP is less confusing than OSPF not have different network types and EIGRP easier to deploy in hub and spoke scenarios. EIGRP uses flat network without areas, this can both be an advantage and disadvantage. OSPF is an open standard's logical choice if multiple vendors. Network administrators usually be more comfortable with OSPF because it's more commonly deployed. Both protocols have advantages and disadvantages. using iBGP, router must have full mesh, or must use a mitigation. Route reflectors are one mitigation. another mitigation similar to you suggest, called confederations. It breaks your AS in sub-ASes uses eBGP between sub-ASes. can search for BGP confederations, find documents, such as IP Routing: BGP Configuration Guide: BGP Routing Domain Confederation One way to reduce internal BGP (iBGP) mesh is to divide autonomous system into multiple subautonomous systems and group them into single confederation. To outside world, confederation looks like a single autonomous system. Each autonomous system is fully meshed within itself has few connections to other autonomous systems in same confederation. Even though peers in different autonomous systems have external BGP (eBGP) sessions, they exchange routing information as if they were iBGP peers. Specifically, next hop, Multi Exit Discriminator (MED) attribute, and local preference information are preserved. This feature allows to retain single Interior Gateway Protocol (IGP) for all autonomous systems. To configure BGP confederation, must specify confederation identifier. To outside world, group of autonomous systems will look like single autonomous system with confederation identifier as autonomous system number. Route reflectors are simpler to configure, easy to screw up confederation design and configurations. If large AS, buying many AS numbers can be problematic, confederations can internally use private AS numbers because do not advertise them outside your AS. Some people like router reflectors, and some people like confederations. Having multiple, real ASes isn't practical.

Executive summary: "root" is actual name of administrator account. "sudo" is a command allows ordinary users to perform administrative tasks. "Sudo" is not a user. Long answer: "root" (aka "superuser") is the name of system administrator account. origins of name are archaic, but doesn't matter. Root user has user id 0 and nominally has unlimited privileges. Root can access any file, run any program, execute any system call, modify any setting. (But see below1). Prior to invention of "sudo" command, if wanted to perform administrative tasks, you had to login as root, either by getting login prompt2, or with su command ("su" short for substitute user. )3 That's hassle, doesn't let give users partial administrative powers. So "sudo" command (short for "substitute user do") was invented. "sudo" command lets you execute commands with superuser privileges as long as your user id is in sudoers file, giving necessary authorization., e. g. sudo vi /etc/hosts would allow you to edit hosts file as if running as root. don't need root password, just your own login password., sudo su would allow you to simply become root. result is same as if logged in as root or executed su command, except you don't need to know root password but do need to be in sudoers file. sudoers file determines who can use sudo command and what they can do with it. sudoers file gives you multiple administrators4. Effectively, your administrators are root, plus everybody listed in sudoers file. Without sudoers file, only administrator is root. In, in organizations where someone else administers your computer for you, common to not know root password of your own computer — as long as you're in sudoers file, it doesn't matter.At one company I worked for, with a ginormous server farm, only very, small number of people knew root passwords. Instead, there was a database of who was allowed to work on which servers. automated process would add you to sudoers files of servers you authorized to access, and remove you when authorization expired. 1: modern Unix versions can now restrict even what root user can do. Under SELinux (Security Enhanced Linux), access control list determines which program can do what, even root can't get past those restrictions. Under Apple's System Integrity Protection (SIP) (aka "rootless") system, certain files and directories are locked down only applications on appropriate whitelist can access them. These systems exist to protect system from a malicious user to obtain root access. (Or in some cases, to prevent users from jailbreaking embedded devices. ) For, extremely difficult to bypass these restrictions, even with root access. 2 "login: " prompt is archaic piece of Unix history, dating back to when used ascii terminals on serial lines, instead of window systems. You can still get a "login: " prompt by typing login in any terminal window, or by opening ssh (or telnet or rsh) connection to computer from elsewhere. could log in as another user from there if wanted. (And if computer have serial ports, can still configure it to allow logins on them. ) 3 possible for individual programs to be given root access. These programs can do anything a user with root access can do, even when run by ordinary user. typically limited to specific tasks. For example, crontab program has root privileges can edit cron tables., "sudo" has root privileges it can do what it does. 4 to cover one point glossed over previously. been using "administrator" and "root" interchangeably, but there are other kinds of administrators.These are often called "role accounts", to say these accounts don't belong to actual humans, but instead exist to perform some specific role on system. If you look at /etc/passwd file on your system, you'll find dozens dozens of such accounts. For example, if mysql was installed on your system, there be a "mysql" user, and all of database files, config files, all owned by that user. Only that user (and root, of) have necessary permissions to access files and run mysql server. In, that user would be an administrator account, but only for mysql. If you needed to perform database administrative tasks, you either become "mysql" with su mysql command, or use sudo where sudoers file give mysql privileges for those specific commands.

root user (UID 0) exists in every Unix or Unix-like operating system. Every process of Unix operating systems must run as a valid user/UID, independently of system processes, daemons, services or user-initiated applications. Every basic system-process runs under UID 0 (root), every system-relevant file is owned by that user. For reasons security, some processes running as different "users" with lesser privileges than superuser root. Such users there for solely purpose to start services, as webserver, database, window server., not every user configured on Unix (or macOS) is a "real" user., most system-users can not log-in interactively. For example webserver (nginx, apache,. ) will started by script running under UID 0 (=root). webserver-process drops privileges to specific UID (in this, it could be user www). www is not a real user cannot be used to log in to system interactively. two ways to "deactivate" a (system) user: set user shell to /bin/false (or non valid-shell) disable users's password, setting it to an invalid, empty or specific value. On macOS non-valid user has empty password and specific property set on local OpenDirectory server. Usually, for request "is valid user" OpenDirectory service in macOS does simple check on requested user returns true (user can log in) or false (user cannot log in)., Apples bug was not to check user's validity but to set it to enabled. On already enabled accounts this had no effect, but disabled accounts became valid, enabled accounts. since disabled user has no password, empty password was accepted as a valid option to log in as superuser/root.

Originally, users intended to correspond to a human using system, hence name. Each process runs as particular user, each file owned by particular user. A special user, called root, is used for things don't belong to any particular human user,. e. operating system itself. Since root corresponds to operating system itself, it has all privileges. Soon people found convenient to create multiple system users, without extensive privileges. This allows isolating various services run on machine, they don't tread on each others' toes. A service account (or “system account”, two terms are synonyms) is one corresponds to service running on system, rather than to someone using the system. generally have a service account for each task running on system has its own set of privileges (e. g. its own files, own network ports, etc. ). no formal definition of human vs system/service account. kernel doesn't care (other than granting lot of privileges to user with UID 0). Most administration commands don't care either. typical differences are: human user has real name like “John Doe”, system user has descriptive name like “Nasal daemon” or none at all. human user has real login shell (e. /bin/sh or /bin/bash or /bin/csh. Some system users have a shell (almost always /bin/sh), others don't, depending on how meant to be used (e. su foo requires foo to have shell). human user often has a password but not always the case, for example remote-only user might only have SSH key. Note on modern unices, password not in /etc/passwd but in some other file such as /etc/shadow. human user's home directory usually under /home (or site-specific location), system user's home directory usually not under /home and might not exist (but exceptions).sites designate range of user IDs for system users and disjoint range for human users. Reserving 100–65533 or 500–65533 or 1000–65533 is typical, most distributions set up to start allocating real user IDs from 500 or 1000. On sites where accounts shared across multiple machines, typically a central server contains user lists, accessible via NIS or LDAP. passwd entry in /etc/nsswitch. conf specifies where to find user information. common to have system users in local /etc/passwd and real users from network-wide database, but sometimes system users in network-wide database (to enforce consistent UIDs, facilitates server and data replication), and sometimes human users in local file (to let them log in even when network is hosed). human-accessible account disguised as system user typically not have real name, but have login shell, and either password set or SSH key, while having user ID in system range. In, better disguise to use actual system account whose removal cause some service to stop working. hard-and-fast rules to detect potential attacks: by definition, attackers don't follow rules. Service accounts and human accounts managed by same commands and recorded in same files. Account creation commands may have options to set reasonable defaults for human vs service users, e. g. to pick user ID in proper range, and to prompt for password for human and disable password authentication for service. For example, adduser vs adduser --system or useradd vs useradd -r on Linux.

Long Answer SDD (Spinning Disc Drive) - a. k. a HDD (Hard Disc Drive) important to know difference between Spinning Disc Drive (SDD) and Solid State Drive (SSD) answer What is a Spinning Disc Drive? Spinning Disc Drives have moving parts Spinning Disc Drives phased out in favor of Solid State Drives (at in consumer applications) SSD (Solid State Drive) SSD means "a hard drive without moving parts" Solid State Drive developed to improve upon Spinning Disc Drives (moving parts not reliable and slow to read from memory) SSD has been around for decades (contrary to popular belief) Recently, technology gotten better, see them in all newer comptuers RAM (Random Access Memory) SSD's originally achieved by using RAM as method to store data RAM requires continuous power to applied to retain data By using RAM, hard drive no longer had moving parts major downside of using RAM: can never turn hard drive off or else lose all data. Historically, RAM was/is used in conjunction with Spinning Disc Drive or Solid State Drive (since RAM cannot retain data once powered off) upside of using RAM: RAM is super fast - faster than SSD's and flash memory Flash Storage Flash storage is old technology, started as way to permanently store information without power continuously applied (in contrast to RAM) Flash storage traditionally had significant aging issues could only write to memory certain number of times before lose section of drive, and performance worse over time.Flash storage improved (in late 2000’s), manufacturers started making SSDs out of Flash memory instead of out of RAM. Modern SSD hard drives are Flash-based, today, not a difference between SSD's and Flash memory., SSD's are simply disks have no moving parts, Flash is implementation allows that to happen USB thumb drives have used Flash storage for long time, but quality of Flash storage in USB's is typically lower than Flash memory used in SSD's. This means worse performance for USB's than SSD's (but believe current USB technology is improving to close gap) SUMMARY SSD means a hard disk doesn’t have moving parts; Flash is type of memory fast and doesn’t require continuous power (non-volatile) SSDs used to use RAM, but now use Flash instead. In, shouldn’t compare Flash to SSD just as shouldn’t compare batteries to lithium-ion. In both cases latter is a type of the former.

It's bit messy, degree of cross-overs, but quick tour, without going into subfolders of these: /etc, /tmp and /var are just symbolic links to subfolders in /private. /etc generally contains configuration files. /tmp is for temporary files used by running processes (also see /var/tmp) /var also used for somewhat temporary files used by running processes, to less temporary more often preserved between runs - e. g. logfiles usually in /var/log. /usr contains binaries (executables) and developer-related files for core unix/BSD utilities. Things user installs themselves should end up in /usr/local. /bin also contains binaries to more OS-fundamental than those in /usr - such as cp, cat, bash. /sbin is as above focused on routine administrative tasks such as mount and shutdown. s=system/superuser, usually need root/superuser rights to use these commands. /. fseventsd used by OS to log file-system change events (such as folder creation) interested parties can be notified when filesystem changes., to run risk of saying what didn't want to say - most of these of little interest, if to use any, most likely to be in /usr/local, /var/log or /tmp. No, Windows offers different recovery features than OS X. Windows is creating automatic (and allowing manual creation of) system restore points. Restore points created to allow users choice of previous system states. Each restore point contains necessary information needed to restore system to chosen state. Restore points are created before key changes made to system. These restore points are actual copies of registry, device drivers, other configuration and take up disk space on system drive. With OS X no such system-level backups are taken (or no control over them given to user). Apple takes different approach protects core system files and configuration by making them immutable or by observing tough control over their modifications. SIP (System Integrity Protection) with to file system protection in ensures applications and unsigned drivers installed by user won't mess or) with core system configuration so it will always boot to good state (and need for restoring to last known good state eliminated). Either Windows or OS X allow system reinstall without deleting user files.
