complement @Polynomial's self-answer: DEP can be enforced on older x86 machines (which predate NX bit), but at a price. easy but limited way to do DEP on old x86 hardware is to use segment registers. With current operating systems on such systems, addresses are 32-bit values in flat 4 GB address space, but internally each memory access implicitly uses a 32-bit address and special 16-bit register, called a "segment register". In protected mode, segment registers point to internal table (the "descriptor table" -- two such tables, technicality) each entry in table specifies characteristics of segment., types of allowed accesses, and size of segment., code execution implicitly uses CS segment register, data access uses mostly DS (and stack access,. g. with push and pop opcodes, uses SS). This allows operating system to split address space into two parts; lower addresses in range for both CS and DS, upper addresses out of range for CS. For instance, segment described by CS is made to be of size 512 MB. means any address beyond 0x20000000 accessible as data (read or written to using DS as base register) but execution attempts will use CS, CPU will raise an exception (which kernel will convert into suitable signal like SIGILL or SIGSEGV, usually implying death of offending process). (Note segments are applied on address space; MMU is still active, on lower layer, trick explained above is per-process. ) This is cheap to do: x86 hardware enforce segments, systematically (and first 80386 was already doing it;, 80286 already had such segments with boundaries, but only 16-bit offsets). can usually forget them because sane operating systems set segments to begin at offset zero and be 4 GB long, but setting them otherwise does not imply overhead we did not already have., as DEP mechanism, is inflexible: when data block requested from kernel, kernel must decide whether is for code or not for code, because boundary is fixed. We cannot decide to dynamically convert any given page between code-mode and data-mode. fun but more expensive way to do DEP uses PaX. To understand it does, one must go into details. MMU on x86 hardware uses in-memory tables, describe status of every 4 kB page in address space. address space is 4 GB, so are 1048576 pages. Each page described by a 32-bit entry in a sub-table; 1024 sub-tables, each holding 1024 entries, and one main table, with 1024 entries point to 1024 sub-tables. Each entry tells where pointed-to object (a sub-table, or page) is in RAM, or whether it is there at all, and what are its access rights. root of issue is access rights are about privilege levels (kernel code vs userland) and only one bit for access type, allowing "read-write" or "read-only". "Execution" is considered to be a kind of read access., MMU has no notion of "execution" distinct from data access. That which is readable, is executable. (Since Pentium Pro, in previous century, x86 processors know of another format for tables, called PAE. It doubles size of entries, leaves room for addressing more physical RAM, and also adding a NX bit -- but specific bit implemented by hardware only around 2004. ), trick. RAM is slow. To perform memory access, processor must first read main table to locate sub-table it must consult, then do another read to that sub-table, only at that point does processor know whether memory access should be allowed or not, and where in physical RAM accessed data is.These are read accesses with full dependency (each access depends on value read by previous) this pays full latency, on modern CPU, can represent hundreds of clock cycles., CPU includes a specific cache contains most recently accessed MMU table entries. This cache is the Translation Lookaside Buffer. From 80486 onwards, x86 CPU do not have one TLB, but two. Caching works on heuristics, heuristics depend on access patterns, access patterns for code tend to differ from access patterns for data. smart people at Intel/AMD/other found it worthwhile to have a TLB dedicated to code access (execution), and another for data access., 80486 has opcode (invlpg) can remove specific entry from TLB. idea is following: make two TLB have different views of same entry. All pages are marked in tables (in RAM) as "absent", triggering exception upon access. kernel traps exception, exception includes data about type of access, in particular whether it was for code execution, or not. kernel then invalidates newly read TLB entry (the one which says "absent"), then fills entry in RAM with rights which allow access, then forces one access of needed type (either data read or code execution), feeds entry into corresponding TLB, only that one. kernel sets entry in RAM back to absent, finally returns to process (back to trying again opcode which triggered exception). net effect is that, when execution comes back to process code, TLB for code or TLB for data contains appropriate entry, but other TLB does not, and will not since tables in RAM still say "absent". At point, kernel is in position to decide whether to allow execution or not, independently from whether it allows data access or not. It can enforce NX-like semantics.Devil hides in details; in this case, room for a whole legion of demons. a dance with hardware is not easy to implement properly. Especially on multi-core systems. overhead is following: when access is performed and TLB does not contain relevant entry, tables in RAM must be accessed, that alone implies losing a few hundred cycles. To cost, PaX adds overhead of exception, and management code which fills right TLB, turning "a few hundred cycles" into "a few thousand cycles". Fortunately, TLB misses are right. PaX people claim to measured slowdown of as little as 2. 7% on a big compilation job (this depends on CPU type,). NX bit makes all of this obsolete. Note PaX patchset also contains other security-related features, such as ASLR, is redundant with some functionality of newer official kernels.

believe WPA was original WPA standard, WPA2 was improved version of it. Some network cards can’t connect to WPA2 networks. From Wikipedia page on WPA: later WPA2 certification mark indicates compliance with full IEEE 802. 11i standard. This advanced protocol not work with some older network cards. Wikipedia article cites white paper from Wi-Fi Alliance: WPA is both forward and backward-compatible designed to run on existing Wi-Fi devices as software download. In nutshell, WPA/WPA2 network will any network card that supports WPA or WPA2 to connect to it; WPA2 only network locks out network cards only support newer standard. don’t think meaningful difference in security., I’ve used WPA2 Personal on my Airport Extreme since bought it, no device ever had problems connecting. Confession: initially misread question as about difference between Personal and Enterprise, wrote this. not directly answering question, include it for interest. “Personal” and “Enterprise” refer to two flavours of WPA and WPA2. From Wi-fi Alliance’s page on WPA2: WPA2 can be enabled in two versions - WPA2 Personal and WPA2 Enterprise. WPA2 - Personal protects unauthorized network access by utilizing set-up password. WPA2 - Enterprise verifies network users through server. WPA2 is backward compatible with WPA. believe WPA and WPA2 both come in these two flavours, hence either/or. Personal is more suitable for home network, but less secure than enterprise. Enterprise connects to “RADIUS server” for authentication. don’t know what that is, but sounds clever and secure. guess device connecting to your Time Capsule sees request for WPA2 password, hence why it doesn’t ask you for WPA2 Personal password.

Both 'WPA' and 'WPA2' use AES to encrypt information transiting WiFi network, but WPA uses TKIP to manage keys to encrypt data. TKIP is vulnerable to attack (it not secure) and should not be used. WPA2 uses AES-CCMP for key management. "WPA/WPA2 Personal", also called mixed-mode, allows negotiation of key management modes and reduces security of network to lowest common denominator. BOTTOM LINE: If concerned about security/privacy of information on networks (wired and wireless), DON'T use WPA or WPA/WPA2. Use WPA2 only., if't, WEP is basically same as no security at all. poster points out 'Enterprise' modes send authentication requests to server before allowing client on network. two big advantages are: central management: I don't have to set keys on every access point, and can disable accounts of individual users. traceability: I know which WiFi device belongs to which user. longer keys (like 2048 bit, versus 128 for 'personal'). This decreases likelihood attacker can figure out key in time it's in use. 'personal' pre-shared key ("PSK") is derived from passphrase you type into client, even if PSK allowed long keys, you'd have to type passphrase most people would object to.
Codeproof MDM supports WPA2-Enterprise WiFi configurations offer 14 days free trial of software.
Internet Sharing now supports WPA2 encryption (and no longer supports WEP,) when sharing wired connection to Wi-Fi.

key thing is WPS isn't a Wireless protocol to secure WiFi connection but a protocol to connect a device (e. your Mac) to a WiFi router. instead of selecting right network and typing WiFi password into device you can press a button (either physical or virtual) on both router and device have them figure out rest themselves. This feature is fairly secure both devices get out of WPS mode after short time even if no connection established), but also a PIN based method each certified WPS product must support. This method can be remotely attacked and broken within hours, giving attacker access to WPA/WPA keys and whole network.'s it's highly recommended to disable the feature, at least after set up a network. In Apple land WPS isn't used much because neither OS X nor iOS support it. Airport Utiltiy 6. x allows to add WPS printers that way (with either button or PIN method) but that's about as support goes. to question: To secure your WiFi network against WPS attacks you must disable the feature on your router/modem (if possible).

terms used differently by different people, but below is generally accepted. Bandwidth is number of bits per second a link can send or receive, including all flows. For example, bandwidth of 100 Mbps connections is 100 Mbps, but doesn't mean it is always sending or receiving 100 Mbps, but is maximum possible on that link. Unlike many people mean by bandwidth, it does not mean data usage. see people say they have a bandwidth limitation (every link does), used all their bandwidth for the month. This incorrect use of term. they mean to say is they have a data usage limitation, used it up for the month. Throughput is amount of data during a time period a flow (process to process) can send or receive. includes all host overhead, and contention on link (multiple flows on link will each use some percentage of bandwidth, reducing throughput of each). Bit rate is closer to bandwidth, but often per host, or source to destination devices. You may have bit rate of 100 Mbps from a host to a switch, but bit rate from a host to a host is less. usually includes multiple flows.

Daily I see peoples specialists in communication do mistakes about three terms: Bandwidth: unit of it is Hz, it is mathematically is: High_Used_Frequency - Low_Used_Frequency., when we measure bandwidth in bps, i. we do mistake. Beside, some guys working in Network field, they treat with bandwidth as Data rate., bandwidth is difference between high and low frequency. For example, bandwidth of a channel in FM is 0. 2MHz, for carrier is WCDMA is 5MHz. Data Rate: unit is bps, we can say data rate of channel is maximum ability of channel can transmit bits in a second. In normal case, can say if we have 5MHz bandwidth, channel capacity (or data rate) is 5Mbps, but also it can be bandwidth is 5MHz but data rate is 10Mbps, or 2. 5Mbps, depends on modulation type and other Technics. Throughput: This term is used in many different systems, shortly, we can define it as: real data that we receive. For example, Bandwidth=5MHz, channel capacity(data rate)=10Mbps, but what we receive exactly is 6Mpbs due to reason, throughput is 6Mbps. Hope gave you an idea.

Not disagreeing with other answers, but important takeaway is people often meaning slightly different things with similar identical words. couple of points worth adding, especially if you do anything numerical like try to work out maximum throughput of a given FTP connection over X Mbit/sec line: Kbit/sec, Mbit/sec etc in data rates are always powers of 10 as I ever seen File sizes equally stated as powers of 2 and often powers of 10, frequently people don't know ("few hundred megabyte" doesn't matter at that accuracy. ) If you get oscilloscope on wire quickly find out symbol rate can be different. 100baseT for example is 125 Mbaud, because it transmits 5 bits on wire for 4 bits of data. In summary, terms used often vary depending on what you emphasising: Throughput emphasises all things which could slow it down, much "net result". Bandwidth emphasises gross bit rate, still have to pay for all framing and overheads before you get throughput. You sometimes see things like "peak throughput" and "average sustained throughput" regard as very helpful. often rates interesting depend entirely on period you average over. PS IEC prefixes kibi, mebi, etc are far from universally used but worth knowing about

depends on how devices connected. Say we three devices connected: A(400) <--> B(800) <--> C(800) Firewire is processed in chips. 800 speed firewire chipsets will pass 400 speed along 800 bus at 400 speeds as data is passed along chain. anything C sends will seen by B and A as 400 speed, and exist as 400 speed on 800 bus between A and B. It doesn't increase 400's total bandwidth, but twice as long to transmit along 800 bus as if B had sent it natively. When B sends to A it at 800 speeds. problem is if A is particularly communicative it will drag down total bandwidth of 800 bus between B and C. If A transmits at full speed, 800 bus becomes a 400 bus. If A transmits 25% of the time, its 100mbps data consumes 200mbps of time on 800 bus. When C sends data to A, it at 400 speeds, use up twice the bandwidth on 800 bus than if transmitting native 800. This is called multi-speed concatenation. When B notices C sending 400 speed data, it passes that data along 800 bus at 400 speeds. When packet done it can immediately send next packet at 800. transition is instantaneous, no additional bandwidth lost, but, if A talks a lot, can reduce total bandwidth on 800 bus significantly. B(800) <--> A(400) <--> C(800) This configuration will reduce total bandwidth through entire bus to 400, regardless of chipset used in each device.

Propagation speed is time for one signal to get from one point to another. Transmission Rate is total amount of data can sent from one place to another in given period of time. Consider two possibilities at opposite extremes: A 300 baud modem. Propagation speed is close to speed of light, but transmission rate is only 300 bits per second (~30 characters per second). If, for example, talking to a machine 3000 miles away, transmitting a single character is close to instant, but transmitting lot of them takes long time (e., one megabyte take close to 10 hours). Propagation speed = ~C, Transmission rate = ~100 KB/hour. A van/small truck full of hard drives. assume vehicle can hold 1000 hard drives. propagation speed is speed limit from source to destination -- assume 60 MPH average. figure transmission rate, assume each hard drive holds 2 terabytes, for total of 2000 Terabytes. Propagation speed = ~60 MPH, transmission rate = ~40 terabytes/hour.

terms used differently by different people, but below is generally accepted. Bandwidth is number of bits per second a link can send or receive, including all flows. For example, bandwidth of 100 Mbps connections is 100 Mbps, but doesn't mean it is always sending or receiving 100 Mbps, but is maximum possible on that link. Unlike many people mean by bandwidth, it does not mean data usage. see people say they have a bandwidth limitation (every link does), used all their bandwidth for the month. This incorrect use of term. they mean to say is they have a data usage limitation, used it up for the month. Throughput is amount of data during a time period a flow (process to process) can send or receive. includes all host overhead, and contention on link (multiple flows on link will each use some percentage of bandwidth, reducing throughput of each). Bit rate is closer to bandwidth, but often per host, or source to destination devices. You may have bit rate of 100 Mbps from a host to a switch, but bit rate from a host to a host is less. usually includes multiple flows.

Daily I see peoples specialists in communication do mistakes about three terms: Bandwidth: unit of it is Hz, it is mathematically is: High_Used_Frequency - Low_Used_Frequency., when we measure bandwidth in bps, i. we do mistake. Beside, some guys working in Network field, they treat with bandwidth as Data rate., bandwidth is difference between high and low frequency. For example, bandwidth of a channel in FM is 0. 2MHz, for carrier is WCDMA is 5MHz. Data Rate: unit is bps, we can say data rate of channel is maximum ability of channel can transmit bits in a second. In normal case, can say if we have 5MHz bandwidth, channel capacity (or data rate) is 5Mbps, but also it can be bandwidth is 5MHz but data rate is 10Mbps, or 2. 5Mbps, depends on modulation type and other Technics. Throughput: This term is used in many different systems, shortly, we can define it as: real data that we receive. For example, Bandwidth=5MHz, channel capacity(data rate)=10Mbps, but what we receive exactly is 6Mpbs due to reason, throughput is 6Mbps. Hope gave you an idea.

Not disagreeing with other answers, but important takeaway is people often meaning slightly different things with similar identical words. couple of points worth adding, especially if you do anything numerical like try to work out maximum throughput of a given FTP connection over X Mbit/sec line: Kbit/sec, Mbit/sec etc in data rates are always powers of 10 as I ever seen File sizes equally stated as powers of 2 and often powers of 10, frequently people don't know ("few hundred megabyte" doesn't matter at that accuracy. ) If you get oscilloscope on wire quickly find out symbol rate can be different. 100baseT for example is 125 Mbaud, because it transmits 5 bits on wire for 4 bits of data. In summary, terms used often vary depending on what you emphasising: Throughput emphasises all things which could slow it down, much "net result". Bandwidth emphasises gross bit rate, still have to pay for all framing and overheads before you get throughput. You sometimes see things like "peak throughput" and "average sustained throughput" regard as very helpful. often rates interesting depend entirely on period you average over. PS IEC prefixes kibi, mebi, etc are far from universally used but worth knowing about

API = Application Programming Interface SDK = Software Development Kit real difference is: an API is no more than an interface to "some service", an SDK is a set of tools, components classes for specific purpose. An SDK presents you with an API to interface with. you might use an API without underlying components, for example when API provided through web service. Examples of APIs: Java API Google Maps API Flash Player API Examples SDKs: JDK GWT Flex SDK

http://www. differencebetween. com/difference-between-api-and-vs-sdk/ What is API? API is an interface allows software programs to interact with each other. It defines set of rules be followed by programs to communicate with other. APIs specify how routines, data structures,. should be defined in for two applications to communicate. APIs differ in the functionality provided by. are general APIs provide library functionalities of a programming language such as Java API. also APIs provides specific functionalities such as Google Maps API. also language dependent APIs, only be used by a specific programming language., language independent APIs could be used with several programming languages. APIs needs to be implemented carefully by exposing only required functionality or data to outside, while keeping the other parts of application inaccessible. Usage of APIs has become popular in internet. It common to allow some of functionality and data through an API to the outside on the Web. This functionality can be combined to offer improved functionality to users. What is SDK? SDK is a set of tools be used to develop software applications targeting a specific platform. SDKs include tools, libraries, documentation and sample code help programmer to develop application. Most of SDKs could be downloaded from the internet and many the SDKs are provided free to encourage programmers to use SDK‘s programming language. Some widely used SDKs are Java SDK (JDK) includes all libraries, debugging utilities, etc., make writing programs easier in Java. SDKs make life of a software developer easy, since no need to look for components/ tools compatible with each other and all are integrated in to a single package is easy to install. My two cents: I believe term API often used incorrectly. An API is an Application Programming Interface. awkward name, it means it's an interface. an application might have an API to allow other applications to communicate with it. piece of software (e. g. a class in an OO system) might offer an API to allow other modules in the system to communicate with it. often term API used as a synonym of "library". don't think's correct use of word. Part of library is an API to allow code to use it, but library isn't an API. an SDK is a kind of library,'s confusion might be.

"SDK" is collective in larger sense than "API". typically find only one SDK to cover entire platform. one MacOS X SDK and one iOS SDK, for example, those each contain API's for many different areas of functionality. "API" was originally used as collective term, still often used that way (MAPI, WSAPI, etc. ), but usually limited to some particular technology. scope implied by "API" to diminished over years; people used to talk about "Mac Toolbox API" or "Windows API, " both of obviously contained a lot of functionality. These days, not uncommon to hear "API" used to mean single system function; new version of operating system might be said to contain hundreds of new API's, and meant is hundreds of new system calls. Neither term very precise without context.

I think it rather falls the lines "All SDKs are APIs but not all APIs are SDKs". An SDK seems to be a complete set of APIs allow you to perform most any action need for creating applications. In an SDK may include other tools for developing for the platform/item it is for. An API is just a series of related methods may be good for a specific purpose. As example, the JDK (Java Development Kit) contains the API compilers, runtimes, other miscellaneous tools. The Java API is all the libraries that make up the core language you can work with out of the box.

the other answers explain an SDK is tooling, but none of directly says an API is a specification. The API for compoonent X is all the information you need in to write some other component will interact with X. An SDK for component X may contain library routines make it easier for to write component, but libraries are not the API: They are merely an embodiment of the API.

comment end of script, can do it like this: #!/bin/sh echo 'hello world' exec true can put whatever we want here \'\"\$\`!#%&()*+, -. /0123456789:;<=>?@ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ[\]^_ abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz{|}~
<command> 2>&1 | read line ; do echo $line | say ; done Replace <command> with normal command outputs what like be spoken.

not a multi-line comment. # is a single line comment. : (colon) is not a comment at all, but rather a shell built-in command is basically a NOP, a null operation does nothing except return true, like true (and setting $? to 0 as a side effect). since it is a command, it can accept arguments, it ignores its arguments, in most cases superficially acts like a comment. main problem with kludge is arguments are still expanded, leading to host of unintended consequences. arguments still affected by syntax errors, redirections still performed so : > file will truncate file, and : $(dangerous command) substitutions will still run. least surprising safe way to insert comments in shell scripts is with #. Stick to that even for multi-line comments. Never attempt to (ab)use : for comments. no dedicated multi-line comment mechanism in shell analogous to slash-star /* */ form in C-like languages. For of completeness, not recommended practice, mention possible to use here-documents to do multi-line "comments": : <<'end_long_comment' This is abuse of null command ':' and here-document syntax to achieve "multi-line comment". According to POSIX spec linked above, if any character in delimiter word ("end_long_comment" in) above is quoted, here-document will not be expanded in any way. **critical**, failing to quote "end_long_comment" will result in problems with unintended expansions described above. All this text in this here-doc goes to standard input of :, does nothing with it, effect is like a comment. little point to doing this besides throwing people off. Just use '#'. end_long_comment

swapping stdout and stderr. >name means redirect output to file name. >&number means redirect output to file descriptor number. & is needed to tell shell you mean a file descriptor, not file name. A file descriptor is a number refers to already open file. standard ones are 0 for standard input, 1 for standard output or 2 for standard error. can also use any other number, create new file descriptor, just like create new variable with var=value. By default, both file descriptor 1 and 2 go to /dev/tty, if run somecommand 3>&1 1>&2 2>&3 in new shell, it doesn't change anything (except now have file descriptor number 3). if earlier in script it does redirection using exec (e. g. exec 2>error. log), or script is run with command line including redirection (e. g. /thescript 2>error. log), swapping stdout and stderr will do something. In specific case, command's having stdout and stderr swapped is dialog. man page, Some widgets, e. g., checklist, will write text to dialog's output. Normally that is standard error perhaps person who wrote script wants dialog's output to go to stdout instead of stderr for reason. See also Order of redirections

numbers are file descriptors first three (starting with zero) have standardized meaning: 0 - stdin 1 - stdout 2 - stderr each these numbers in command refer to a file descriptor. can redirect a file descriptor to a file with > or redirect it to another file descriptor with >& 3>&1 in command line will create new file descriptor and redirect it to 1 which is STDOUT. Now 1>&2 redirect file descriptor 1 to STDERR and 2>&3 redirect file descriptor 2 to 3 which is STDOUT. you switched STDOUT and STDERR, steps: Create new fd 3 and point it to fd 1 Redirect file descriptor 1 to file descriptor 2. If wouldn't saved file descriptor in 3 would lose target. Redirect file descriptor 2 to file descriptor 3. Now file descriptors one and two are switched. if program prints something to file descriptor 1, it will be printed to file descriptor 2 and vice versa.

Both applications: built-in Apple Terminal and iTerm2 are only terminal emulators. They do not implement commands, just take care of the display. When you open a Terminal or iTerm2 window, it automatically runs a shell (like bash or ksh). This is program interprets most commands you know as CLI. When you type a command into shell, it first tries to match it with its internal set of commands and interprets it accordingly. If command is not found, shell will try to find a program which name matches command. This is might perceive aa "unix commands", they are just standalone programs. For example: If you run a Terminal on a Mac, it runs bash shell by default. Then if you type date, shell will find it not internal shell command, it search the disk (it search only in places defined in "PATH environment variable") and most likely find a program in following place /bin/date. shell will execute this program. Terminal will print standard output of date command in its window. iTerm2 does not use Terminal in background, but it will run the same shell. flow is: iTerm2 runs bash (by default), bash executes a date command and date command send output to iTerm2 display the characters for user.

Not everything counts from 1970. Its standard time of Unix. Unix time, or POSIX time, is a system for describing points in time, defined as number of seconds elapsed since midnight proleptic Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) of January 1, 1970, not counting leap seconds. Unix Time Early versions of unix measured system time in 1/60 s intervals. This meant a 32-bit unsigned integer could only represent span of time less than 829 days. For this reason, time represented by number 0 (called the epoch) had to be set in recent past. in early 1970s, epoch was set to 1971-1-1. Later, system time changed to increment every second, increased span of time represented by 32-bit unsigned integer to around 136 years. As no longer important to squeeze every second counter, epoch was rounded down to nearest decade, becoming 1970-1-1. assume this was considered a bit neater than 1971-1-1. 32-bit signed integer using 1970-1-1 as epoch can represent dates up to 2038-1-19, date it will wrap around to 1901-12-13. Both applications: built-in Apple Terminal and iTerm2 are only terminal emulators. They do not implement commands, just take care of the display. When you open a Terminal or iTerm2 window, it automatically runs a shell (like bash or ksh). This is program interprets most commands you know as CLI. When you type a command into shell, it first tries to match it with its internal set of commands and interprets it accordingly. If command is not found, shell will try to find a program which name matches command. This is might perceive aa "unix commands", they are just standalone programs. For example: If you run a Terminal on a Mac, it runs bash shell by default. Then if you type date, shell will find it not internal shell command, it search the disk (it search only in places defined in "PATH environment variable") and most likely find a program in following place /bin/date. shell will execute this program. Terminal will print standard output of date command in its window. iTerm2 does not use Terminal in background, but it will run the same shell. flow is: iTerm2 runs bash (by default), bash executes a date command and date command send output to iTerm2 display the characters for user.

Usually, vector and array are same thing used interchangeably when programming. in most places, shouldn't worry much about it most of time., language is imprecise sometimes have words different meanings in different contexts up meaning same thing, or one word two or more different meanings. In C an array is series of data elements same type stored in memory contiguously. Java inherited that meaning. not the same as a List or a Vector, arrays are more basic than those. A vector is a mathematical construct defined as object can be added to another object of same type, or multiplied by any real (or complex) number resulting in another vector of same type. It has few other properties useful. A vector has dimension. minimum number of different vectors to be combined to get every possible vector of type. Velocity and acceleration are 3-dimensional vectors because space has 3 base directions by adding multiples of those three base directions can get any position in space. Position in a plane is a 2-dimensional vector, individual numbers are 1-dimensional vectors. One way to represent vector of dimension n is by using array of n elements each one representing how much of each base vector you to add to get to your vector. can represent a vector using arra of elements, with time, two concepts were equated., in many places, they simply are the same thing in some languages arrays are called vectors. Another case where one word has two different meanings is, for instance, dimension. wikipedia definition of a vector as 1-dimensional array is example. not talking of vector dimension here. talking about computer representation of data structure. A 3-Dimensional vector can be represented by "1-dimensional" array of size 3. 3 numbers in line. A 3x3 matrix can be represented by a "2-dimensional" array, what programmers call an array of arrays.3x3 matrix is also a mathematical vector of dimension 9 (since it has all properties of vector) and has 9 numbers. Confusing, huh?, answer is simply: don't worry. depends on context. two words have different origins, but in context of data structures, when they say vector they mean exactly array.

From Wikipedia: initialization vector has different security requirements than a key, so IV usually not need to be secret. However, in most cases, important initialization vector never reused under same key. For CBC and CFB, reusing IV leaks information about first block of plaintext, and about any common prefix shared by two messages. You don't need to keep IV secret, but it must be random and unique.

depends on algorithms used. AES is a fast algorithm, but also depends on mode of operation. Assume Apple used AES or 3DES because they are standardized. Now, computation of plaintext only possible (at moment) with exhaustive search attack. attacker can manipulate plaintext. But not do much good in counter-terrorism operation. Never corrupt data if it is important. If attacker was spying using software as VNC, (if software exists for iOS), or advanced touch Keylogger, unless he had access by ssh, he would probably not have able to install Keylogger, unless he had previous info on UI decryption key (not for hardware decryption). If he gets an image of device, he can perform online attack on UI encryption, but can't change code, without data corruption. This means he will be locked out after several failed attempts. If attacker manages to get a hold of disk, he can perform offline attack. But this much harder, as hardware encryption is on. attacker will eventually win, but will it do any good?

If I encrypt some data with randomly generated Key and Initialization Vector, store all three pieces of information in same table row; is it necessary to encrypt the IV as well as the Key? No, only the key may need to be stored encrypted; not necessary to encrypt random IV. (secret) key needs to be kept secret. If do that using encryption (i. e. shifting burden to another key or key pair) or any other method is up to architect. However, if to store it next to database good key wrapping method such as AES-WRAP, AES-SIV is a logical choice as part of securing your key at rest. Other security mechanisms such as access control / protection against side channel attacks need to be in place when using key. IV needs to be unpredictable to adversary for CBC mode. If's not the case then CBC fails under active attack using ciphertext oracle. In should assume that such an oracle exists. For instance, assume attacker can send messages to your DB, you encrypt and store in database for attacker to read back. random IV generated by well seeded cryptographically secure (pseudo-) random number generator (CSPRNG) - such as /dev/urandom - avoids this of problem. Encrypting the IV is dangerous practice as IV gets XOR'ed with plaintext. If do should encrypt it with different key, otherwise may harm security of CBC mode. If to use your current key should use resulting ciphertext as IV instead of plaintext input., for a random IV that's completely unnecessary: you can just store it next to ciphertext without protection. Supplemental: message integrity & authenticity In always good idea to verify integrity and authenticity of stored messages before using it. Using mode of operation such as GCM or EAX should be preferred.Note neither GCM nor EAX need unpredictable IV; IV just needs to be unique - no other requirements apart from size; using a fully random IV/nonce of 128 bit is fine. They automatically will include IV into the calculation of authentication tag. Using a HMAC over ciphertext (also known as encrypt-then-MAC) has proven successful to provide integrity / authenticity but please note you should include the IV in the calculation* if you decide to go with HMAC.

in your case the IV should be okay in plaintext in the DB, a severe vulnerability if you allow user to control the IV. IV in decryption is used (and used) to XOR the first block into final plaintext - if attacker can control the IV they can arbitrarily control the first block of data, the rest of plaintext will survive without modification. If attacker knows original plaintext of first block, problem is magnified as attacker can choose arbitrary data for first block without trial and error. This particularly important in case where encrypted data is transmitted through untrusted channels with IV, maybe into a browser or an app etc.

difference between class variables and instance variables, is a question of who knows what?. An instance variable is only known (= bound) to concrete instance - hence the name. public class Person { private String firstName; private String lastName; [. ] } definition of a class is like a blueprint for building concrete objects. Perhaps point confuses you. But writing it this way, every variable bound to its concrete object:. Every person has its own firstName A class variable is - as name says - known to each and every member of a class; or known/ bound at class level. typical example is a counter of how many objects, you created - problematic example; but doesn't matter at this early stage. public class Person { private String firstName; private String lastName; [. ] static int numberOfPersons = 0 } numberOfPersons is declared static is keyword to distingush between class variables and instance variabes. variable is declared like others within class definition. But static keyword signals, it is different. firstName, lastName are instance variables and bound to concrete instance numberOfPersons is bound to class, so every instance could access this variable. tl;dr place where variables are defined is the class definition. Class variables are known at/bound to class level,. each concrete instance has access to it. To define a class variable, use keyword static. Instance variables only known at instance level. define them without static keyword. Further documentation for Java is here

both are member variables, both associated with a class., differences between two: Instance variables: belong to instance of a class, object. every instance of class has's own copy of variable. Changes to variable don't reflect in other instances of class. public class Product { public int Barcode; } Class variables: also known as static member variables only one copy of variable shared with all instances of class. If changes made to variable, all other instances see effect of changes. public class Product { public static int Barcode; } Full example: // INSTANCE VARIABLE public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { Product prod1 = new Product(); prod1. Barcode = 123456; Product prod2 = new Product(); prod2. Barcode = 987654; System. out. println(prod1. Barcode); System. out. println(prod2. Barcode); } } public class Product { public int Barcode; } output: 123456 987654, change instance variable to a class variable by making it static: //CLASS VARIABLE public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { Product prod1 = new Product(); prod1. setBarcode(123456); Product prod2 = new Product(); prod2. setBarcode(987654); System. out. println(prod1. getBarcode()); System. out. println(prod2. getBarcode()); } } public class Product { public static int Barcode; public int getBarcode() { return Barcode; } public void setBarcode(int value){ Barcode = value; } } used non-static methods to get and set value of Barcode to call it from object not from class. output following: 987654 987654

Instance Variable: Instance variables declared in class, outside method, constructor or block. Instance variable belongs to instance class or belongs object. Instance variable separate value of each instance of class. Class InstanceDemo { // instance variable visible for any child class. public String name = "Testing"; count variable visible in Demo class only. private int count = 2; } Method to access instance variable: InstanceDemo demo = new InstanceDemo (); System. out. println("Access Instance variable: " + demo. count + ", "+demo. name ); Output: 2, Testing Class Variable: Class variable belongs to class. class variable created by adding “static” keyword before variable. Also called static variable. important class variable maintain single shared value for all instance of class, even if no instance object class exists. Class ClassDemo { // count variable is Same for all instance of class public static int count = 2; } Method to access class variable: System. out. println("Access Class variable: " + ClassDemo. count ); //class variable directly refer with class name Output: 2 Brief Difference Between Class Variable and Instance Variable: Instance variables have separate values for each instance of class. Class variables maintain single shared value for all instances class, even if no instance object class exists. use static keyword to change instance variable into class variable. Both instance and class variables declared at class level, not within methods.

explained here (with example Bicycle class with class variable numberOfBicycles and instance variables cadence, speed, gear & id): Sometimes, want to have variables common to all objects. This accomplished with static modifier. Fields have static modifier in declaration are called static fields or class variables. associated with class, rather than with any object. Every instance of class shares class variable, in one fixed location in memory. Any object can change value of class variable, but class variables can be manipulated without creating instance of class. class variable (declared static) is a location common to all instances. In example, numberOfBicycles is a class variable (since declared static). only one such variable (i. location) common to all instances and to class. if modify numberOfBicycles in one method, other methods see new value (even for different Bicycle objects) In contrast gear & id are instance variables (because declaration has no static modifier). Every Bicycle object has its own one. If modify gear for some Bicycle a, if b is another instance, modifying a. gear has no effect on b. gear Each Java object is distinct memory zone with meta data (e. reference to its class) and its own instance variables (perhaps inherited from superclass). But class variables are common to class shared by all instances. See also Object (computer science) & Instance variable wikipages.

Java Pattern objects are thread safe and immutable (its the matchers not thread safe)., no reason not to make them static if to used by each instance of class (or again in another method in the class). Making them instance variables, no matter how short (or long) their life time means you recompiling regular expression each time you create an instance of class. key reasons for this structure (Pattern being a factory for Matcher objects) is compiling regular expression into its finite automata is a moderately expensive action. However, one finds often same regular expression is used again and again in a given class (either through multiple invocations of same method or different spots in class). Matcher, on is rather light - it points to state of pattern within Pattern and location within character array for string. For a singleton, it shouldn't matter too much, because after, there's only one instance of it sits around you aren't recreating singleton again and again (wait, 'lifetime of singleton isn't that long'? Does this mean you instantiating it multiple times over course of application?) However, find some static source code analyzers don't recognize something is a singleton and will complain you creating instances of patterns from constants for each instance of class. problem with this is it is a not good (its not bad for a singleton either) choice and you may start ignoring other warnings for compiler and analysis tools tell you about (read more about broken windows). difference between class variables and instance variables, is a question of who knows what?. An instance variable is only known (= bound) to concrete instance - hence the name. public class Person { private String firstName; private String lastName; [. ] } definition of a class is like a blueprint for building concrete objects. Perhaps point confuses you. But writing it this way, every variable bound to its concrete object:. Every person has its own firstName A class variable is - as name says - known to each and every member of a class; or known/ bound at class level. typical example is a counter of how many objects, you created - problematic example; but doesn't matter at this early stage. public class Person { private String firstName; private String lastName; [. ] static int numberOfPersons = 0 } numberOfPersons is declared static is keyword to distingush between class variables and instance variabes. variable is declared like others within class definition. But static keyword signals, it is different. firstName, lastName are instance variables and bound to concrete instance numberOfPersons is bound to class, so every instance could access this variable. tl;dr place where variables are defined is the class definition. Class variables are known at/bound to class level,. each concrete instance has access to it. To define a class variable, use keyword static. Instance variables only known at instance level. define them without static keyword. Further documentation for Java is here

both are member variables, both associated with a class., differences between two: Instance variables: belong to instance of a class, object. every instance of class has's own copy of variable. Changes to variable don't reflect in other instances of class. public class Product { public int Barcode; } Class variables: also known as static member variables only one copy of variable shared with all instances of class. If changes made to variable, all other instances see effect of changes. public class Product { public static int Barcode; } Full example: // INSTANCE VARIABLE public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { Product prod1 = new Product(); prod1. Barcode = 123456; Product prod2 = new Product(); prod2. Barcode = 987654; System. out. println(prod1. Barcode); System. out. println(prod2. Barcode); } } public class Product { public int Barcode; } output: 123456 987654, change instance variable to a class variable by making it static: //CLASS VARIABLE public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { Product prod1 = new Product(); prod1. setBarcode(123456); Product prod2 = new Product(); prod2. setBarcode(987654); System. out. println(prod1. getBarcode()); System. out. println(prod2. getBarcode()); } } public class Product { public static int Barcode; public int getBarcode() { return Barcode; } public void setBarcode(int value){ Barcode = value; } } used non-static methods to get and set value of Barcode to call it from object not from class. output following: 987654 987654

Instance Variable: Instance variables declared in class, outside method, constructor or block. Instance variable belongs to instance class or belongs object. Class InstanceDemo { // instance variable visible for any child class. public String name = "Testing"; count variable visible in Demo class only. private int count = 2; } Method to access instance variable: InstanceDemo demo = new InstanceDemo (); System. out. println("Access Instance variable: " + demo. count + ", "+demo. name ); Output: 2, Testing Class Variable: Class variable belongs to class. class variable created by adding “static” keyword before variable. Also called static variable. important class variable maintain single shared value for all instance of class, even if no instance object class exists. explained here (with example Bicycle class with class variable numberOfBicycles and instance variables cadence, speed, gear & id): Sometimes, want to have variables common to all objects. This accomplished with static modifier. Fields have static modifier in declaration are called static fields or class variables. associated with class, rather than with any object. Every instance of class shares class variable, in one fixed location in memory. Any object can change value of class variable, but class variables can be manipulated without creating instance of class. class variable (declared static) is a location common to all instances. In example, numberOfBicycles is a class variable (since declared static). only one such variable (i. location) common to all instances and to class. if modify numberOfBicycles in one method, other methods see new value (even for different Bicycle objects) In contrast gear & id are instance variables (because declaration has no static modifier). Every Bicycle object has its own one. If modify gear for some Bicycle a, if b is another instance, modifying a. gear has no effect on b. gear Each Java object is distinct memory zone with meta data (e. reference to its class) and its own instance variables (perhaps inherited from superclass). But class variables are common to class shared by all instances. See also Object (computer science) & Instance variable wikipages.

Heres super easy fix. Take lightening to 3. 5mm adaptor came with your iPhone. In 1997, Sun Microsystems approached ECMA to formalize Java but soon withdrew from process. Java standard is controlled through Java Community Process. in 2006, most of Java was released by Sun Microsystems under terms of GPL but current official implementation is owned by Oracle. Java lacks formal standardization recognized by ECMA, ISO/IEC, ANSI, or other third-party standards organization, Oracle implementation is defacto standard., alternative implementations like GNU Compiler for Java, GNU Classpath, IcedTea-Web, etc.

core of many important languages written in C, but things changing: reference implementation of Python (CPython) is written in C (but other implementations written in other languages, e. g. Jython / Java, PyPy / Python, IronPython / C#. ) PHP Zend Engine written in C first Java compiler developed by Sun Microsystems was written in C, but now class libraries always written in Java (since intended to be run using Java VM). Certain libraries using JNI (Java Native Interface) may be partially written in variety of other languages, intended to used OUTSIDE JVM. Sun/Oracle VM written in C++. BEA/Weblogic/Oracle VM written in C. But JVM written in Java, Lisp, SmallTalk (IBM). Perl implemented as core interpreter, written in C, together with large collection of modules, written in Perl and C (but Pugs, a compiler and interpreter for Perl 6 programming language, written in Haskell) official Ruby interpreter, referred to as Matz's Ruby Interpreter or MRI, written in C uses its own Ruby-specific virtual machine (but JRuby, a Java implementation runs on Java virtual machine; Rubinius, a C++ bytecode virtual machine uses LLVM to compile to machine code at runtime. ) about 50% of R written in C and, of, C is (was) written in C! (but first C compiler, targeted to PDP-11, was a mix of B and assembler). many reasons why C often chosen: performance, portability, experience. last most important: Python started in 1991, PHP in 1994/1995, Perl in 1988, Ruby in 1995. In those years Java was just released and C++ not yet well standardized. related: Is functional language without runtime written in C possible?

"Hostname" used specifically in context TCP/IP suite. Other protocols operating systems (MS Windows) often use term "server name. " for example, device could be referred to by its Server Name in Windows, but by its Hostname using DNS. names can be different. Often two terms used interchangeably.

For hostname read domain name such as apple. stackexchange. com, john-pc. local or localhost localhost is a static local hostname only accessible to limited area (in this case single device), by tradition, assigned to same ip address: 127. 0. 0. 1. john-pc. local is (potentially) a dynamic local hostname while it will always refer to same pc, device's ip address will vary*. IP address can broken down into two parts, Network Address and Host Address. In example, /29 refers to Subnet Mask 29 bits of total 32 bits from MSB to LSB are all 1's, i. e., 255. 255. 255. 248. This allow for 8 addresses per subnet. first address in subnet, 178. 18. 230. 120 is Network Address and - last address, is all 1's - i. e., 172. 18. 230. 127 is the Broadcast Address. host address can range anywhere between Network and Broadcast Address, i. e., 172. 18. 230. 121 to 172. 18. 230. 126. arrive at these addresses by performing logical AND on IP address and Subnet Mask. first IP address usually reserved for Network address and last one in block is for Broadcast address, remaining ones used as Host addresses. Loopback address is special reserved IP address, usually referred to as localhost - 127. 0. 0. 1 used to communicate with localhost. Edited: can convert IP addresses into binary form and perform logical AND., easier and less time consuming to have them in Decimal representation. 178. 18. 230. 127 (AND) 255. 255. 255. 248 -------------------- **178. 18. 230. 120** -----> **Network Address** -------------------- 178. 18. 230. 127 (AND) 255. 255. 255. 255 -------------------- **178. 18. 230. 127** -----> **Broadcast Address** -------------------- Keep in first and last one in a block are always Network and Broadcast Addresses(reserved). Host Addresses: Any other address between Network and Broadcast Addresses are Host Addressable, can be assigned to a Host and NOT reserved for any specific purpose, unlike Network and Broadcast Addresses.

three different hostnames macOS/OS X uses: ComputerName HostName LocalHostName Each these values found in /Library/Preferences/SystemConfiguration/preferences. plist ComputerName scutil --get ComputerName This is Apple "friendly" name for computer found in System Preferences >> Sharing >> Computer Name. According to man page for scutil, it described as "The user-friendly name for system. " According to Apple, ComputerName is The AppleTalk name and default name used for SLP/DA1. It's a zero-configuraiton protocol allows to set up simple network without DNS/DHCP server to reach different resources via host name. HostName scutil --get HostName According to scutil man page, HostName is "the name associated with hostname(1) and gethostname(3)". This name can come from of sources: name provided by DHCP or BootP server for primary IP address first name returned by reverse DNS (address-to-name) query for primary IP address local hostname The name “localhost” (In my virgin install of El Capitan, HostName defaulted to LocalHostName) LocalHostName scutil --get LocalHostName This is for Bonjour2 services on LAN. how, on small LAN without DNS/DHCP, Apple computers can discover and interact with resources such as file sharing on other machines, printers, etc. This name gets set when you initially configure Mac. TL;DR It using "the first name you ever set" because during initial setup, it set LocalHostName it assumed would forever be. When re-configured using GUI, changed ComputerName did not modify LocalHostName. If wish to fix this in router, set your LocalHostName using command: scutil --set LocalHostName MyNewComputerName. domain 1 SLP/DA Service Location Protocol/Directory Agent. Service Location Protocol is service discovery protocol allows computers and other devices to find services in local area network without prior configuration.2 Bonjour Apple's implementation of zero-configuration networking, group of technologies includes service discovery, address assignment, hostname resolution.

Devices in different subnets can communicate. purpose of a router. Routers route packets between different networks. Even if devices in different networks on same layer-2 broadcast domain, you need a router to let devices communicate at layer-3. because each host will compare destination layer-3 address and its own layer-3 address and mask to see if they on same network. If destination host is on different network, host will send packets in layer-2 frames to its configured gateway (router). host must assume destination network could be across world from its network, gateway is the host on network that knows how to forward packets toward destination network.

If you have access to system want to check whether it's blocked or open, you can use netstat -tuplen | grep 25 to see if service is on and listening to IP address or not. can also try to use iptables -nL | grep <port number> to see if any rule set by firewall. If saw nothing wrong, finally you can do what already done by using telnet yourTarget 25or nc yourTarget 25, if get a message saying connection is refused, it might be blocked and filtered by ISP since most ISPs block default SMTP port 25. In case you can change default port - if need it - to alternative. other option, is to use Nmap ↴ can use nmap -sT localhost to determine which ports listening for TCP connections from network. To check for UDP ports, use -sU option. To check for port 25, can use nmap -p25 localhost. if not have access to system, can use nmap -sS -p25 yourTargetIP. N. B. Nmap is a super-powerful tool, but should know how to use it. For instance, sometimes might be in need of using -Pn option for pingless scan.

'Filtered port' statement from nmap differs according scan method. standard scan (TCP Scan if unprivileged user, or Half-Open scan -sS if superuser) relies on TCP protocol. (named 3-way hanshake) client (you) issues a SYN, if server replies SYN/ACK : it means port is open ! You issue a SYN, if server replies RST : it means port is close ! You issue a SYN, if server not reply, or replies with ICMP error : it means port is filtered. Likely IDS / statefull firewall block request) To figure real status of port, can : use -sV, or -A option (version detection, help to determine status port. use --tcp-flags SYN, FIN to try bypassing fw. use other scan types (http://nmap. org/book/man-port-scanning-techniques. html) "Nmap Network Discovery" book, written by creator Fyodor explains this well. I quote filtered : Nmap cannot determine whether port is open because packet filtering prevents probes from reaching port. filtering could be from dedicated firewall device, router rules, or host-based firewall software. These ports frustrate attackers because provide little information. respond with ICMP error messages as type 3 code 13 (destination unreachable: communication administratively prohibited), but filters that drop probes without responding are more common. This forces Nmap to retry several times in case probe was dropped due to network congestion rather than filtering. This filtering slows scans down dramatically. open|filtered : Nmap places ports in this state when unable to determine whether port is open or filtered. This occurs for scan types in which open ports give no response. lack of response could also mean packet filter dropped probe or response elicited. Nmap does not know for sure whether port is open or filtered.UDP, IP protocol, FIN, NULL, and Xmas scans classify ports this way. closed|filtered : state used when Nmap unable to determine port closed or filtered. only used for IP ID Idle scan discussed in Section 5. 10, "TCP Idle Scan (-sl)

Traditionally a virus is malware uses infected host to replicate itself to other systems,. by infecting files shared, copying itself to network drives or USB sticks. gets usually not knowingly executed by user but executed when user opens infected file, runs infected program. A trojan is a malware claims to be something different, like some malware claiming to be a virus scanner. It counts on user to execute it knowingly by believing what software claims to be. In common language often any malware is simply called virus,. real viruses, trojans, ransomware etc. For a virus scanner cares about all types of malware, not only viruses.

simple words, What Is a Virus? It's piece of code attaches to a program or file enabling it to spread to several computers, infecting computers as spreads. Like a human virus basically. What is a Trojan A Trojan is a harmful piece software looks legitimate. Users typically tricked into loading executing it on systems. After it activated, can achieve any number of attacks on host. Trojans known to create back doors to give malicious users access to system.

A computer virus is malware capable of infecting computer but rely on other means to propagate. true virus can spread from infected computer to non-infected computer only by attaching to executable code passed between them. For example, a virus could be hidden in a PDF file attached to an e-mail message. difficult to better definition for Trojan horse malware than Ed Skoudis and Lenny Zelter in book Malware: Fighting Malicious Code: "A trojan horse is program appears to useful or benign purpose, but masks hidden malicious functionality. " Trojan horse malware cloaks destructive payload during installation and program execution, preventing anti-malware from recognizing malcode. concealment techniques include: Renaming malware to resemble files normally present. Corrupting installed anti-malware to not respond when malware located. Using Polymorphic code to alter malware's signature faster than defensive software can retrieve new signature files. Vundo is a prime example; creates popup advertising for rogue anti-spyware programs, degrades system performance, interferes with Web browsing. Typically, a malware scanner installed on a LiveCD is required to detect and remove it.

If you intentionally download something turns to harmful or not expecting, it's generally considered a Trojan. This on account of fact you invited it inside your perimeter, as in story of Trojan Horse. This (potentially harmful) program commonly downloaded via email attachment or sometimes attached to fake or pirated commercial software. It's often form of key-logger or improvised remote administration tool designed to subvert victims personal or financial privacy. virus is generally semi-autonomous, self replicating, usually designed to spread to many machines possible. not necessarily harmful to infected hosts. Viruses and Trojans aren't necessarily exclusive factions. Theoretically, possible to be both, if criteria met. They're just names assigned to generalised groups of attributes to facilitate easier communication of ideas. Hope that helps.

Abstract Data Type: ADT may be defined as a set of data values and associated operations precisely specified independent of implementation. an Abstract Data Type is an organized collection of information and a set of operations to manage information. The set of operations defines interface of ADT. as ADT fulfills conditions of interface, it doesn’t matter how ADT is implemented., in ADT, data values and operations are defined with mathematical precision, rather than as implementation in computer language, we may reason about effects of operations, relations to other abstract data types whether program implements data type etc. simplest abstract data type is the stack data type for functions might be provided to create empty stack, to push values onto a stack and pop values from a stack. basic difference between abstract data type (ADT) and concrete data type is latter allow us to look at concrete representation, former hide representation from us. An ADT may be pure ADT or Updatable ADT. A pure ADT is one where all operations are pure functions. means operations have no side effects. In, they do not modify or update input arguments. They just use these arguments to generate output, are fresh values of ADT (or of other types). Most concrete types are pure. For example, no operation on integers modifies an integer. Instead, all operations like ‘+’ produce fresh outputs. An updatable ADT is one where some operations change values of ADT. For example, suppose operation called ‘pop’ that took a stack as argument modified it., “destructively”) by removing highest priority item. This operation would be considered impure and whole ADT would be impure also. An ADT may be user defined ADT. an Abstract Data Type is a data type that satisfies following two conditions: representation, or definition, of type and operations are contained in a single syntactic unit.representation of objects of type is hidden from program units use type, only direct operations possible on objects are provided in type’s definition. user defined Abstract Data Type should provide: type definition that allows program units to declare variables of type, but hides representation of these variables. set of operations for manipulating objects of type. example of user defined abstract data type is structure. ’C’ provides four basic types: int, char, float and double., ‘C’ also provides programmer ability to define his/her own types. Structure is one such example. structure is an aggregate of different parts, each part is of some existing type. struct abc {int x; float y; }; above structure definition does not create variables, rather creates new type. Variables of this type may be created in similar way to variables of built in type. struct abc a; typedef keyword allows to create new type names for new types. For example: typedef struct abc AB; where AB is new type name can now be used to create new types. AB b; Data Structures: characteristic features of data structures: contains component data items, may be atomic or another data structure (still domain). set of operations on one or more of component items. Defines rules as to how components relates to each other and to structure as a whole (assertions). Data Structures: data structure may be static or dynamic. static data structure has fixed size. meaning different from meaning of static modifier. Arrays are static; once define number of elements can hold, number doesn’t change. dynamic data structure grows and shrinks at execution time as required by contents. dynamic data structure implemented using links. Data structures may be categorized into linear data structures and non-linear data structures.In linear data structures every component has unique predecessor successor, except first and last elements, in non-linear data structures, no such restriction as elements may be arranged in any desired fashion restricted by way we use to represent such types.

Apple calls the area in storage of iOS device containing media (music, video) for built-in apps to play the iPod library. iOS provides interface App Store apps can call to use iPod library, but basically limited to playback and search., apps' access to storage is restricted by sandboxing. From Apple's "iOS App Programming Guide": For security reasons, iOS places each app (including its preferences and data) in a sandbox at install time. A sandbox is set of fine controls limit app’s access to files, preferences, network resources, hardware, so on. As part of sandboxing process, system installs each app in its own sandbox directory, acts as the home for the app and its data. This means third party apps from App Store can't directly access files other than their own (like iPod library), they can't save files they download anywhere but their own directories. In addition to sandboxing, Apple also has a mandatory review and approval process for apps to go into App Store, apps that don't follow guidelines aren't available. In, not really a restriction "in the OS", because Apple can change review process and newly-allowed apps can be downloaded and used immediately without change to iOS., iOS app developers can get their own apps signed to test on their own iOS devices, before review process. from of average user, what restrictions are enforced by sandboxing and what are only App Store guidelines is academic. On jailbroken devices, applications not approved by Apple can be installed, jailbreaks modify iOS so apps can operate outside of sandbox restrictions. possible for app that understands current iPod library file formats (for recent versions iFile) to add music directly to the library.

Use of these different environments, depends on your needs. From your comment that "staging == UAT", it sounds as if you a very small application with no QA team, only couple of developers. Larger application environments might have an integration test environment, a QA environment, former where developers run integration tests and latter where QA team run their tests. There might be a training environment has stock data restored before each training session. staging environment under control of operations team, to ensure roll-outs occur properly. user-acceptance-test (UAT) environment be used by the customer team. There might also be a production-snapshot environment for reproducing customer issues. point is to beware the single viewpoint when determining environments you need.

Adding to @EightBitTony's answer: Kali is a special distro aimed at pentesting, quite different from standard Linux distro. For instance: System supposed to be used as root in a single-user environment Network services disabled by default not persist across reboots Custom kernel, assuming you manage to download and install all Kali packages on your Debian, you'll have something still significantly different, in essence and in behavior, than a standard Kali install. advice not to mix the two use real thing (Kali) if/when you really need it.

list of Kali considers distinguishing features are set out here. Flexibility, customisation, portability security all balanced on unstable Debian Kernel. differences. Kali intended to be a Swiss army knife (often booted from USB) with specific intent for specialist users, Debian intended to be a reliable permanent install for everyday armchair use by Joe/Jane Public. Kali includes tools meaningless to Joe and Jane, "bleeding edge" updates which may break certain things Kali considers unimportant to target user base (like LibreOffice?). If this happens on machine running mission critical tasks for Joe or Jane in office they will panic) wonder which idiot installed Kali instead of Debian for them. Kali tools can be installed on civilised Debian machine to "weaponise" it, or Kali install can be "tamed" to become more civilised animal by anyone with interest, experience time to, but you will retain kernel of original choice. I tried both ways (taming Kali and corrupting Debian). Tamed Kali works for me.

Terminal is actual hardware with keyboard and output devices connected to mainframe. Console - Special type of terminal directly connected to Mainframe for purpose OS Administration. tty - TeleTypewriter used to send and receive data to and from Mainframe. Used before Video Terminals were available. conventionally it still named as tty. short answer is via iCloud Drive. WhatsApp backup(s) stored in hidden folder of iCloud Drive on your MacBook (if signed into iCloud and turned on iCloud Drive). To find WhatsApp backup(s): Launch Terminal (in /Applications/Utilities folder) Type following commands cd ~/Library/Mobile\ Documents/ find *whatsapp* You should see all files related to WhatsApp backup(s). If don’t see anything, make sure iCloud drive is turned on. If only see *. icloud files, turn off “optimize mac storage” in icloud system preferences. knowledge, can’t access directly messages as stored in encrypted SQLite database. documents, pictures and videos stored in separate, unencrypted archives: Document. tar (PDFs and other attachments) Media. tar (pictures) Video. tar (videos) To extract in there, copy files to desktop via terminal command: cp *whatsapp*/Accounts/*/backup/*. tar ~/Desktop Then, double-click on. tar files to extract folder structure containing files organised by conversation. Note: If multiple WhatsApp accounts backed up to same iCloud account, need to replace ‘*’ between “Accounts/” and “/backup” by desired phone number. Hope this helps!

No, no difference in internal structure of such programs. GTK and Qt are user interface toolkits and frameworks. They are libraries developers use to design graphical interfaces. When a graphical (GUI) program is written, first its core internals are developed. This makes program run. never see core, they execute in background. On top of this core, a User Interface (UI) is designed., developers could design complete interface from scratch, or re-use designs by others. Re-using design has major advantage. allows all programs in computer to look similar., they use GUI toolkits. GTK and Qt are two common GUI toolkits. GTK is standard toolkit for GNOME Qt used by KDE. From user's point of view, it's just the looks that differ. program remains the same at heart.

In general, difference from user perspective should be purely cosmetic. Qt and GTK set themes independently (via, e. g., qtconfig or gtk-chtheme) harmonized by some desktop environments. GNU/Linux tends to be more GTK oriented than Qt in former is more commonly used, so you may want to prefer it when given choice; exception be under KDE, which uses Qt for its own applications -- none of these factors very important. more significant issue be in contexts with limited RAM (as in, < 1/4 GB); in this case you probably want system to use exclusively GTK or Qt, but not both. On most modern desktops with gigabytes of memory, this is not a concern -- using both extensively might cost you extra (wild guess) 50-100 MB. Note different versions of both GTK (2 and 3) and Qt (3 and 4) still widely used but not backward compatible (so Qt 3 application cannot use Qt 4 libraries)., both versions may exist on system at same time and serious consequence of potential for confusion and more memory bloat.
