reason is simple: it not have good bindings to all mainstream languages, not magically always appropriate for job at hand. Use right tool for job. If I'm writing a simple command-line application, why I bloat up with Qt just for sake of it? more general answer (which I can give because'm relevant here), some programmers will simply never have given it a go and decided to use it. In some cases no particular reason other than programmer never found need for it and looked into it.

I don't intend this to be a bashing answer, but these reasons I do not personally use Qt. plenty of good things to say about it -- API works most of time, it seamlessly bridge platforms. But I do not use Qt, because: In some cases, it doesn't look like native programs look. Designing a single UI for all platforms not to look right when moved from machine to machine, for various visual styling reasons. For example, on Mac machines, split bars are usually thick, buttons small and rounded with icons. On Windows machines, split bars typically narrow, buttons more textual, with more square designs. you can write one UI for every platform not mean you should for most applications. Qt is not just a link-able set of C++ libraries. build system used requires translation of certain files into extra source files, makes build process more complicated compared with most other libraries. result of (2), C++ IDEs and tools can flag Qt expressions as errors, because they do not understand Qt's specifics. This forces use of QtCreator or a textual only editor like vim. Qt is large amount of source, must be present and preinstalled on any machine before compiling. can make setting up build environment tedious. Parts mostly licensed under LGPL, makes difficult to use single-binary-deployment when needs to release under more restrictive or less restrictive license. It produces extremely large compiled binaries when compared with similarly written "plain old native applications" (excepting applications written for KDE).

I like Qt, but it's a bit heavyweight for of applications. Sometimes you don't need that level of complexity. Sometimes need something simple without all overhead of Qt. Not every application needs to be event driven and C++ provides reasonable set of templates. Boost provides another good set includes low-level functionality (file, socket, managed pointers, etc) that QT does. Other applications have licensing requirements don't play nice with GPL, LGPL or Qt's commercial license. GPL inappropriate for commercial software. LGPL inappropriate for statically linked software and commercial license costs money - many unwilling to pay. Some have security or stability considerations don't allow complex libraries like Qt. need to run moc to pre-process sources. not a huge issue, but can be daunting for new user. programmers think you need to use qmake with Qt, but's a misnomer. possible to plug Qt into other build systems easily. Some targets are memory or CPU constrained. some platform-specific gotchas in it. Most of gotchas are undocumented. Build sufficiently large application and you will run into them and wonder what's going on (disclaimer, last time I used Qt in anger was over 18 months ago, it may have improved). It's C++ only. Other language bindings exist, but they tend to hide or poorly expose of functionality'd want Qt for. of reasons to not use Qt, that's why there are alternatives. If all you have is a hammer every problem will look like a nail.

. gtkrc is configuration file for Gtk, GUI library used by GNOME applications others. Gtk 1. x programs read ~/. gtkrc; Gtk 2. x programs read ~/. gtkrc-2. 0. Gnome settings program may have created one these files for you. If hasn't, can create one yourself. documentation of syntax options in Gtk developer manual, under “resource files”.

I agree Qt is a nice framework to work with. Still, a number of issues I have with it: It is written in C++, a low level language. fact it is C++ will make every Qt programmer less productive compared to Frameworks written in other languages. main beef with C++ as a GUI development language is it has next to no notion of automatic memory management, makes development process more prone to errors. not introspective, makes debugging difficult. Most other major GUI toolkits have some notion of automatic memory management and introspection. Every cross-platform toolkit suffers from problem it only can implement least common denominator of all supported platforms. That, and different UI guidelines on different platforms questions desirability of cross-platform GUIs at whole. Qt is centered on coding up all your UI. Even can use QtDesigner to build some parts of UI, it lacking in comparison to, (Cocoa/Obj-C) Interface Builder or. Net tools. Even Qt include lot of low-level application functionality, it can not compare to framework hand-tailored for a certain platform. native operating system libraries for both Windows and OSX are more powerful than Qt's implementations. (Think audio frameworks, low level file system access etc. ), I love using PyQt for rapid application prototyping or in-house applications. Using Python to do all coding alleviates concerns with C++ and makes Qt a pleasant place. Edit, in response to comments: When wrote about Qt being written in C++, not much complaining about Qt itself, but more about the environment it lives in. true Qt manages its own resources well, but all your GUI-related-but-not-Qt code has to be written in C++, too. Even there, Qt provides many nice tools, but ultimately, you have to deal with C++ at that level. Qt makes C++ bearable, but it is still C++.As for introspection, I mean is this: hardest cases to debug are when you have a pointer to object that not behave the way you think it should. With C++, your debugger might to look inside object bit (if it happens to have type information at thwt point), but even that not always work. Take, on other hand, Cocoa in same situation. In Cocoa/Obj-C, you able to send messages ('call functions') to object right within debugger. You can change objects state, can query it for its attributes, ask it for its type and function names. This can make debugging more convenient. Qt/C++ has nothing close to that.

people say, each tool fits to each problem and situation. But if you're C++ programmer, Qt is your framework. No rival. We develop a complex medical imaging commercial application, Qt holds on. don't say 'cons' people say about it are false, but feeling they don't have tried Qt for long time (its continously improving on each new version. ), mostly all issues they comment are not a problem if you take care. UI platform inconsistency: only if use UI widgets 'as they are', with no customization or custom art. Qt preprocessor overload: Only if you abuse of signal-slot mechanism, or QObject inheritance, when no really need., We still write applications in C#. NET, been doing it for long time. think I have enouch perspective. said, each tool for each situation, but Qt is no doubt a consistent useful framework.

term forwarding is used to describe moving any protocol across network, it decides which exit interface to use to send packet to next hop. Routing is process of forwarding packets at L3 of OSI model. based on knowing where destination is and to which interface layer 3 device should send it to. Switching is process of forwarding frames at Layer 2 of OSI based on Destination Address.
Routing - Packets forwarded by layer 3 gateway, router. Switching - Frames forwarded by layer 2 switch. Forwarding - Protocol Data Units forwarded by networked / networking device.

I see it, forwarding applies to forwarding at any layer. A frame/packet/cell arrives at a device, a header address is inspected address is looked up in forwarding table, forwarding decision is made and datagram is sent out of interface on its way. Routing describes this function when forwarding decision is made at layer 3, using IP destination address. Switching and bridging refer to forwarding decision made at layer 2, using destination MAC address. some confusion around this as seen layer 3 forwarding referred to as switching when carried out on an L3 switch.

Router describes general technical function (layer-3 forwarding) or hardware device intended for that purpose, gateway describes function for local segment (providing connectivity to elsewhere). You could also state "you set up router as gateway". Another term is hop describes forwarding in between subnets. It's just matter of perspective, device is same.

, forwarding refers to a device sending a datagram to next device in path to destination, switching refers to moving a datagram from one interface to another within device, routing refers to process a layer-3 device uses to decide on what to with a layer-3 packet. A host sending data to another host through ethernet interface will place a frame on wire. If next device is a bridge (a switch is a bridge), bridge will inspect the frame for source and destination MAC addresses. bridge use source MAC address in its MAC address table so it knows host with that MAC address is connected to interface where frame entered bridge. It will also try to look up destination MAC address in MAC address table to see to which interface it should switch the frame. If it finds MAC address in MAC address table, it will switch frame to interface indicated in MAC address table, otherwise it will flood frame to all other interfaces, forwarding frame to device(s) on other end(s) of interface(s) link(s). A router receiving a frame on interface will strip frame from packet. router try to look up destination IP address in routing table. If it doesn't find a match, even default route, it will drop the packet. If it finds one or more matches, it will switch packet to interface of the longest match in routing table. router prepare a new frame for packet on new interface (the link on new interface may or may not use MAC addresses), router will forward the new frame containing original packet over next hop interface toward destination. The whole process router uses is called routing, but within router, it switches packets before forwarding them to next hop device.

exact difference between router and gateway? A router is a device/service provides function of routing IP packets between networks. A gateway (in network terms) is a router provides access for IP packets into and/or out of local network. In Network configuration we set gateway ip address, but in reality we call device configured with that ip address as router?, gateway likely referring to is default gateway is the router to which client (or source device) sends IP packets destined somewhere other than local network for client has no "better" route. A gateway always has to be a router, but a router does not have to be a gateway.

router is layer 3 device i. e It cannot modify IP address of packet, can only change MAC Address can route packet, gateway could be NAT capable, or can act as a firewall in case of NAT-capable gateway can change packet's IP address more capable gateways can block traffic Layer2 Devices - Switches Layer3 Devices - Routers Layer2- Layer7 Devices - Gateways/Firewalls/IDC (usually implement DPI -deep packet inspection) Gateways distinct from routers or switches communicate using more than one protocol can operate at any layer of 7 layer OSI model of networking. - Wikipedia

Communication between different subnets packet reach router or layer3 devices to process packet. If another networks directly connected forwards packets on basis of ARP table. If destination on another networks forwards packet to next hops on basis route entry Configured on network. layer2 device understand IP address. Only same subnets traffic handle by layer2 device, traffic forwarded based on mac-address table

If you point static route to broadcast interface, route inserted into routing table only when broadcast interface is up. This configuration not recommended because when next hop of static route points to interface, router considers each hosts within range of route to be directly connected through interface. For example, ip route 0. 0. 0. 0 0. 0. 0. 0 Ethernet0. With this type configuration, router performs Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) on Ethernet for every destination router finds through default route because router considers all destinations as directly connected to Ethernet 0. This default route, especially if used by lot of packets to many different destination subnets, can cause high processor utilization large ARP cache (along with attendant memory allocation failures). Specifying numerical next hop on directly connected interface prevents router from performing ARP or each destination address. However, if interface with next hop goes down and numerical next hop is reachable through recursive route, should specify both next hop IP address and interface through which next hop should be found. For example, ip route 0. 0. 0. 0 0. 0. 0. 0 Serial 3/3 192. 168. 20. 1. Excerpt from Specifying a Next Hop IP Address for Static Routes at cisco. com

I think reason OOP is difficult for many is because tools don't facilitate it. Computer languages today are an abstraction of what is going on in computer. OOP is an abstracted way to represent abstractions. we using an abstraction to build abstractions with an abstraction. Add to we abstracting are usually very complex physical/social interactions, no wonder.

Object Oriented Programming in is not hard. hard part comes in doing it well. Where to put cut between code easily move things to common base object, extend them later? How to make your code usable by others (extend classes, wrap in proxies, override method) without jumping through hoops to. That is hard part, if done right can be very elegant, if done badly can be very clumsy. personal experience it requires lot of practice to been in all situations where you would WISH you did it differently, in order to do it well enough this time.

I have a blog called "Struggles in Object Oriented Programming, " born out of my struggles with learning it. it difficult for to understand because I spent much time using procedural programming, had tough time getting my head around idea that an object could be represented by a collection of attributes and behaviors (I used to simply a collection of variables and methods)., lot of concepts that make a language object oriented - inheritance, interfaces, polymorphism, composition, etc. a lot to learn about theory of it before you can write code effectively, in object-oriented way, whereas with procedural programming, it's simply a matter of understanding things like memory allocation for variables, and entry point calls to other methods.

I don't think it difficult to understand but may be lot of programmers querying are new to concept, coming from procedural languages. From what I seen/read lots of people (in forums) look for a 'result' from OOP. If you a procedural programmer who doesn't go back modify extend code it can probably be hard to understand benefits. Also, there lot of bad OOP out there, if people reading/seeing that easy to see why they might find it difficult. IMO need to wait until it 'clicks' or be taught by someone with real knowledge, don't think you can rush.

many programmers have difficulty with upfront design planning to begin. Even if someone does all design for you, still possible to break away from OOP principles. If I take of spaghetti code dump it into class, is that really OOP? Someone doesn't understand OOP can still program in Java., don't confuse difficulty to understand with not willing to follow certain methodolgy or disagreeing with it.

I personally found mechanics of OOP easy to grasp. hard part for was the "why" of it. When first exposed to it, it seemed like a solution in search of problem. few reasons why most people find it hard: IMHO teaching OO from beginning is a terrible idea. Procedural coding is not a "bad habit" right tool for some jobs. Individual methods in OO program tend to be pretty procedural looking anyhow., before learning procedural programming well enough for its limitations to become visible, OO doesn't seem useful to student. Before can grasp OO, need to know basics of data structures and late binding/higher order functions.'s hard to grok polymorphism (which is passing around pointer to data and a bunch of functions operate on data) if don't understand concepts of structuring data instead of just using primitives passing around higher order functions/pointers to functions. Design patterns should be taught as something fundamental to OO, not more advanced. Design patterns help you to see forest through trees give concrete examples of where OO can simplify real problems, you to want to learn them eventually anyhow., once you really get OO, most design patterns become obvious in hindsight.
OOP requires ability think abstractly; gift/curse few people, even professional programmers, really have.

paradigm requires certain push "over the edge" to grasp, for most people. By definition, it's a new mode of thought requires a letting go of old notions and fully grasping why new notions are useful. problem is methods used to teach computer programming are poor in general. OOP is common now it's not as noticeable, but still see it often in functional programming: important concepts hidden behind odd names (FP: What's a monad? OOP: Why do they call them functions sometimes and methods other times?) odd concepts are explained in metaphor instead of in terms of what they actually do, or why you'd use them, or why anyone thought to use them (FP: A monad is a spacesuit, it wraps up code. OOP: An object is like a duck, it can make noise, walk and inherits from Animal) good stuff varies from person to person,'s not clear what tipping point for student, often teacher can't remember. (FP:, monads let you hide something in type itself carry it on without having to explicitly write out what's happening each time. OOP:, objects let you keep functions for of data with that data. ) worst of is, as question indicates, some people will immediately snap to understanding why concept is good, and some won't. It depends on tipping point is. For me, grasping that objects store data and methods for that data was key, after that everything else just fit as natural extension. Then had later jumps like realizing method call from an object is similar to making a static call with that object as first parameter. little jumps later on help refine understanding, but it's initial one that takes a person from "OOP doesn't make sense, why do people do this?" to "OOP is the best, why do people do anything else?"

basic explanation of OOP has, little to do with how it's used in field. Most programs for teaching it try to use a physical model, such as "Think of a car as object, wheels as objects, doors, transmission. ", but outside of some obscure cases of simulation programming, objects are more often used to represent non-physical concepts or to introduce indirection. effect is it makes people understand it intuitively in wrong way. Teaching from design patterns is better way to describe OOP, it shows programmers how actual modeling problems can be attacked with objects, rather than describing it in abstract.

Motivation. harder to learn something when you don't see why, and when can't look at what you did figure whether did it right or not. needed is small projects that use OO to do useful things. suggest looking through a book on design patterns come up with one obviously useful and works well with OO. Since Unix was a powerful part of development of modern programming, C was dragged along into infamy with it., answer to your question is "No". C is based off of language called ALGOL, many competitors both with ALGOL (FORTRAN, Lisp, COBOL) and C (none to mind). Object-oriented programming, biggest paradigm-shift in programming design, did not originate with C - despite C++ being a popular OOP language (it showed up first in Lisp or Simula 67, depending on). By time OOP came about, C was popular language it didn't need to be first - so popular that C++ "expansion", became one of primary OOP languages too. It remains in modern use mainly because of its powerful memory control features (you can directly allocate and deallocate memory structures create), allowing it to create programs on tight memory budgets (think video games) and highly optimized compiler (obviously depending on the compiler)., even these features losing ground as Java JIT compilation and in-language memory managers become more advanced.

I personally found mechanics of OOP easy to grasp. hard part for was the "why" of it. When first exposed to it, it seemed like a solution in search of problem. few reasons why most people find it hard: IMHO teaching OO from beginning is a terrible idea. Procedural coding is not a "bad habit" right tool for some jobs. Individual methods in OO program tend to be pretty procedural looking anyhow., before learning procedural programming well enough for its limitations to become visible, OO doesn't seem useful to student. Before can grasp OO, need to know basics of data structures and late binding/higher order functions.'s hard to grok polymorphism (which is passing around pointer to data and a bunch of functions operate on data) if don't understand concepts of structuring data instead of just using primitives passing around higher order functions/pointers to functions. Design patterns should be taught as something fundamental to OO, not more advanced. Design patterns help you to see forest through trees give concrete examples of where OO can simplify real problems, you to want to learn them eventually anyhow., once you really get OO, most design patterns become obvious in hindsight.

HTML and XML are both markup languages (hence the *ML). XML is a generic markup language suitable for representing arbitrary data, HTML is a specific markup language suitable only for representing web pages. HTML and XHTML are both subsets of SGML, except XHTML has additional specifications it also validates as XML. XML as XHTML's influential godfather. Because of relationship to SGML across all 3 these languages, of similarities, but they are all considered different languages., defines these languages is their restrictions on SGML. HTML restricts SGML by defining a list of tags allowed to used. XML restricts SGML by not allowing unclosed or empty start and end tags, forces attributes to be explicit. XML has additional restrictions not found in SGML. XHTML restricts SGML with tags from HTML (with some exclusions, as frameset,), and with tag and entity restrictions from XML. may find this document helpful, technical terms may be hard to digest. http://www. w3. org/TR/NOTE-sgml-xml-971215 XML is not a metalanguage for defining markup languages.'s just SGML. XML is simply a data formatting markup language. Your quoted source is using technical terms imprecisely, confusing. Purposes XML is for defining your own data format. If to pass data between two systems, XML is often the way to do it. If, for example, needed to pass a sales order from website to billing system, could create this XML payload: <order id="12345"> <name>John Doe</name> <item id="443">Adult Diapers</item> </order> Your website would send that XML to your billing system, which could parse data from XML. XHTML and HTML are just for web pages. XHTML's primary purpose is to remove ambiguity in previous years (decades) of web development.Back late 90s I started, we using HTML 3. 2 allowed for seriously sloppy code. HTML 4+ and XHTML try remedy by strongly suggesting or enforcing explicit closing tags, explicit attributes, and disallowed tags, makes easier on both browsers and humans, avoids unexpected differences in behaviour cross-browser.

XHTML is updated version HTML but with some rules put it place so it also correct XML. notes on how HTML 5 Standard works with other specifications. http://dev. w3. org/html5/spec/Overview. html#compliance-with-other-specifications not sure of differences between SGML and XML or when use one over the other. XML to commonly used one. For XHTML and HTML better off always using XHTML. Errors easier to find and bonus it also be valid XML.

three concepts overlap somewhat, get endless arguments whether XSLT is a programming language or Python is a scripting language or not. A markup language is a language represent structured data in textual format, HTML is most well-known, but numerous formats for various purposes, like SVG for graphics, WSDL for describing web service interfaces, resx for resouce files in. net and so on. rule of thumb is markup language not describe a process or algorithm (like programming language does) but is pure data. But fundamental CS insight no fundamental difference between code and data. Some markup languages like XSLT has loops and conditionals like "real" programming language, and some programming languages like Prolog are almost pure data with no process specified in code. Lisp blurs line it treats its own code as a structured data format. for distinction between programming language and scripting language, is a historical distinction almost obsolete today. In olden days we had compiled stand-alone programs written in C, and then had scripting languages like shell scripts or Word Basic, were interpreted and designed to manipulate other programs and tool. Today line is blurred with lot of middle ground, since various levels of compilation and interpretation (bytecode compilation, JIT-compilation etc. ), and various language-independent API's. distinction not that useful.

history of these might enlighten you here. talking about meta-languages, profiles, subsets instances is little dry ! try to keep it short and simple. SGML evolved from GML (Generalized Markup Language) devised by 3 IBM engineers in 1960s means of storing elaborate legal, government, industrial military documents. GML gradually refined till standardized as SGML in 1986. GML/SGML is not a language per se. It is rather a meta-language,. language to define conforming languages or "rules" by which formatting of variety of elaborate documents could be designed in generally consistent way. Each different type of document would define its own SGML conforming set of tag names plus associated attributes, defined formal public identifiers/namespaces, schemas, etc. Each format defined like became a distinct data storage language for document type concerned. Because of consistency between all documents conforming to SGML rules, possible to write code to collate/process data within documents and transfer data between documents sharing common format. SGML was found overly elaborate for numerous smaller-sized document. XML developed between 1996 and 2006 as a subset (the word profile means same as subset) of SGML that could handle both small and large documents. Being a subset of meta-language, XML is itself a meta-language, though simpler one. XML provides basis for designing document formats suitable for easy storage and transfer between systems on network. After standardization of SGML before simplified to XML, internet emerged with need for document format that enabled easy transfer and display of both documents and loose data. result was HTML language, instance (occasionally referred to as application) of SGML with 18 pre-defined tags providing standardized way to display variety of data types, e. g. text, images, audio, etc. HTML exploited SGML's allowing some elements to omit start- or end-tags.Subsequent versions of HTML added new tags attributes made obsolete existing ones. Until HTML 5, changes to HTML made so it always remained a child language of SGML. After XML standardized, instance it called XHTML came out combined existing HTML tag names with XML's rigor on tag closing, namespaces, schemas, etc. XHTML initially held promise of useful for storage, transfer display of data. It seemed to be about to replace HTML as commonest way to display web material - until HTML 5 came out. HTML 5 had syntactic features beyond defined in SGML to provide richer data display, especially for multimedia laden websites. As time went on, additional features added to HTML 5 enriched more its use for data display/use to it unlikely to be superseded by new XHTML versions, display of data. standards for HTML & XHTML are done by W3C working groups, actual propagation of languages "on ground" is done by progressive web designers none more progressive than those working in media (advertising/PR/marketing) sector: look at creativity of advertising agency sites compared to other sites. This sector took to new HTML 5 language, delighted in exploiting its capacity for SVG, audio, video new APIs. ready adoption of HTML 5 led to its popularity among web designers in, process accelerated by online exchange of skills tricks on YouTube various other sites. updated XHTML version, XHTML5, has emerged but it not really a strict XML derivative but rather a version of HTML5 is XML-serialized. Only a small proportion of sites appear to have use for it. That's the story behind these data languages. I hope it helps you distinguish the meaning and purpose of them all.Philosophically, story shows essential enabling tool (SGML) for new technology (internet) can, in new environment with increasingly varied demands, outgrow original limits become conceptually simpler, applicably more versatile impactfully more powerful.

That's actually a broad question. In the basic sense, a web API works when a client (like a Web browser) makes an HTTP request to a Web server. server examines request to figure out what user wants, and then returns data in format (like a page) that client then examines to get what it wants. These are about the only things Web APIs have in common; realize this doesn't answer your question, but wanted to give reason why question is broad. all of ways a client could format its request, or a server could format its response, in for any it to make sense, client and server have to agree on basic rules. Generally speaking, two general styles get used for this thing. Remote Procedure Call (RPC) In RPC style API,'s usually just one URL for the whole API. You call it by POSTing a document of contains information about what you want to do, server returns document that has what you want. In general computing terms, request document typically has a function name and some arguments. standards for this style of API include XML-RPC and SOAP. These standards attempt to create format can be used to describe the function calls, or to describe the whole API. REpresentational State Transfer (REST) In REST style API, you don't much have a URL for API as a name space: a server, or a folder inside of a server, where of different objects reside, every URL within this namespace becomes part of the API. Rather than telling server you want to use API, the URL tells server what you want to use the API on. You then use the HTTP method, and possibly request body, to explain what you want to do to that object: GET (retrieve something already there), POST (create something new), PUT (replace something's already there), or DELETE (get rid of something that's already there). There are few other verbs you can use, but those are by the most common.So far, I haven't mentioned standard formats for REST. In theory, you could use any format. HTTP provides for saying what you want to do to it, so format of request body could be anything: some representation of the object you want to create or replace. But in practice, REST authors tend to agree on a format anyway, because it difficult to make sense of every possible format.

It defines set of rules be followed by programs to communicate with other. APIs specify how routines, data structures,. should be defined in for two applications to communicate. APIs differ in the functionality provided by. are general APIs provide library functionalities of a programming language such as Java API. also APIs provides specific functionalities such as Google Maps API. also language dependent APIs, only be used by a specific programming language., language independent APIs could be used with several programming languages. APIs needs to be implemented carefully by exposing only required functionality or data to outside, while keeping the other parts of application inaccessible. Usage of APIs has become popular in internet. It common to allow some of functionality and data through an API to the outside on the Web. This functionality can be combined to offer improved functionality to users. What is SDK? SDK is a set of tools be used to develop software applications targeting a specific platform. SDKs include tools, libraries, documentation and sample code help programmer to develop application. Most of SDKs could be downloaded from the internet and many the SDKs are provided free to encourage programmers to use SDK‘s programming language. Some widely used SDKs are Java SDK (JDK) includes all libraries, debugging utilities, etc., make writing programs easier in Java. SDKs make life of a software developer easy, since no need to look for components/ tools compatible with each other and all are integrated in to a single package is easy to install. API is an interface allows software programs to interact with each other, a SDK is a set of tools can be used to develop software applications targeting a specific platform.simplest version of a SDK could be API contains files required to interact with a specific programming language. So an API can be seen as simple SDK without debugging support, etc.

At its simplest, you create set of GET/POST requests anyone can call and publish information on URLs, parameters and effects. GET requests for read-only tasks and POST requests for anything change data on server. Add in authentication system if needed and you have yourself simple Web API. Web API is just an Interface to allow access to your system (such as site) via standard HTTP request methods. data usually wrapped in standard format (such as JSON or XML) to make easy to handle. example Web API for 'TextWise'

I'm developing an API for my company's virtualization platform now. can go about them in few different ways, but my favorite (and fastest route to getting something working people understand) is using simple HTTP GET requests returning a JSON response. My URL's look like this: domain. com/method/call/subcall?key=key&data=something I then break down HTTP GET variables, do what caller wants done with them. of reasons I signed up as a beta user to Stack Exchange API development was knew it would be a tremendous learning experience, and indeed it was. Usually, I return two JSON encoded arrays, one being result, which just says if call was successful and gives error code / error string if not. The other is usually just called data, contents of described in documentation of call., GET based API's are easier to test and debug. of other formats exist, such as SOAP / XMLRPC, find chosing JSON gives simplicity and freedom of choice. For instance, if I need to send a lot of fields don't want to deal with ton of GET variables, can just do this (example in PHP) $to_send = base64_encode(json_encode($some_array)); easily decoded on other side, giving me dozens of variables to work with, while still only accepting 2 - 3 GET variables via API. I try to keep methods and calls short and succinct, design it in way where each call returns a uniform 'worked or failed' response, followed by data requested.

My two cents: I believe term API often used incorrectly. An API is an Application Programming Interface. awkward name, it means it's an interface. an application might have an API to allow other applications to communicate with it. piece of software (e. g. a class in an OO system) might offer an API to allow other modules in the system to communicate with it. often term API used as a synonym of "library". don't think's correct use of word. Part of library is an API to allow code to use it, but library isn't an API. an SDK is a kind of library,'s confusion might be.

the other answers explain an SDK is tooling, but none of directly says an API is a specification. The API for compoonent X is all the information you need in to write some other component will interact with X. An SDK for component X may contain library routines make it easier for to write component, but libraries are not the API: They are merely an embodiment of the API.

"SDK" is collective in larger sense than "API". typically find only one SDK to cover entire platform. one MacOS X SDK and one iOS SDK, for example, those each contain API's for many different areas of functionality. "API" was originally used as collective term, still often used that way (MAPI, WSAPI, etc. ), but usually limited to some particular technology. scope implied by "API" to diminished over years; people used to talk about "Mac Toolbox API" or "Windows API, " both of obviously contained a lot of functionality. These days, not uncommon to hear "API" used to mean single system function; new version of operating system might be said to contain hundreds of new API's, and meant is hundreds of new system calls. Neither term very precise without context.

API = Application Programming Interface SDK = Software Development Kit real difference is: an API is no more than an interface to "some service", an SDK is a set of tools, components classes for specific purpose. An SDK presents you with an API to interface with. you might use an API without underlying components, for example when API provided through web service. Examples of APIs: Java API Google Maps API Flash Player API Examples SDKs: JDK GWT Flex SDK

I think it rather falls the lines "All SDKs are APIs but not all APIs are SDKs". An SDK seems to be a complete set of APIs allow you to perform most any action need for creating applications. In an SDK may include other tools for developing for the platform/item it is for. An API is just a series of related methods may be good for a specific purpose. As example, the JDK (Java Development Kit) contains the API compilers, runtimes, other miscellaneous tools. The Java API is all the libraries that make up the core language you can work with out of the box.

API → documented interface (at certain point in time, for certain audience. Documentation might be incomplete/or unavailable to general public might be on purpose, but not dimish fact it meant to be documented for third parties to use it. ) SDK → interface documentation ( + examples & tools )

native VLAN only relevant to 802. 1q, yes it untagged by default, but can be tagged if required. Ports assigned to native VLAN if no other config present. It's ok to keep it as VLAN 1, but can be changed, to remember to shut down unused ports. by, if I plugged my evil hacker laptop into working port left as VLAN 1, I could potentially be to span across your entire network, whereas you could change native VLAN to VLAN 10, and then not assign VLAN 10 to any ports. ISL has no concept of native VLAN.

access links presented to any device without tags. when traffic leaves vlan going into switch for destination not on same vlan it gets tag of vlan added to each frame, to allow switch to forward it correctly. speak of native vlan, it is common vlan two devices agree to send non tag packets. default vlan on cisco switches is vlan 1. Devices need common untag network to communicate on. Tags are for forwarding purposes. provide no value within vlan.

They very much different. lot terms (megabit, megabyte, memory, hard drive, etc) get miscommunicated. Often customers asking us to move a vlan from one site to another, when they want is to move subnet over. You get used to it, I try and correct them (politely)

used interchangeably then used incorrectly. Subnet refers to particular IP network, such as 192. 0. 2. 0/28. VLAN refers to 802. 1Q standard, give each port unique MAC address table, separating them from each other. VLAN may transport one or more subnet (but not have to, may be transporting something else than IP entirely). Subnet may be configured for VLAN, but not have to be, could be without 802. 1Q or over different L2 technology than ethernet.

Vlan is broadcast domain. default hosts in single Vlan communicates each other. different Vlans won't communicate each other, ensure communication between different Vlans host routing between Vlans mandatory for Configuring routing between Vlan layer3 device required. inter-Vlan routing or using layer3 device SVi can be configured with different Vlans make them talk to each.

In many implementations IPv4 subnet and a VLAN closely correlated on 1:1 basis. A subnet, is a portion of IPv4 address space from may assign addresses to hosts. differentiated from a "prefix" a term in common parlance or a supernet, may be a larger portion of IP address space comprised of many subnets. reason for correlation is a single VLAN and single subnet both represent a single broadcast domain., these two tend to be overlaid in most implementations. described in earlier answers, a VLAN is a layer 2 entity. All hosts on given VLAN can communicate with each other, but no hosts on one VLAN can communicate to hosts on another without form routing or in rare cases, bridging.

often confused point for people new to Networking, in particular to people up Cisco track, due to Cisco's over emphasis on this point. It more just a terminology thing. explain. 802. 1q standard defines method of tagging traffic between two switches to distinguish which traffic belongs to which VLANs. In Cisco terms, this is what happens on a "trunk" port. other vendors refer to this as a "tagged" port. In context, it means same: adding identifier to frames to indicate what VLAN frame belongs to. Terminology aside, main thing to in is VLAN tag is necessary, because often traffic traversing two switches belongs to multiple VLANs, must be way to determine which 1's and 0's belong to which VLAN. But what happens if a trunk port, expecting to receive traffic includes VLAN tag, receives traffic with no tag? In predecessor to 802. 1q, known as ISL (cisco proprietary, but archaic, no one supports it anymore, not even Cisco), untagged traffic on trunk would simply be dropped. 802. 1q however, provided for a way to not only receive this traffic, but also associate it to a VLAN of your choosing. This method is known as setting a Native VLAN., configure your trunk port with Native VLAN, whatever traffic arrives on port without existing VLAN tag, gets associated to your Native VLAN. As with all configuration items, if do not explicitly configure, usually default behavior exists. In case of Cisco (and most vendors), Default Native VLAN is VLAN 1. to, if not set Native VLAN explicitly, any untagged traffic received on trunk port is automatically placed in VLAN 1. trunk port is "opposite" from an Access Port. access port sends and expects to receive traffic with no VLAN tag.this work, an access port only sends and expects to receive traffic belonging to one VLAN. access port is statically configured for a particular VLAN, any traffic received on that port is internally associated on Switch as belonging to a particular VLAN (despite not tagging traffic for that VLAN when it leaves switch port)., to add to confusing mix. Cisco books refer to "default VLAN". The Default VLAN is the VLAN all Access Ports are assigned to until explicitly placed in another VLAN. In of Cisco switches (and most other Vendors, Default VLAN is usually VLAN 1. Typically, this VLAN is only relevant on an Access port, a port that sends and expects to receive traffic without a VLAN tag (also referred to an 'untagged port' by other vendors)., to summarize: Native VLAN can change. can set it to anything you like. Access Port VLAN can change. can set it to anything you like. Default Native VLAN is always 1, can not be change, because its set that way by Cisco Default VLAN is always 1, can not be changed, because it set that way by Cisco forgot other questions, can it / should it be changed? This is largely an opinion question. to agree with this school of thought: All unused ports should be in a specific VLAN. All active ports should be explicitly set on to a particular VLAN. Your switch should prevent traffic from traversing uplink into rest of network if traffic belongs on VLAN1, or VLAN you using for unused ports. Everything else should be allowed up the uplink. many different theories behind this. differing requirements would prevent restricted switch policy (scale, resources, etc).For instance, if a switch going into part of a network only one VLAN not VLAN 1, is possible to make "default" / native VLAN on all ports a particular VLAN using one global command, or preferred method to make all ports access ports and set access VLAN to 10 on each? You can not change default Cisco configurations. can use "interface range" to put all ports in different VLAN in one go. don't need to change Native VLAN on uplink trunk, so long as other switch is using same Native VLAN. If want to spare the switch from adding VLAN Tag, you could get creative do following (although, probably not recommended). Leave all access ports in the VLAN1. Leave Native VLAN at its default (VLAN1). On uplink switch, set the port as a trunk port. set its Native VLAN to the VLAN you want lower switch to be a part of. Since lower switch will send traffic to upper switch untagged, upper switch will receive it and associate it with it considers Native VLAN.

terminal is at end of electric wire, shell is home of turtle, tty is strange abbreviation and console is kind of cabinet., etymologically speaking, anyway. In unix terminology, short answer is terminal = tty = text input/output environment console = physical terminal shell = command line interpreter Console, terminal and tty are closely related. Originally, they meant piece of equipment through which interact with computer: in early days of unix, meant teleprinter-style device resembling typewriter, sometimes called teletypewriter, or “tty” in shorthand. name “terminal” came from electronic point of view, and name “console” from furniture point of view. early in unix history, electronic keyboards and displays became norm for terminals. In unix terminology, tty is particular kind of device file implements number of additional commands (ioctls) beyond read and write. In most common meaning, terminal is synonymous with tty. Some ttys provided by kernel on behalf of hardware device, for example with input from keyboard and output to text mode screen, or with input and output transmitted over serial line. Other ttys, sometimes called pseudo-ttys, are provided (through thin kernel layer) by programs called terminal emulators, such as Xterm (running in X Window System), Screen (which provides layer of isolation between program and another terminal), Ssh (which connects terminal on one machine with programs on another machine), Expect (for scripting terminal interactions), etc. word terminal can also have more traditional meaning of device through which one interacts with computer, typically with keyboard and display. For example X terminal is kind of thin client, special-purpose computer only purpose is to drive keyboard, display, mouse and occasionally other human interaction peripherals, with actual applications running on another, more powerful computer. console is generally a terminal in physical sense is by some definition primary terminal directly connected to machine.console appears to operating system as a (kernel-implemented) tty. On some systems, Linux and FreeBSD, console appears as several ttys (special key combinations switch between these ttys); to confuse, name given to each tty can be “console”, ”virtual console”, ”virtual terminal”, and other variations. See also Why is a Virtual Terminal “virtual”, and what/why/where is the “real” Terminal?. shell is primary interface users see when log in, primary purpose is to start other programs. (I don't know whether original metaphor is shell is home environment for user, or shell is what other programs running in. In unix circles, shell specialized to mean command-line shell, centered around entering name of application wants to start, followed by names of files or other objects application should act on, pressing Enter key. Other types of environments don't use word “shell”; for, window systems involve “window managers” and “desktop environments”, not a “shell”. many different unix shells. Popular shells for interactive use include Bash default on most Linux installations, zsh power and customizability) and fish simplicity). Command-line shells include flow control constructs to combine commands. In addition to typing commands at interactive prompt, users can write scripts. most common shells have common syntax based on Bourne_shell. When discussing “shell programming”, shell is almost always implied to be a Bourne-style shell. Some shells often used for scripting but lack advanced interactive features include Korn shell (ksh) and many ash variants. any Unix-like system has a Bourne-style shell installed as /bin/sh, usually ash, ksh or bash. In unix system administration, user's shell is program invoked when they log in.Normal user accounts have a command-line shell, but users with restricted access may have restricted shell or other specific command (e. g. for file-transfer-only accounts). division of labor between terminal and shell not obvious. their main tasks. Input: terminal converts keys into control sequences (e. g. Left → \e[D). shell converts control sequences into commands (e. g. \e[D → backward-char). Line editing, input history and completion are provided by shell. terminal may provide its own line editing, history and completion instead, only send a line to shell when ready to be executed. only common terminal operates in this way is M-x shell in Emacs. Output: shell emits instructions as “display foo”, “switch foreground color to green”, “move cursor to next line”,. terminal acts on these instructions. prompt is purely a shell concept. shell never sees output of commands it runs (unless redirected). Output history (scrollback) is purely a terminal concept. Inter-application copy-paste provided by terminal (usually with mouse or key sequences Ctrl+Shift+V or Shift+Insert). shell may have its own internal copy-paste mechanism (e. Meta+W and Ctrl+Y). Job control (launching programs in background and managing them) mostly performed by shell., it terminal handles key combinations like Ctrl+C to kill foreground job and Ctrl+Z to suspend it.

Some ttys provided by kernel on behalf of hardware device, for example with input from keyboard and output to text mode screen, or with input and output transmitted over serial line. Other ttys, sometimes called pseudo-ttys, are provided (through thin kernel layer) by programs called terminal emulators, such as Xterm (running in X Window System), Screen (which provides layer of isolation between program and another terminal), Ssh (which connects terminal on one machine with programs on another machine), Expect (for scripting terminal interactions), etc. word terminal can also have more traditional meaning of device through which one interacts with computer, typically with keyboard and display. For example X terminal is kind of thin client, special-purpose computer only purpose is to drive keyboard, display, mouse and occasionally other human interaction peripherals, with actual applications running on another, more powerful computer. console is generally a terminal in physical sense is by some definition primary terminal directly connected to machine.console appears to operating system as a (kernel-implemented) tty. On some systems, Linux and FreeBSD, console appears as several ttys (special key combinations switch between these ttys); to confuse, name given to each tty can be “console”, ”virtual console”, ”virtual terminal”, and other variations. See also Why is a Virtual Terminal “virtual”, and what/why/where is the “real” Terminal?. shell is primary interface users see when log in, primary purpose is to start other programs. (I don't know whether original metaphor is shell is home environment for user, or shell is what other programs running in. In unix circles, shell specialized to mean command-line shell, centered around entering name of application wants to start, followed by names of files or other objects application should act on, pressing Enter key. Other types of environments don't use word “shell”; for, window systems involve “window managers” and “desktop environments”, not a “shell”. many different unix shells. Popular shells for interactive use include Bash default on most Linux installations, zsh power and customizability) and fish simplicity). Command-line shells include flow control constructs to combine commands. In addition to typing commands at interactive prompt, users can write scripts. most common shells have common syntax based on Bourne_shell. When discussing “shell programming”, shell is almost always implied to be a Bourne-style shell. Some shells often used for scripting but lack advanced interactive features include Korn shell (ksh) and many ash variants. any Unix-like system has a Bourne-style shell installed as /bin/sh, usually ash, ksh or bash. In unix system administration, user's shell is program invoked when they log in.Normal user accounts have a command-line shell, but users with restricted access may have restricted shell or other specific command (e. g. for file-transfer-only accounts). division of labor between terminal and shell not obvious. their main tasks. Input: terminal converts keys into control sequences (e. g. Left → \e[D). shell converts control sequences into commands (e. g. \e[D → backward-char). Line editing, input history and completion are provided by shell. terminal may provide its own line editing, history and completion instead, only send a line to shell when ready to be executed. only common terminal operates in this way is M-x shell in Emacs. Output: shell emits instructions as “display foo”, “switch foreground color to green”, “move cursor to next line”,. terminal acts on these instructions. prompt is purely a shell concept. shell never sees output of commands it runs (unless redirected). Output history (scrollback) is purely a terminal concept. Inter-application copy-paste provided by terminal (usually with mouse or key sequences Ctrl+Shift+V or Shift+Insert). shell may have its own internal copy-paste mechanism (e. Meta+W and Ctrl+Y). Job control (launching programs in background and managing them) mostly performed by shell., it terminal handles key combinations like Ctrl+C to kill foreground job and Ctrl+Z to suspend it.

'Filtered port' statement from nmap differs according scan method. standard scan (TCP Scan if unprivileged user, or Half-Open scan -sS if superuser) relies on TCP protocol. (named 3-way hanshake) client (you) issues a SYN, if server replies SYN/ACK : it means port is open ! You issue a SYN, if server replies RST : it means port is close ! You issue a SYN, if server not reply, or replies with ICMP error : it means port is filtered. Likely IDS / statefull firewall block request) To figure real status of port, can : use -sV, or -A option (version detection, help to determine status port. use --tcp-flags SYN, FIN to try bypassing fw. use other scan types (http://nmap. org/book/man-port-scanning-techniques. html) "Nmap Network Discovery" book, written by creator Fyodor explains this well. I quote filtered : Nmap cannot determine whether port is open because packet filtering prevents probes from reaching port. filtering could be from dedicated firewall device, router rules, or host-based firewall software. These ports frustrate attackers because provide little information. respond with ICMP error messages as type 3 code 13 (destination unreachable: communication administratively prohibited), but filters that drop probes without responding are more common. This forces Nmap to retry several times in case probe was dropped due to network congestion rather than filtering. This filtering slows scans down dramatically. open|filtered : Nmap places ports in this state when unable to determine whether port is open or filtered. This occurs for scan types in which open ports give no response. lack of response could also mean packet filter dropped probe or response elicited. Nmap does not know for sure whether port is open or filtered.UDP, IP protocol, FIN, NULL, and Xmas scans classify ports this way. closed|filtered : state used when Nmap unable to determine port closed or filtered. only used for IP ID Idle scan discussed in Section 5. 10, "TCP Idle Scan (-sl)

list available file systems differs by platform operation. Refer to product documentation or use show file systems EXEC command to determine prefixes available on your platform. File system prefixes listed: bootflash: Boot Flash memory. Bootflash generic term used for flash of route flash and switch flash. disk0: Rotating media. flash: Flash memory. This prefix available on all platforms. For platforms not device named flash:, prefix flash: is aliased to slot0:., use prefix flash: to refer to main Flash memory storage area on all platforms. flh: Flash load helper log files. ftp: FTP network server. null: Null destination for copies. copy remote file to null to determine size. nvram: NVRAM. where configuration saved when copy run start. rcp: Remote copy protocol network server. slavebootflash: Internal Flash memory on slave RSP card of router configured for high system availability (HSA). slavenvram: NVRAM on slave Route/Switch Processor (RSP) card of router configured for HSA. slaveslot0: First PCMCIA card on slave RSP card router configured for HSA. slaveslot1: Second PCMCIA card on slave RSP card router configured for HSA. slot0: First PCMCIA Flash memory card. slot1: Second PCMCIA Flash memory card. system: Contains system memory, including running configuration. tftp: TFTP network server. xmodem: Obtain file from network machine using Xmodem protocol. ymodem: Obtain file from network machine using Ymodem protocol. Source: https://www. cisco. com/c/en/us/td/docs/ios/12_2/configfun/configuration/guide/ffun_c/fcf006. html

1. Flash memory is the technology, not the product. Everyone to focus on size aspect, but "flash memory" is really just the technology, not an end product. It used in both USB storage and SSDs (the difference being quality of NAND memory) unfortunate that name got tagged automatically associated with a particular product (USB then, SSD now) — just like how mention of "Wiki" reminds one of Wikipedia, although it only refers to technology underneath. For example, this article from Seagate, leading manufacturer of SSDs and HDDs, does not differentiate two terms as different products. look at Apple's tech specs, they use term flash storage, not flash memory, is just their way of calling it. 2. Marketing — "flash" conveys notions of lightning speed believe this primary reason — word "drive" conjures up images of something in motion. From marketing point of view, exact opposite of image you wish to convey when tout things as not having movable parts. compare that with "flash", conveys notions of transience, speed (think Flash Gordon), etc. Given Apple's meticulous care for detail, wouldn't be surprised if they consciously decided to ditch word "SSD" because of this.

Depends on speed of flash. Most flash drives allow faster read then write since writing to flash is "destructive operation" site like http://usbspeed. nirsoft. net/ might provide further information. example SSD drives are rates at number Input/Output Operations/s (IOPS) commonly read faster then on best most expensive drives.

benefit of using flash memory in Macbook Air? How use flash memory compare to SSDs? benefits? Macbook Air uses an SSD. Apple markets it as merely flash memory because in consumer market only two storage types - flash and hard drives. typical consumer Apple aiming for not know what SSD is, nor they care. But they know what a "flash drive" is, due to aggressive marketing they believe it's better than alternative. It's a custom form-factor SSD, it uses SATA flash controller, Air reads it as if any other SATA drive. OS X does, understand it as an SSD and treats it slightly differently from a hard drive in to use it to full potential, but in every other respect it's just a custom form factor SSD. reason Apple uses custom form factor SSD is for size, weight, and - important to Apple - cost. They have both Toshiba and Samsung on line for supplying these SSDs. When they get poor price from one, they go to the other. They need this because SSD is one of few in Air requires custom PCB layout comes from multiple suppliers. pinouts and circuitry different between samsung and toshiba flash controllers, they can't build them into main PCB as Apple prefer, without locking them into one vendor or other. flash market is volatile they can't lock themselves into just one supplier, especially since 80% of Apple's revenue comes from products use copious amounts of flash. If they thought they could get better price manufacturing their own flash, they'd have their own plant - or ten. Instead it's cheaper to play major flash producers against each other to get lowest cost. Storage in the Air is a SATA interfaced SSD not on the main PCB to ability to use different parts from different suppliers It's not a 2. 5", 1.8", or SATA slim interface they needed it to be smaller - designed their own interface, but it's still SATA, with different low insertion force connector aren't using latest greatest chipsets due to cost power consumption aren't using hard drives due to size, weight, power consumption

https://tools. ietf. org/html/rfc2131#page-13 servers receive DHCPREQUEST broadcast from client. Those servers not selected by DHCPREQUEST message use message as notification that client has declined server's offer. protocol assumes may be multiple DHCP servers. By broadcasting request message, all servers may have issued an offer can be aware of client's choice.
Because until server sends DHCPACK, client still doesn’t have IP address. possible for a DHCP server to respond to a request with a DHCPNACK.

Be aware of broadcast flag, see RFC2131 (page 24): A client cannot receive unicast IP datagrams until protocol software configured with an IP address SHOULD set BROADCAST bit in 'flags' field to 1 in any DHCPDISCOVER or DHCPREQUEST messages client sends. BROADCAST bit will provide hint to DHCP server and BOOTP relay agent to broadcast any messages to client on client's subnet. EDIT A client that can receive unicast IP datagrams before protocol software configured SHOULD clear BROADCAST bit to 0. BOOTP clarifications document discusses ramifications of use of BROADCAST bit. Added rest of RFC. According to entire paragraph, it could be either broadcast, or unicast or even both.

https://www. ietf. org/rfc/rfc2131. txt per this RFC: Droms Standards Track [Page 24] RFC 2131 Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol March 1997 Normally, DHCP servers and BOOTP relay agents attempt to deliver DHCPOFFER, DHCPACK and DHCPNAK messages directly to client using uicast delivery. IP destination address (in IP header) is set to DHCP 'yiaddr' address and link-layer destination address set to DHCP 'chaddr' address., some client implementations unable to receive unicast IP datagrams until implementation configured with a valid IP address (leading to a deadlock in client's IP address cannot be delivered until client configured with an IP address). client that cannot receive unicast IP datagrams until protocol software configured with an IP address SHOULD set BROADCAST bit in 'flags' field to 1 in any DHCPDISCOVER or DHCPREQUEST messages client sends. BROADCAST bit provide hint to DHCP server and BOOTP relay agent to broadcast messages to client on client's subnet. client that can receive unicast IP datagrams before protocol software configured SHOULD clear BROADCAST bit to 0. BOOTP clarifications document discusses ramifications of use of BROADCAST bit [21]. A server or relay agent sending or relaying DHCP message directly to DHCP client (i., not to a relay agent specified in 'giaddr' field) SHOULD examine BROADCAST bit in 'flags' field. If this bit is set to 1, DHCP message SHOULD be sent as an IP broadcast using IP broadcast address (preferably 0xffffffff) as IP destination address and link-layer broadcast address as link-layer destination address.If BROADCAST bit cleared to 0, message SHOULD be sent as an IP unicast to IP address specified in 'yiaddr' field and link-layer address specified in 'chaddr' field. If unicasting not possible, message MAY be sent as an IP broadcast using IP broadcast address (preferably 0xffffffff) as IP destination address and link- layer broadcast address as link-layer destination address.

DHCP for helping new clients network get IP address dynamically. (Without IP address, they're helpless. ) Dynamic NAT for translating clients already on network to different IP addresses dynamically. Using this, they appear to outside world like they have different address than they really do. only common thread between two is word "dynamic". When DHCP hands out addresses, it does so dynamically, means you might get different IP address next time. When NAT translates you, it does so dynamically, means might get translated to different port number or IP address next time.

DHCP server answering with DHCP OFFER to provide IP address. It knows target MAC and IP, hence will use unicast IP packet, toward originating Ethernet address, hence unicast Ethernet frame too. If want to see it for real, enter following command on DHCP server: tcpdump -imy_ethernet_device-e src port bootps where my_ethernet_device is name of Ethernet interface on which DHCP server is replying to your network.

answer is it can be either broadcast or unicast - and in some cases both unicast and broadcast before it reaches client when ip helper-address is used. client doesn't have IP address until DISCOVER-OFFER-REQUEST-ACK exchange is completed. possible (although unlikely) to situation arise where server will resond to REQUEST with a NAK. However, since unicast is generally preferred over broadcast, many clients will accept unicast reply that matches their L2 address.

DHCP and NAT have nothing in common (above "IP-related things"). elaborate what they do you find similar. DHCP assigns IP address, NAT mangles IP addresses (and higher level ports, like TCP/UDP), e. g. translates them to different address range.

When message sent using iMessage, from Apple device to an Apple device, message bubble will be blue. When message sent using SMS, in your instance this be from your Apple device to non-Apple device, message bubble will be green. This to show you message was sent but your device can't obtain a read receipt or let you know message was delivered.

When bubble is blue, message is send as an iMessage. If it turn green, it is send as a regular SMS. iMessages have build in delivery report will tell you tings like 'delivered' or 'read' when message gets delivered/read. However, regular SMS doesn't provide these options, you'll have to install 3th party software to get this of feedback. to trust your provider to make sure message gets delivered. If you have jailbroken your device, SMS Delivery Report repository in Cydia. If you don't like iMessages to be sent as regular text, can simply turn this feature off in Settings < Messages < Send As SMS

Basically, your message has been sent, from your end, to another iPhone or Apple apparatus (it appears in Blue and not Green) but not delivered to your recipient. "Delivered" may not appear for several reasons. most likely, and only I confirmed, is recipient cannot receive data. This happens when a phone is off or out of service range,. It also happens frequently if they talking on the phone. When someone is talking voice, and out of a WiFi area, they may not be able to receive text messages, because they may drop or lose some of data, so it is conveniently held onto for them until they're freed up (i. off the phone). It can also happen when WiFi access is spotty, when other apps are running in background,. reason you may be experiencing this but still receiving responses is once a response is sent (in exchange) "Delivered" or "Read" message vanishes. you're probably not seeing it change to Delivered to Read before you see a response. Another possibility explain both, unconfirmed by, is "Do Not Disturb" feature is toggled on recipients phone. aware, this prevents them from receiving notifications of messages, haven't test it out. It's one of the above for sure. Hope it helps.

No zsh has differences with bash., if you never write scripts, like just do things from command line, likely worth using zsh over bash because it has nice features and many utilities related to autocompletion support it. HOWEVER, if you write scripts, probably want to avoid learn 2 scripting languages stick with bash since it is nowadays ubiquitous, you don't want to to install zsh everywhere you go.

from Zsh FAQ: 2. 5: Similarities with bash The Bourne-Again Shell, bash, is another enhanced Bourne-like shell; obvious difference from zsh is it does not attempt to emulate Korn shell. Since both shells under active development probably not sensible to be too specific here. Broadly, bash has paid more attention to standards compliancy (i. e. POSIX) for longer, avoided more abstruse interactive features (programmable completion, etc. ) that zsh has. I've used them both, but prefer Bash now days because machines I work on default to bash consistently. standards-compliancy comment important to because means consistency between OSes. Zsh has nice autocompletion abilities, but kept finding cases where it didn't know what I wanted. several years ago, might have improved since then. found enabling "vi-mode" (set -o vi) in Bash makes it nicer command-line environment normally, I do that immediately in my. bashrc file. When writing shell scripts I don't ever program in either bash or zsh - I program using sh (/bin/sh), because it's lowest common denominator and least likely to have compatibility issues. old habit stood me well.

Zsh can run most Bourne, POSIX or ksh88 scripts if in right emulation mode (emulate sh or emulate ksh). It doesn't support all features of bash or ksh93. Zsh has most features of bash, but in many cases with different syntax. shell you use interactively is irrelevant for any script. shell that runs scripts is one indicated in first line, shebang line. For example, if script starts with #!/bin/bash, it executed by bash. If customized bash, you won't just rename your. bashrc to. zshrc. Some things can be shared, for example aliases and functions, stick to intersection between two shells (the intersection is close to ksh88 and pdksh). Other things, as prompt settings, completion functions and most options, will need to be completely rewritten. If writing snippet for people to source from. bashrc or. zshrc don't want to maintain two versions, stick to common subset of bash and zsh features, which includes most of bash's programming features. Put whole code in functions, put following line at top of each function: if [ -n "$ZSH_VERSION" ]; then emulate -L ksh; can use emulate sh instead of emulate ksh to be closer to plain sh syntax, need for. profile.
