Barcode = 123456; Product prod2 = new Product(); prod2. Barcode = 987654; System. out. println(prod1. Barcode); System. out. println(prod2. difference between class variables and instance variables, is a question of who knows what?. An instance variable is only known (= bound) to concrete instance - hence the name. public class Person { private String firstName; private String lastName; [. ] } definition of a class is like a blueprint for building concrete objects. Perhaps point confuses you. But writing it this way, every variable bound to its concrete object:. Every person has its own firstName A class variable is - as name says - known to each and every member of a class; or known/ bound at class level. typical example is a counter of how many objects, you created - problematic example; but doesn't matter at this early stage. public class Person { private String firstName; private String lastName; [. ] static int numberOfPersons = 0 } numberOfPersons is declared static is keyword to distingush between class variables and instance variabes. variable is declared like others within class definition. But static keyword signals, it is different. firstName, lastName are instance variables and bound to concrete instance numberOfPersons is bound to class, so every instance could access this variable. tl;dr place where variables are defined is the class definition. Class variables are known at/bound to class level,. each concrete instance has access to it. To define a class variable, use keyword static. Instance variables only known at instance level. define them without static keyword. Further documentation for Java is here

explained here (with example Bicycle class with class variable numberOfBicycles and instance variables cadence, speed, gear & id): Sometimes, want to have variables common to all objects. This accomplished with static modifier. Fields have static modifier in declaration are called static fields or class variables. associated with class, rather than with any object. Every instance of class shares class variable, in one fixed location in memory. Any object can change value of class variable, but class variables can be manipulated without creating instance of class. class variable (declared static) is a location common to all instances. In example, numberOfBicycles is a class variable (since declared static). only one such variable (i. location) common to all instances and to class. if modify numberOfBicycles in one method, other methods see new value (even for different Bicycle objects) In contrast gear & id are instance variables (because declaration has no static modifier). Every Bicycle object has its own one. If modify gear for some Bicycle a, if b is another instance, modifying a. gear has no effect on b. gear Each Java object is distinct memory zone with meta data (e. reference to its class) and its own instance variables (perhaps inherited from superclass). But class variables are common to class shared by all instances. See also Object (computer science) & Instance variable wikipages.

In ITU-T-X. 509-201210 explained in section 8. 5. 3. 1 (Reason code extension) as: – unspecified can be used to revoke certificates for reasons other than specific codes. – keyCompromise is used in revoking an end-entity certificate; it indicates known or suspected subject's private key, or other aspects of subject validated in certificate, have been compromised. – cACompromise used in revoking a CA-certificate; indicates known or suspected that subject's private key, or other aspects of subject validated in certificate, have been compromised. – affiliationChanged indicates the subject's name or other information in the certificate has been modified but no cause to suspect private key has been compromised. – superseded indicates certificate has been superseded but no cause to suspect private key has been compromised. – cessationOfOperation indicates certificate is no longer needed for purpose for it was issued but no cause to suspect private key been compromised. – privilegeWithdrawn indicates certificate (public-key or attribute certificate) was revoked because privilege contained within certificate has been withdrawn. – aACompromise indicates known or suspected that aspects of AA validated in the attribute certificate have been compromised. they also explain hold and remove; but hold just means "temporarily revoked" and "remove" is placed on delta-CRLs to say "uh, hold was cancelled". Per X. 509 subsequent "full" CRL won't list certificate any longer. noteworthy technically this extension is entirely optional. Both RFCs 3280 and 5280 say a conforming CA "SHOULD" provide reason code. X. 509 has little to say about when to use it, just what it means if it was used.

[Disclaimer: I work as software developer on software powers trusted public CAs, and many corporate internal PKIs] tl;dr to my knowledge, no formal guidelines for which revocation reason should be used in which situation, it's up to discretion of administrator or operator of each CA. Typically, cert revocations are done by humans to choose revocation reasons from drop-down menu in GUI. deciding which bucket certain edge-case falls into may vary from one organization / CA to another, or may be entirely up to discretion of IT guy revoking certificate for ID badge, email access, web server, wtv. In corporate Windows Active Directory CAs: found old article by Microsoft giving text description of each reason -- search for "Revocation Reasons" on page. (Microsoft built CA software as part of Active Directory suite, assume this is accompanying documentation intended for Windows Domain Admins). See Appendix A at bottom for full list. In public internet TLS PKI CA/Browser Forum (CAB Forum) dictates policy for how publicly-trusted CAs and browsers need to behave with respect to certificates. CA/Browser Forum Baseline Requirements for Issuance and Management of Publicly-Trusted Certificates, v. 1. 2. 5, April 2015. If go to section 13. 1. 5 Reasons for Revoking a Subscriber Certificate (see Appendix B below), list of situations in which CA required to revoke a certificate, but no mention of which reason code they supposed to use. tl;dr to my knowledge, no formal guidelines for which revocation reason should be used in which situation, it's up to discretion of administrator or operator of each CA. Appendix A: guidance from Microsoft on when to use each revocation reason: KeyCompromise. The token or disk location where private key associated with certificate has compromised and in possession of unauthorized individual.can include case where a laptop is stolen, or smart card lost. CACompromise. token or disk location where CA's private key is stored has compromised and in possession of unauthorized individual. When a CA's private key is revoked, this results in all certificates issued by CA signed using private key associated with revoked certificate being considered revoked. AffiliationChanged. user has terminated his or her relationship with organization indicated in Distinguished Name attribute of certificate. This revocation code typically used when individual is terminated or has resigned from organization. do not have to revoke a certificate when user changes departments, unless security policy requires different certificate be issued by departmental CA. Superseded. replacement certificate issued to user, reason does not fall under previous reasons. This revocation reason is typically used when smart card fails, password for token is forgotten by user, or user has changed legal name. CessationOfOperation. If a CA is decommissioned, no longer to be used, CA's certificate should be revoked with this reason code. Do not revoke CA's certificate if CA no longer issues new certificates, yet still publishes CRLs for currently issued certificates. CertificateHold. temporary revocation indicates CA will not vouch for a certificate at specific point in time. Once certificate is revoked with CertificateHold reason code, certificate can then be revoked with another Reason Code, or unrevoked and returned to use. Note: While CertificateHold allows certificate to be "unrevoked", it not recommended to place a hold on certificate, as it becomes difficult to determine if a certificate was valid for specific time. RemoveFromCRL. If certificate is revoked with CertificateHold reason code, it possible to "unrevoke" a certificate. unrevoking process still lists certificate in CRL, but with reason code set to RemoveFromCRL.Note: This specific to CertificateHold reason only used in DeltaCRLs. Unspecified. possible to revoke a certificate without providing specific reason code. possible to revoke certificate with Unspecified reason code, not recommended, as does not provide audit trail to why certificate is revoked. Appendix B: 13. 1. 5 Reasons for Revoking a Subscriber Certificate from CA/Browser Forum Baseline Requirements for Issuance and Management of Publicly-Trusted Certificates, v. 1. 2. 5, April 2015: CA/Browser Forum Baseline Requirements for Issuance and Management of Publicly-Trusted Certificates, v. 1. 2. 5, April 2015CA/Browser Forum Baseline Requirements for Issuance and Management of Publicly-Trusted Certificates, v. 1. 2. 5, April 2015: Subscriber requests in writing CA revoke Certificate; Subscriber notifies CA that original certificate request was not authorized and does not retroactively grant authorization; CA obtains evidence that Subscriber’s Private Key corresponding to Public Key in Certificate suffered a Key Compromise (also see Section 10. 2. 4) or no longer complies with requirements of Appendix A; CA obtains evidence Certificate was misused; CA made aware Subscriber has violated one or more of material obligations under Subscriber or Terms of Use Agreement; CA made aware of any circumstance indicating use of Fully-Qualified Domain Name or IP address in Certificate is no longer legally permitted (e. g.a court or arbitrator revoked a Domain Name Registrant’s right to use Domain Name, a relevant licensing or services agreement between Domain Name Registrant and Applicant has terminated, or Domain Name Registrant failed to renew Domain Name); CA made aware a Wildcard Certificate used to authenticate a fraudulently misleading subordinate Fully-Qualified Domain Name; CA made aware of a material change in information in the Certificate; CA made aware Certificate was not issued in accordance with these Requirements or the CA’s Certificate Policy or Certification Practice Statement; CA determines information in the Certificate is inaccurate or misleading; CA ceases operations for any reason and not made arrangements for another CA to provide revocation support for Certificate; CA’s right to issue Certificates under these Requirements expires or is revoked or terminated, unless CA made arrangements to continue maintaining the CRL/OCSP Repository; CA made aware of a possible compromise of Private Key of Subordinate CA used for issuing Certificate; Revocation required by CA’s Certificate Policy and/or Certification Practice Statement; or technical content or format of Certificate presents an unacceptable risk to Application Software Suppliers or Relying Parties (e. g. CA/Browser Forum might determine deprecated cryptographic/signature algorithm or key size presents unacceptable risk and such Certificates should be revoked and replaced by CAs within a given period of time).

What is crl why Should it be revoked From RFC 3280 A certificate revocation list (CRL) is time-stamped listidentifying revoked certificates signed by a CA or CRL issuerand made freely available in publicrepository. Each revoked certificate is identified in CRL by itscertificate serial number. When certificate-using system uses a certificate (e., for verifying remote user's digital signature), system not checks certificate signatureand validity acquires a suitably recent CRL checks certificate serial number is not on that CRL. From RFC 5280 meaning of "suitably recent" may vary with local policy, but it usuallymeans most recently issued CRLA new CRL is issued on regular periodic basis (e., hourly, daily, or weekly). entryis added to CRL as part of next update following notification of revocation. entry MUST NOT be removed from CRL until it appears on one regularly scheduled CRL issued beyondthe revoked certificate's validity period. advantage of revocation method is CRLs may be distributed by same means as certificates, via untrusted servers and untrusted communications. CRl's would revoke when private key of asymmetric encryption key pair (whose public key certified by CA) is stolen. In situation, anybody with private key could decrypt all communication between user and certified entity. CRLs issued periodically, certificates expired may be tagged as revoked, or may be issued as soon as certificate is revoked. To keep CRLs from being faked, they are signed by public key of CA and contain timestamp, after which CRLs expire. Reasons for revocation : According to ietf common reasons for revocation were : keyCompromise CACompromise affiliationChanged superseded cessationOfOperation certificateHold removeFromCRL privilegeWithdrawn AACompromise Reference 2 Reference 3

Both RFCs 3280 and 5280 say a conforming CA "SHOULD" provide reason code. X. 509 has little to say about when to use it, just what it means if it was used.

If go to section 13. 1. 5 Reasons for Revoking a Subscriber Certificate (see Appendix B below), list of situations in which CA required to revoke a certificate, but no mention of which reason code they supposed to use. tl;dr to my knowledge, no formal guidelines for which revocation reason should be used in which situation, it's up to discretion of administrator or operator of each CA. Appendix A: guidance from Microsoft on when to use each revocation reason: KeyCompromise. The token or disk location where private key associated with certificate has compromised and in possession of unauthorized individual.can include case where a laptop is stolen, or smart card lost. CACompromise. token or disk location where CA's private key is stored has compromised and in possession of unauthorized individual. When a CA's private key is revoked, this results in all certificates issued by CA signed using private key associated with revoked certificate being considered revoked. AffiliationChanged. user has terminated his or her relationship with organization indicated in Distinguished Name attribute of certificate. This revocation code typically used when individual is terminated or has resigned from organization. do not have to revoke a certificate when user changes departments, unless security policy requires different certificate be issued by departmental CA. Superseded. replacement certificate issued to user, reason does not fall under previous reasons. This revocation reason is typically used when smart card fails, password for token is forgotten by user, or user has changed legal name. CessationOfOperation. If a CA is decommissioned, no longer to be used, CA's certificate should be revoked with this reason code. Do not revoke CA's certificate if CA no longer issues new certificates, yet still publishes CRLs for currently issued certificates. CertificateHold. temporary revocation indicates CA will not vouch for a certificate at specific point in time. Once certificate is revoked with CertificateHold reason code, certificate can then be revoked with another Reason Code, or unrevoked and returned to use. Note: While CertificateHold allows certificate to be "unrevoked", it not recommended to place a hold on certificate, as it becomes difficult to determine if a certificate was valid for specific time. If certificate is revoked with CertificateHold reason code, it possible to "unrevoke" a certificate. unrevoking process still lists certificate in CRL, but with reason code set to RemoveFromCRL.Note: This specific to CertificateHold reason only used in DeltaCRLs. Unspecified. possible to revoke a certificate without providing specific reason code. possible to revoke certificate with Unspecified reason code, not recommended, as does not provide audit trail to why certificate is revoked. What is crl why Should it be revoked From RFC 3280 A certificate revocation list (CRL) is time-stamped listidentifying revoked certificates signed by a CA or CRL issuerand made freely available in publicrepository. Each revoked certificate is identified in CRL by itscertificate serial number. When certificate-using system uses a certificate (e., for verifying remote user's digital signature), system not checks certificate signatureand validity acquires a suitably recent CRL checks certificate serial number is not on that CRL. From RFC 5280 meaning of "suitably recent" may vary with local policy, but it usuallymeans most recently issued CRLA new CRL is issued on regular periodic basis (e., hourly, daily, or weekly). entryis added to CRL as part of next update following notification of revocation. entry MUST NOT be removed from CRL until it appears on one regularly scheduled CRL issued beyondthe revoked certificate's validity period. advantage of revocation method is CRLs may be distributed by same means as certificates, via untrusted servers and untrusted communications. CRl's would revoke when private key of asymmetric encryption key pair (whose public key certified by CA) is stolen. In situation, anybody with private key could decrypt all communication between user and certified entity. CRLs issued periodically, certificates expired may be tagged as revoked, or may be issued as soon as certificate is revoked. To keep CRLs from being faked, they are signed by public key of CA and contain timestamp, after which CRLs expire. Two separate VLANs must communicate through a layer-3 device, like a router. Devices on a VLAN communicate with each other using layer-2. Layer-3 must used to communicate between separate layer-2 domains. Assuming most common communications (layer-2 is ethernet and layer-3 is IP), when a host on a VLAN wants to communicate with another host on same VLAN, it discovers other hosts layer-2 (e. g. MAC) address with like ARP, sends frame to MAC address. When a host on one VLAN wants to send something to host on another VLAN, it must use a layer-3 (e. g. IP) address. host use layer-2 to send frames to its defined gateway (router). router will strip off layer-2 frame inspect layer-3 packet for destination layer-3 address. router will then look up next hop for layer-3 address. create a new layer-2 frame for layer-3 packet based on layer-2 LAN on interface where it needs to send packet for next hop. Other routers in path to end LAN repeat this process until frame is placed on final VLAN, where receiving host gets the frame. In many implementations IPv4 subnet and a VLAN closely correlated on 1:1 basis. A subnet, is a portion of IPv4 address space from may assign addresses to hosts. differentiated from a "prefix" a term in common parlance or a supernet, may be a larger portion of IP address space comprised of many subnets. reason for correlation is a single VLAN and single subnet both represent a single broadcast domain., these two tend to be overlaid in most implementations. described in earlier answers, a VLAN is a layer 2 entity. All hosts on given VLAN can communicate with each other, but no hosts on one VLAN can communicate to hosts on another without form routing or in rare cases, bridging.

A VLAN is Ethernet level concept, a subnet is IP level concept. VLAN splits Ethernet network into multiple logically seperate Ethernet networks. subnet defines which hosts host will try to communicate with directly verses which hosts need to go via a router. It also defines "network" and "broadcast" addresses. common practice to have 1:1 mapping between subnets and VLANs but possible to have multiple subnets on same VLAN. possible to use proxy arp to split a subnet between multiple VLANs or have two VLANs using same IP subnet for different purposes.

These need to be in same L2 domain but not in same IP subnet, since IP is not required. In case may be practical to use VLANS without considering IP/Subnetting of.

Subnets (L3) and VLANs (L2) on different layers. terms not used interchangeably. A VLAN can contain one or more L3 prefixes ("Subnets"). For layman this could cause confusion. Often people don't understand these two connected but not same. People might say host located in our server subnet or server located in DMZ VLAN mean same thing.

informal way of looking at difference between VLANs and subnets, but not inaccurate (just incomplete). may help networking newcomers get closer to right mental picture. Two different VLANs on a single switch or host are like two physically separate switches. They partition MAC address space, in communications between two parties on single VLAN or on single physical switch don't involve other parties on MAC-level (layer 2) network. VLAN or physical switch limits extent MAC-level message propagation, keeping it as local as possible. In contrast, IP subnets exist at layer 3 and partition IP address space, not MAC address space, but with similar purpose: to limit extent of message propagation. Any partitioning at MAC-level layer 2 network below is transparent to layer 3, VLANs and/or separate physical switches can be treated as one single continuous layer 2 medium from point of IP-level networking. Conversely, switches and VLANs don't see IP addresses nor IP subnetting (with some minor provisos can complicate picture). Everything at layer 3 and higher is just payload to them at layer 2 MAC level. In summary: VLANs and subnets partition different layers of network model. no circumstance in they interchangeable terms.

Switches don't exchange MAC address information through VTP or other protocol. only way a switch can learn destination port and VLAN of MAC address is by recording source MAC address and VLAN of inbound frames. For VLAN trunks, tagging required to show which VLAN frame and source MAC address belong to. VTP's purpose automate creation of VLANs on a switch. With VTP, once VLAN created on VTP server, clients (and other servers) have VLAN created in databases, with same VLAN ID and name as VTP server. VTP doesn't contain port VLAN information or MAC address tables.

often confused point for people new to Networking, in particular to people up Cisco track, due to Cisco's over emphasis on this point. It more just a terminology thing. explain. 802. 1q standard defines method of tagging traffic between two switches to distinguish which traffic belongs to which VLANs. In Cisco terms, this is what happens on a "trunk" port. other vendors refer to this as a "tagged" port. In context, it means same: adding identifier to frames to indicate what VLAN frame belongs to. Terminology aside, main thing to in is VLAN tag is necessary, because often traffic traversing two switches belongs to multiple VLANs, must be way to determine which 1's and 0's belong to which VLAN. But what happens if a trunk port, expecting to receive traffic includes VLAN tag, receives traffic with no tag? In predecessor to 802. 1q, known as ISL (cisco proprietary, but archaic, no one supports it anymore, not even Cisco), untagged traffic on trunk would simply be dropped. 802. 1q however, provided for a way to not only receive this traffic, but also associate it to a VLAN of your choosing. This method is known as setting a Native VLAN., configure your trunk port with Native VLAN, whatever traffic arrives on port without existing VLAN tag, gets associated to your Native VLAN. As with all configuration items, if do not explicitly configure, usually default behavior exists. In case of Cisco (and most vendors), Default Native VLAN is VLAN 1. to, if not set Native VLAN explicitly, any untagged traffic received on trunk port is automatically placed in VLAN 1. trunk port is "opposite" from an Access Port. access port sends and expects to receive traffic with no VLAN tag.this work, an access port only sends and expects to receive traffic belonging to one VLAN. access port is statically configured for a particular VLAN, any traffic received on that port is internally associated on Switch as belonging to a particular VLAN (despite not tagging traffic for that VLAN when it leaves switch port)., to add to confusing mix. Cisco books refer to "default VLAN". The Default VLAN is the VLAN all Access Ports are assigned to until explicitly placed in another VLAN. In of Cisco switches (and most other Vendors, Default VLAN is usually VLAN 1. Typically, this VLAN is only relevant on an Access port, a port that sends and expects to receive traffic without a VLAN tag (also referred to an 'untagged port' by other vendors)., to summarize: Native VLAN can change. can set it to anything you like. Access Port VLAN can change. can set it to anything you like. Default Native VLAN is always 1, can not be change, because its set that way by Cisco Default VLAN is always 1, can not be changed, because it set that way by Cisco forgot other questions, can it / should it be changed? This is largely an opinion question. to agree with this school of thought: All unused ports should be in a specific VLAN. All active ports should be explicitly set on to a particular VLAN. Your switch should prevent traffic from traversing uplink into rest of network if traffic belongs on VLAN1, or VLAN you using for unused ports. Everything else should be allowed up the uplink. many different theories behind this. differing requirements would prevent restricted switch policy (scale, resources, etc).For instance, if a switch going into part of a network only one VLAN not VLAN 1, is possible to make "default" / native VLAN on all ports a particular VLAN using one global command, or preferred method to make all ports access ports and set access VLAN to 10 on each? You can not change default Cisco configurations. can use "interface range" to put all ports in different VLAN in one go. don't need to change Native VLAN on uplink trunk, so long as other switch is using same Native VLAN. If want to spare the switch from adding VLAN Tag, you could get creative do following (although, probably not recommended). Leave all access ports in the VLAN1. Leave Native VLAN at its default (VLAN1). On uplink switch, set the port as a trunk port. set its Native VLAN to the VLAN you want lower switch to be a part of. Since lower switch will send traffic to upper switch untagged, upper switch will receive it and associate it with it considers Native VLAN.

echo and printf are built-in commands (printf Bash built-in since v2. 0. 2, 1998). echo exits with 0 status, prints arguments followed by end of line character on standard output, printf allows for definition of formatting string and gives non-zero exit status code upon failure. printf has more control over output format. It can be used to specify field width for item, various formatting choices for numbers (such output base use, to print an exponent, print sign, how many digits to print after decimal point). This done by supplying format string, controls how and where to print other arguments same syntax as C language (%03d, %e, %+d,. ). means must escape percent symbol when not talking about format (%%)., if add newline character that echo uses by default (except using -n option) you'll get same effect. printf "blah
" >/dev/udp/localhost/8125 Concerning performance, echo was faster than printf because later has to read string and format it. testing them with time (also built-in) results say otherwise: $ time for i in {1. 999999}; do echo "$i" >/dev/null; done real 0m10. 191s user 0m4. 940s sys 0m1. 710s $ time for i in {1. 999999}; do printf "$i" >/dev/null; done real 0m9. 073s user 0m4. 690s sys 0m1. 310s Telling printf to add newline characters, just as echo does by default: $ time for i in {1. 999999}; do printf "$i
" >/dev/null; done real 0m8. 940s user 0m4. 230s sys 0m1.460s obviously slower than without printing 
, but yet faster than echo.
difference is echo sends a newline at the end of its output. no way to "send" an EOF.

echo prints its argument followed by newline. With multiple arguments, separated by spaces. Depending on unix variant, shell and shell options, it may also interpret some escape sequences beginning with \, and may treat first argument(s) as options if start with -. printf interprets first argument as format, subsequent arguments as arguments to % specifiers. No newline added unless you specify one. In first argument, all characters except two interpreted literally: % starts printf specifier, and \ starts escape sequence (e. g. \n for newline character). different shells work differently, echo "$string" does not always print specified string plus newline. reliable way of printing string is printf %s "$string". If want newline after string, write printf '%s\n' "$string". In your case, assuming blah doesn't start with a - or contain % or \, only difference between two commands is echo adds newline and printf doesn't.

For trivial messages (no escape sequences, no options), echo is fine. soon need something more complex, shoud use printf is portable (i. e. behave same regardless of OS) allows better formatting, designed from same name C function. want to call echo in your example, correct way would be either: echo -n "blah" >/dev/udp/localhost/8125 or echo "blah\c" >/dev/udp/localhost/8125 depending on echo implementation you use.

Many bugs been fixed since.

Echo is a binary program (/bin/echo) builtin command in some shells bash and sh. As man echo states, Some shells may provide builtin echo command similar or iden- tical to this utility. notably, builtin echo in sh(1) does not accept -n option. Consult builtin(1) manual page. to fix this, you can change your script to use bash by setting first line to #!/bin/bash Or change invocation of echo to /bin/echo -n "$b "

described in Application Usage section of POSIX description of echo command, -n option and escape sequences not portable (due to different support in various branches of Unix family tree). printf command (which, like echo, also builtin to most shells, available as external command) is more reliably standardized (though syntax not the same; e. g. need to watch for % in first argument, multiple arguments not automatically joined with space): printf 'Some text \e[0;32m in color \e[0m no more color\n' printf '%s\e[0;32m%s\e[0m %s\n' 'Some text' 'in color' 'no more color'
echo not portable as you experienced. suggest use POSIX alternative printf: printf "$b " Note in general case, if you don't know in advance what contains $b, should use instead: printf "%s " "$b"
